Just as the Buddha spoke of the praise [of the Dhamma] with nine terms through the word "viññūhi" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.28), so too He spoke of the praise of this Ekayana Magga with seven terms starting with "sattānaṃ visuddhiyā."

Why did He speak in this way? It was to generate enthusiasm (ussāha) in those monks. For upon hearing the praise, those monks will think: "This path dispels the four misfortunes—sorrow (soka) which is the burning of the heart, lamentation (parideva) which is verbal wailing, pain (dukkha) which is bodily unpleasantness, and grief (domanassa) which is mental unpleasantness; it brings about the three special benefits—purification (visuddhi), the Noble Path (ñāya), and Nibbāna." Thus, becoming enthusiastic, they will learn, study, memorize, and recite this Dhamma teaching, and they will consider that this path should be developed. Thus, He spoke the praise to generate enthusiasm in those monks, just as a blanket merchant speaks of the praise of blankets and such.

For example, even when a merchant of a pale-red blanket (paṇḍukambala) worth a hundred thousand [pieces of money] proclaims, "Buy this blanket!", people do not yet know what kind of blanket it is. This is because blankets made of human hair or animal hair, which are foul-smelling and rough to the touch, are also called "blankets." But when he proclaims, "This is a red blanket from Gandhara, fine, bright, and pleasant to the touch," then those who can afford it buy it. Those who cannot afford it also desire to see it. In the same way, even when it is said, "Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path (ekāyano maggo)," it is not yet clear what kind of path it is. This is because various paths that do not lead out [of saṃsāra] are also called "paths." But when it is said, "For the purification of beings," etc., they become enthusiastic, thinking, "This path dispels the four misfortunes and brings the three special benefits," and they will learn, study, memorize, and recite this Dhamma teaching, and consider that this path should be developed. Intending this, He spoke the praise, saying "sattānaṃ visuddhiyā" and so on. Just as with the simile of the merchant of the pale-red blanket worth a hundred thousand, so too the similes of merchants of red Jambūnada gold, water-clearing gem-jewels, very pure pearl-jewels, washed coral-jewels, etc., should be brought in here.

"Yadidaṃ" is a particle, meaning "which is this." "Cattāro" (four) is a numerical limitation; by this, He shows the limit of the foundations of mindfulness, neither less nor more than that. "Satipaṭṭhānā" refers to the three foundations of mindfulness (the objects of mindfulness), as well as the state of the Teacher being beyond resentment and attraction (paṭighānunayavītivattatā) towards disciples who practice in three ways, and also mindfulness itself.
243:
"Bhikkhus, I will teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen to that... Bhikkhus, what is the arising of the body (kāya)? With the arising of nutriment (āhāra) comes the arising of the body." In such passages from the Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 3.408), the object of mindfulness is called "satipaṭṭhāna." Likewise, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭis. M. 3.35), it is said: "The body is the foundation (paṭṭhāna), not mindfulness. Mindfulness is both the foundation and mindfulness."

Its meaning is: because mindfulness stands in this object, it is called "paṭṭhāna" (foundation). What stands? Mindfulness stands. Because it is the foundation of mindfulness, it is "satipaṭṭhāna" (satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ). Alternatively, it is "paṭṭhāna" because it is a principal place. Like an elephant-stable (hatthiṭṭhāna) or a horse-stable (assaṭṭhāna), because it is the place of mindfulness, it is called "satipaṭṭhāna."

"There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One (the Buddha) frequents, frequenting which the Teacher is worthy to instruct a group of disciples." In this passage from the Majjhima Nikāya (MN 3.311), the state of the Teacher being free from resentment and attraction towards disciples who practice in three ways is called "satipaṭṭhāna." Its meaning is: it is "paṭṭhāna" because it is to be established (paṭṭhapetabbato) or to be set in motion. By what is it established? It is established by mindfulness. Because it is established by mindfulness, it is "satipaṭṭhāna."

"The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment." In such passages from the Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 5.989), mindfulness itself is called "satipaṭṭhāna." Its meaning is: it is "paṭṭhāna" because it stands (patiṭṭhāti), meaning it appears (upaṭṭhāti) by entering into and leaping into [the object]. Mindfulness itself is the foundation, thus "satipaṭṭhāna." Or else, it is "sati" in the sense of remembering (saraṇa) and "paṭṭhāna" in the sense of appearing (upaṭṭhāna). Thus, because it is both mindfulness and the foundation, it is "satipaṭṭhāna." This is the meaning intended here [in this Sutta].

If that is so, why is the plural "satipaṭṭhānā" used? Because mindfulness is manifold. Due to the diversity of objects, these mindfulnesses are many. But why is the singular "maggo" (path) used? Because it is one in the sense of being a path. For all these four mindfulnesses become one in the sense of being a path.

It has been said: "In what sense is a path called a path? In the sense of going to Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought (maggannīya) by those who desire Nibbāna." These four mindfulnesses also, in the subsequent stage, accomplish their task regarding the objects such as the body and go to Nibbāna. And from the beginning, they are sought by those who desire Nibbāna. Therefore, all four are called a single path (eko maggo).

By using [the terms] in this way, the teaching becomes one with a proper connection of words. It is like the teaching (SN 5.224): "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the path that crushes Mara's army. Listen to that... And what, bhikkhus, is the path that crushes Mara's army? It is these seven factors of enlightenment." Just as in that case, "the path that crushes Mara's army" and "the seven factors of enlightenment" are the same in meaning, and only the phrasing (byañjana) is different; so too here, "ekāyano maggo" and "cattāro satipaṭṭhānā" are...
244:
Although it is one in meaning, only the phrasing (expression) is different here. Therefore, it should be understood that the singular form (maggo) is used because of the oneness in the sense of the path, and the plural form (satipaṭṭhānā) is used because of the multiplicity of mindfulness by way of the variety of objects.

Why did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither more nor less? It is for the benefit of those to be led (veneyya). Among those with a craving temperament (taṇhācarita), those with a wrong-view temperament (diṭṭhicarita), those who follow the vehicle of serenity (samathayānika), and those who follow the vehicle of insight (vipassanāyānika), there are two types each: those with dull faculties (manda) and those with sharp faculties (tikkha). For a person of dull faculties with a craving temperament, the coarse contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) is the path of purification. For a person of sharp faculties with a craving temperament, the subtle contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā) is the path of purification. For a person of dull faculties with a wrong-view temperament, the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā), which is not very diversified, is the path of purification. For a person of sharp faculties with a wrong-view temperament, the highly diversified contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) is the path of purification. For a person of dull faculties following the vehicle of serenity, the first foundation of mindfulness, which has a sign to be attained without difficulty, is the path of purification. For a person of sharp faculties, the second foundation of mindfulness is the path, because they do not settle on coarse objects. For a person of dull faculties following the vehicle of insight, the third foundation of mindfulness, which has an object that is not very diversified, is the path of purification. For a person of sharp faculties, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, which has a highly diversified object, is the path of purification. Thus, exactly four are taught, neither more nor less.

Alternatively, they are taught to abandon the four perversions (vipallāsa): the notions of beauty (subha), happiness (sukha), permanence (nicca), and self (atta). Although the body (kāya) is foul (asubha), beings have the perverted view that it is beautiful. To abandon that perversion by showing them the foul nature of the body, the first foundation of mindfulness was taught. Although they hold feelings and so forth to be happy, permanent, and self, feelings are suffering (dukkha), the mind is impermanent (anicca), and phenomena (dhamma) are non-self (anatta). To abandon those perversions by showing beings who have the perverted views of happiness, permanence, and self the nature of suffering and so forth, the remaining three foundations of mindfulness were taught. Thus, it should be understood that exactly four are taught, neither more nor less, to abandon the four perversions.

It should be understood that they are taught as four not only to abandon the perversions but also to abandon the four floods (ogha), the four bonds (yoga), the four taints (āsava), the four ties (gantha), the four clingings (upādāna), the four wrong courses (agati), and for the full understanding of the four nutriments (āhāra). This is the method of the exposition (pakaraṇanaya).

In the Commentary, however, it is said that the foundation of mindfulness is only one by way of its meaning as mindfulness and by way of its convergence into a single state, but it is four by way of its objects. For example, in a city with four gates, people coming from the east take goods produced in the eastern direction and enter the city through the eastern gate. Those coming from the south, west, and north take goods produced in the northern direction and enter the city through the northern gate. This should be understood in the same way. Like the city...
245:
Nibbāna is like the great city. The supramundane Eightfold Path is like the gate. The body and so forth are like the eastern direction and so forth.

Just as people coming from the east take goods produced in the east and enter the city through the eastern gate, similarly, those who come through the door of contemplation of the body, having developed the contemplation of the body in its fourteen ways, enter the single Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path arisen through the power of the development of the contemplation of the body.

Just as people coming from the south take goods produced in the south and enter the city through the southern gate, similarly, those who come through the door of contemplation of feeling, having developed the contemplation of feeling in its nine ways, enter the single Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path arisen through the power of the development of the contemplation of feeling.

Just as people coming from the west take goods produced in the west and enter the city through the western gate, similarly, those who come through the door of contemplation of the mind, having developed the contemplation of the mind in its sixteen ways, enter the single Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path arisen through the power of the development of the contemplation of the mind.

Just as people coming from the north take goods produced in the north and enter the city through the northern gate, similarly, those who come through the door of contemplation of phenomena, having developed the contemplation of phenomena in its five ways, enter the single Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path arisen through the power of the development of the contemplation of phenomena.

Thus, it should be understood that the single foundation of mindfulness is taught as four by way of its objects, both by way of its nature as a group and by way of its convergence into the single Nibbāna.

The phrase "Which four?" is a question asked with the desire to explain. "In this" means in this Dispensation (sāsana) of the Buddha. "Monks" is an address to the persons receiving the Dhamma. "A monk" is an illustration of a person who fulfills the practice. Although other deities and humans also fulfill the practice, it is said "a monk" because of the excellence of the practice and to show the state of a monk. Among those who receive the Blessed One's instruction, a monk is the best because he is a suitable vessel for all kinds of instruction; therefore, he is called "a monk" due to his excellence. When he is mentioned, the rest of the assembly is also included, just as when a king's departure is mentioned, his retinue is also included. Whoever undertakes this practice is called a monk.
246:
He is called a 'bhikkhu' because he demonstrates the state of a monk through his practice. Indeed, whether a deva or a human, one who follows the practice is known as a 'bhikkhu'. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Even if he is adorned, if he lives in peace, is calm, restrained, established in the Path, leading a holy life, and has laid aside the rod towards all beings—he is a Brahmin, he is a recluse (samaṇa), he is a monk (bhikkhu).' (Dhp. 142)

'Kāye' refers to the material body (rūpakāya). In this context, the material body is intended as 'kāya' in the sense of a collection (samūha) of major and minor limbs and things such as hair, etc., just like an elephant-corps or a chariot-corps. Just as it is called 'kāya' in the sense of a collection, it is also called 'kāya' because it is the place of origin (āya) of loathsome things (kucchita). 'Āya' means the place of arising. Here, the word-definition is: it is called 'āya' because they arise from that place. What arises? Loathsome things such as hair and so forth. Thus, it is called 'kāya' because it is the place of origin of loathsome things. 'Kāyānupassī' means one who has the habit of contemplating the body repeatedly, or one who is contemplating the body.

It should be understood that although 'kāye' has been said, the inclusion of the word 'kāya' for a second time in 'kāyānupassī' is intended to show the determination [of the object] without mixing it with other things, and to show the breaking down of the perception of compactness (ghana-vinibbhoga). By saying so, it is shown that one is not contemplating feelings (vedanā) in the body, nor contemplating the mind (citta) or mental objects (dhamma), but rather contemplating only the body in the object known as the body, thereby showing the determination without mixing. Likewise, one does not contemplate a single dhamma apart from the major and minor limbs in the body, nor does one contemplate a woman or a man apart from the hair, body hair, and so forth. Even in this body, which is called a collection of primary elements and derived matter such as hair, body hair, etc., one does not contemplate a single dhamma apart from the primary elements and derived matter. Rather, one is only a contemplator of the collection of major and minor limbs, like one contemplating the parts of a chariot; one is only a contemplator of the collection of hair, body hair, etc., like one contemplating the parts of a city; and one is only a contemplator of the collection of primary elements and derived matter, like one peeling the layers of a banana trunk or like one opening an empty fist. Thus, by showing the object known as the body through various parts and by way of a collection, the breaking down of the perception of compactness (ghana-vinibbhoga) is demonstrated. In this body, there is no body, no woman, no man, nor any other dhamma apart from the aforementioned collection.
247:
In reality, it is only in the aforementioned collection of dhammas that beings wrongly perceive [a self] in various ways. Therefore, the ancient teachers (porāṇā) said:

'What one sees (with wrong view), that is not the seen (the actual visible object); what is the seen, that one does not see (with wisdom). Not seeing (the truth), the fool is bound; being bound, he is not liberated (from saṃsāra).'

It was said that this is for the purpose of showing the breaking down of the perception of compactness and so forth. By the word 'ādi' (and so forth), this meaning should also be understood: this person contemplates only the body in this single body, not contemplating other dhammas. What is meant? Just as people contemplate water in a mirage that is not actually water, it is not like that here; rather, in this body which is indeed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul, one does not contemplate it as permanent, pleasant, self, and beautiful. Instead, being a contemplator of the body (kāyānupassī), one only contemplates the collection of aspects of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.

Alternatively, it refers to the body from the out-breath and in-breath down to the skeleton, as taught later in the passage: 'Here, monks, a monk having gone to the forest... he, mindful, breathes out,' and so forth. Also, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is said: 'Here, someone contemplates the earth-body (pathavīkāya) as impermanent; he contemplates the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, the hair-body, the body-hair-body, the outer-skin-body, the inner-skin-body, the flesh-body, the blood-body, the tendon-body, the bone-body, and the marrow-body as impermanent.' Because one contemplates all those collections in this very body, the meaning should be understood as 'kāye kāyānupassī'.

In another way, because one does not contemplate anything in the body as 'I' or 'mine', but contemplates only that specific collection of various dhammas such as hair, body hair, etc., the meaning should be understood as 'one who contemplates the body known as the collection of dhammas such as hair, etc., in the body'. Furthermore, because one contemplates the body known as the collection of aspects such as the characteristic of impermanence, according to the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'In this body, he contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent,' and so forth, the meaning should also be understood as 'kāye kāyānupassī'.

This is indeed true. A monk who has entered upon the practice of contemplation of the body in this body contemplates this body as impermanent, not as permanent, by virtue of the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). He contemplates it as suffering, not as pleasant.
248: One contemplates as non-self, not as self. One becomes weary, not delighted. One becomes dispassionate, not passionate. One causes cessation, not arising. One relinquishes, does not grasp. It should be understood that as that person repeatedly contemplates that material body as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā); as he repeatedly contemplates it as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā); as he repeatedly contemplates it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self (atta-saññā); as he becomes weary, he abandons delight (nandī); as he becomes dispassionate, he abandons lust (rāga); as he causes cessation, he abandons the cause of arising (samudaya); and as he relinquishes, he abandons grasping (ādāna).## 'Viharati' means dwelling (through the four postures). 'Ātāpī' means 'ātāpa' because it burns away the defilements in the three realms of existence; this is a name for energy (vīriya). Because he possesses that ardent energy, he is called 'ātāpī'. 'Sampajāno' means being endowed with the wisdom known as clear comprehension (sampajañña). 'Satimā' means being endowed with mindfulness (sati) that grasps the body. This person, having grasped the object with mindfulness, contemplates it repeatedly with wisdom. Indeed, for one devoid of mindfulness, there is no such thing as contemplation (anupassanā). For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Monks, I say that mindfulness is useful in all circumstances." Therefore, by saying here, "he dwells contemplating the body in the body," the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna) is already stated. Alternatively, for one who lacks ardent energy, internal indolence becomes an obstacle; one who lacks clear comprehension becomes confused in grasping the right means and avoiding the wrong means; and one who is forgetful is unable to relinquish the wrong means and grasp the right means. If that is the case, the meditation subject cannot be accomplished for him. Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "ātāpī sampajāno satimā" is spoken to show those qualities by whose power that meditation subject can be accomplished.## Having thus shown the mindfulness of the body and its associated factors (sampayogaṅga), the phrase "removing covetousness and grief in the world" is now spoken to show the factors to be abandoned (pahaṇaṅga). In that phrase, 'vineyya' means having removed either by the removal of a factor (tadaṅga-vinaya) or by removal through suppression (vikkhambhana-vinaya). 'Loke' (in the world) means in that very body. Here, the body is intended as 'the world' (loka) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating. However, since covetousness and grief are abandoned for him not only regarding the body but also regarding feelings and so forth, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga that "the five aggregates of clinging are the world." Or, because those states are called the world, this is stated by the method of extracting the meaning. That which was said, "Therein, what is the world? That very body is the world," has this same meaning. It should be seen as connected thus: "removing covetousness and grief in that world." Since by taking covetousness here...
249: By taking covetousness (abhijjhā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is included; by taking grief (domanassa), ill-will (byāpāda) is included. Therefore, it should be understood that by showing these two powerful states included among the hindrances, the abandonment of all hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is meant.## Specifically here, by the removal of covetousness, the abandonment of attraction (anurodha) based on the perfection of the body is stated; by the removal of grief, the abandonment of aversion (virodha) based on the failure of the body is stated. Furthermore, by the removal of covetousness, the abandonment of delight in the body is stated; by the removal of grief, the abandonment of lack of delight in the development of the body (kāya-bhāvanā) is stated. By the removal of covetousness, the abandonment of the false attribution of beauty, pleasure, etc., to the body is stated; and by the removal of grief, the abandonment of the removal of the actual qualities of foulness, suffering, etc., from the body is stated. By stating such abandonment, the power and capability of the practitioner (yogāvacara) in meditation are demonstrated. Indeed, this is the power of meditation: that one becomes free from attraction and aversion, able to endure both delight and lack of delight, and free from attributing what is false and removing what is true. That person who is free from attraction and aversion, who can endure delight and lack of delight, who does not attribute what is false and does not remove what is true, is one capable of practicing meditation.## In another way, in the phrase "kāye kāyānupassī," the meditation subject is stated by 'contemplation' (anupassanā). In the word "viharati," the maintenance of the body of the practitioner through the stated mode of dwelling is mentioned. In the words beginning with "ātāpī": by 'ardour' (ātāpa), right effort (samma-ppadhāna) is meant; by 'mindfulness and clear comprehension', the meditation subject useful in all circumstances (sabbatthika-kammaṭṭhāna) or the means of maintaining the meditation subject is meant; or, by 'mindfulness', the tranquillity (samatha) obtained through the power of contemplating the body is meant; by 'clear comprehension', insight (vipassanā) is meant; and by 'removing covetousness and grief', the fruit of development (bhāvanā-phala) is meant. Thus it should be understood.## In the Vibhaṅga, regarding the term "anupassī": therein, what is contemplation? It is the wisdom, the act of understanding... right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). This is called contemplation. One is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, furnished with, provided with, and accompanied by this contemplation. Therefore, one is called 'anupassī'.## "Viharati" means one proceeds, occurs, protects, sustains, maintains, practices, and dwells. Therefore, it is called 'viharati'.## In the term "ātāpī": therein, what is ardour (ātāpa)? It is the mental inception of energy... right effort (sammā-vāyāma). This is called ardour. One is endowed with... accompanied by this ardour. Therefore, one is called 'ātāpī'.
250:
In the word "sampajāno," what is clear comprehension (sampajañña)? It is the wisdom that clearly knows, the act of clearly knowing... (extensively)... it is right view (sammādiṭṭhi). This is called clear comprehension. One is endowed with this clear comprehension... (extensively)... is fully possessed of it. Therefore, one is called "sampajāno."

In the word "satimā," what is mindfulness (sati)? It is the mindfulness that remembers things done or spoken long ago, the repeated recollection (anussati)... (extensively)... it is right mindfulness (sammāsati). This is called mindfulness. One is endowed with this mindfulness... (extensively)... is fully possessed of it. Therefore, one is called "satimā."

In the phrase "having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world," what is the "world" (loka)? One's own body (rūpakāya), which is the object of that mindfulness, is itself called the world; the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) are also called the world. This is called the world. Among those three—the world, covetousness, and displeasure—what is covetousness (abhijjhā)? It is the lust (rāga) that attaches to an object, the intense infatuation (sārāga), the repeated fawning (anunaya), the compliance (anurodha), the delight (nandī), the delight and lust (nandīrāga), the intense infatuation of the mind. This is called covetousness. Therein, what is displeasure (domanassa)? It is the mental unpleasantness (asāta), the mental pain (dukkha) that is difficult to endure, the unpleasantness born of mental contact... (extensively)... it is painful feeling (dukkhā vedanā). This is called displeasure. Thus, both this covetousness and this displeasure are removed, abandoned, calmed, specifically calmed, brought to an end, specifically brought to an end, extinguished, thoroughly extinguished, destroyed, specifically destroyed, dried up, specifically dried up, and made non-existent in this world. Therefore, it is said, "having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world" (Vibhaṅga 356). Thus, the meaning of these words has been stated. This method of the Commentary should be understood as it accords with that Vibhaṅga Pali.

This is the explanation of the meaning of the brief summary (uddesa) of the contemplation of the body in the foundations of mindfulness.

In the words "contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, he dwells... (extensively)... having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world," the purpose of repeating "feelings" and so on in the words "contemplating feelings" etc., should be understood in the same way as explained in the contemplation of the body. In the phrase "contemplating feelings in feelings, mind in mind, phenomena in phenomena," "feelings" refers to the three types of feelings, and these are only mundane (lokiya) feelings. The mind is also only mundane, and likewise the phenomena. Their classification will become clear in the exposition (niddesavāra). However, in this Dispensation, how feelings should be contemplated—one who contemplates them in that way is to be understood as "one who contemplates feelings in feelings." This method is the same for the mind and phenomena. How should feelings be contemplated? Firstly, pleasant feeling (sukha vedanā) should be contemplated as suffering (dukkha), painful feeling (dukkha vedanā) as a dart (salla), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha vedanā) as impermanent (anicca). As the Blessed One said:
251:
"He who sees pleasure as pain, and sees pain as a dart, and sees the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent—that bhikkhu, seeing rightly, will wander truly at peace." (SN 4.253).

All these feelings should also be contemplated simply as "suffering." For has it not been said: "Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering"? (SN 4.259). They should also be contemplated in terms of pleasure and pain. As it is said: "Pleasant feeling is pleasant when it persists and painful when it changes" (MN 1.464). All this should be expanded upon. Furthermore, they should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence. The remaining meanings will become clear in the exposition (niddesavāra).

Regarding mind and phenomena: the mind should be contemplated by way of its various aspects such as object (ārammaṇa), predominance (adhipati), conascence (sahajāta), plane (bhūmi), kamma, resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya); by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence; and by way of the divisions such as "with lust" (sarāga) mentioned in the Niddesavāra. Phenomena (dhamma) should be contemplated by way of their individual characteristics (salakkhaṇa), general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), as void phenomena (suññatadhamma), by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence, and by way of the divisions such as "present" (santa) and "not present" (asanta) mentioned in the Niddesavāra. The remaining terms are as previously explained. Indeed, in this Dispensation, for one who has abandoned covetousness and displeasure in the "world" called the body, they are also abandoned in the "worlds" of feelings and so on. However, it is taught in all [four] categories for the sake of different individuals and by way of the development of mindfulness in various distinct moments of consciousness. Or, when abandoned in one place, they are abandoned in the rest as well. Therefore, it should be understood that this is stated to show the abandonment in those [feelings, etc.] as well.

## The Explanation of the Brief Summary (Uddesavāra) is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing in the Contemplation of the Body

Now, for example, just as a skilled bamboo worker, wishing to make various utensils such as large mats, fine mats, baskets, boxes, and cases, would take a large bamboo, split it into four parts, and then take each part to split further to make those respective utensils; in the same way, the Blessed One, wishing to enable beings to attain many kinds of special distinctions through the teaching of the foundations of mindfulness, divided the single right mindfulness into four by way of the objects, saying: "There are four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body..." and then, taking each foundation of mindfulness and analyzing it, he began to speak the exposition (niddesavāra) in the manner starting with: "And how, bhikkhus, [is a bhikkhu a contemplator of the body in the body]?"
252:
In this section of the exposition, the term "How (kathañca)" and so forth is a question asked with the intention of providing a detailed explanation. The summary of the meaning here is: Monks, in what manner does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? This method applies to all sections where questions are raised. "Here, monks, a monk (idha bhikkhave bhikkhu)" means, monks, a monk in this Dispensation (Sāsana). In this context, the word "idha" (here) indicates the Dispensation which is the support for the person who develops the contemplation of the body in all its aspects, and it excludes such a state in other dispensations. For it has been said: "Monks, only here is there an ascetic (samaṇa)... other doctrines are void of ascetics" (as stated in the Majjhima Nikāya). Therefore, it is said, "a monk in this Dispensation."

"Gone to the forest... or gone to an empty hut"—this statement indicates the selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā). For the mind of this monk, having long wandered among sense objects such as visible forms, does not wish to enter the path of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). It runs off the track like a chariot yoked to a wild ox. Therefore, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a wild calf that has grown up drinking all the milk of a wild cow, would take it away from the cow and tie it with a rope to a large post planted in a certain place; and then that calf, struggling this way and that but unable to run away, would eventually sit down or lie down by that very post; in the same way, this monk, wishing to tame the corrupt mind that has grown up drinking the nectar of sense objects such as visible forms, should remove it from those sense objects, make it enter a forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty hut, and tie it with the rope of mindfulness to the post of the object of the foundations of mindfulness. Thus, even if his mind struggles this way and that, no longer obtaining the objects it was previously accustomed to, and being unable to break the rope of mindfulness and run away, it settles down and lies down upon that very object of mindfulness by way of access concentration (upacāra) and absorption concentration (appanā).

Hence, the ancients said:

"Just as a man here would tie a calf,
To a post in order to tame it,
So should one tie one's own mind,
Firmly to the object with mindfulness."

In this way, that dwelling becomes suitable for meditation. Therefore, it is said, "this indicates the selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness."
253:
Furthermore, this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-kammaṭṭhāna), which is the pinnacle of the contemplation of the body and the basis for the attainment of distinction and dwelling in happiness in the present life for all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddhas, is not easy to accomplish without abandoning the vicinity of a village crowded with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, and so forth. This is because sound is a thorn to meditative absorption (jhana).

However, in a forest far from a village, it is easy for a practitioner (yogāvacara) to take up this meditation subject, produce the fourth jhana of mindfulness of breathing, and then, using that very jhana as a basis, to comprehend conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) and reach the supreme fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing him a suitable dwelling, said "gone to the forest" and so forth.

Indeed, the Blessed One is like a master of site-selection (vatthuvijjācariya). Just as a master of site-selection, having seen and thoroughly examined a site for a city, instructs, "Build the city here," and when the city is safely completed, he receives great honor from the royal family; in the same way, the Blessed One, having examined the dwelling suitable for a practitioner, instructs, "The meditation subject should be practiced here." Then, when the meditating monk practicing the meditation subject in that place reaches Arahantship in due course, he pays great honor to the Blessed One, saying, "The Blessed One is indeed the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)."

This monk is said to be like a leopard. Just as a great king of leopards hides in the forest, in a thicket of grass, a thicket of trees, or a mountain cleft to catch wild buffaloes, elks, pigs, and other animals; in the same way, this monk practicing the meditation subject in the forest and so forth catches the four Paths and the four Noble Fruits in due course. Therefore, the ancients said:

"Just as the leopard,
By hiding, catches its prey,
Even so, this son of the Buddha,
An insightful practitioner of yoga,
Having entered the forest,
Catches the supreme Fruit."

Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the forest dwelling as the suitable ground for the speed of his exertion, said "gone to the forest" and so forth. What remains to be said in this section on mindfulness of breathing has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Regarding his practice: "Breathing in long, he knows 'I breathe in long'... training himself, 'I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation'"—in this manner...
254:
For one who practices by way of the aforementioned in-breaths and out-breaths, the four jhānas arise in the sign (nimitta) of the in-breaths and out-breaths. Having emerged from the jhāna, that person grasps either the in-breaths and out-breaths or the jhāna factors. Among those two, the one who strives with the in-breaths and out-breaths contemplates: 'On what do these in-breaths and out-breaths depend? They depend on the base (vatthu). The base is the physical body (karajakāya). The physical body consists of the four great elements and derived materiality (upādārūpa).' In this way, he grasps materiality. Thereafter, he grasps mentality-materiality by identifying the group of five factors starting with contact (phassa) that take that materiality as an object as 'mentality' (nāma). While searching for the cause of that mentality-materiality, he sees Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) starting with ignorance (avijjā) and, having overcome doubt by realizing 'This is merely a phenomenon of causes and produced effects; there is no other being or person,' he applies the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) to the mentality-materiality along with its causes. As he develops insight (vipassanā), he gradually reaches the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). This is the path of exit (niyyānamukha) leading to Arahantship for one monk.

The one who strives with jhāna also defines mentality-materiality by contemplating: 'On what do these jhāna factors depend? They depend on the base. The base is the physical body. The jhāna factors are mentality, and the physical body is materiality.' While searching for the cause of that mentality-materiality, he sees the nature of Dependent Origination starting with ignorance and, having overcome doubt by realizing 'This is merely a phenomenon of causes and produced effects; there is no other being or person,' he applies the three characteristics to the mentality-materiality along with its causes. As he develops insight, he gradually reaches the fruit of Arahantship. This is the path of exit leading to Arahantship for one monk.

'Thus, internally...' means he dwells frequently contemplating the body in his own group of in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Or externally...' means (contemplating) in the group of in-breaths and out-breaths of another. 'Or internally and externally...' means (contemplating) sometimes in his own and sometimes in another's group of in-breaths and out-breaths. By this statement, the time of moving back and forth without abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in which the monk is proficient is described. At one single time, however, both cannot be obtained.

'Or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising...' means that just as wind moves back and forth depending on the blacksmith's bellows, the skin-tube, and the appropriate effort, even so, the group of in-breaths and out-breaths moves back and forth for the monk depending on the physical body, the nostrils, and the mind. Phenomena such as the body are the causes of arising; one who sees these phenomena is said to 'dwell contemplating the nature of arising in the body.' 'Or he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing...' means that just as when the bellows are removed, or the skin-tube is broken, or there is no appropriate effort, that wind does not occur, even so, when the body is broken, or the nostrils are destroyed...
255:
...and when the mind ceases, the group of in-breaths and out-breaths does not occur. Thus, one who sees the cessation of in-breaths and out-breaths due to the cessation of the body and so forth is said to 'dwell contemplating the nature of vanishing in the body.' 'Contemplating the nature of both arising and vanishing' means contemplating arising at one time and vanishing at another time. Alternatively, mindfulness is established for that monk as 'There is only a body; there is no being, no person, no woman, no man, no self, no property belonging to a self, no I, no mine, no someone, and no property belonging to someone.'

The phrase 'yāvad eva' (only to the extent) defines the limit of the purpose. This is what is meant: the mindfulness that is established is not for any other purpose, but only for the sake of mere knowledge, for the sake of the measure of further and higher knowledge, for the sake of the measure of mindfulness, and for the sake of the growth of mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña). He dwells independent through the power of the independence from the supports of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). He does not cling to anything in the world, not grasping any materiality... or consciousness in the world as 'This is my self' or 'This is my property.' In the term 'evampi', the syllable 'pi' has the sense of inclusion, taking the aforementioned meaning. With this word, the Blessed One concludes and shows the teaching on the section on breathing (ānāpānapabba).

In that context, the mindfulness that grasps the in-breaths and out-breaths is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca). The preceding craving that originates that mindfulness is the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca). The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca). The Noble Path (ariyamagga) which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and takes cessation as its object is the Truth of the Path (maggasacca). Thus, having striven by way of the Four Noble Truths, he reaches Nibbāna, the state of peace. This is the path of exit leading to Arahantship for a certain monk who strives by way of in-breaths and out-breaths.

## The Explanation of the Section on Breathing is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Postures

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of in-breaths and out-breaths, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with 'puna caparaṃ' (again, further) in order to analyze it by way of postures (iriyāpatha). In that regard, even dogs, jackals, and so forth, when they are going, know 'we are going.' However, this was not spoken with reference to that kind of knowing. For that kind of knowing does not abandon the perception of a being and does not [abandon] the notion of a self...
256:
Without removing (the perception of "my body"), there is no meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) or development of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā). However, the understanding of this monk abandons the perception of a being, removes the perception of "my body," and both the meditation subject and the development of mindfulness occur. This is said with reference to the analytical understanding (sampajānana): "Who goes? Whose going is it? For what reason does one go?" The same method applies to standing and so forth.

In that regard, "Who goes?" means no being or person goes. "Whose going is it?" means there is no going of any being or person. "For what reason does one go?" means one goes because of the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the mind. Therefore, this practitioner understands thus: the mind "I will go" arises; that mind produces the air element; the air element produces intimation (viññatti). Thus, the bringing forward of the whole body through the diffusion of the air element produced by the mind is called "going." The same method applies to standing and so forth.

In those cases as well, the mind "I will stand" arises; that mind produces the air element; the air element produces intimation. The state of being erect from the lower extremity of the whole body through the diffusion of the air element produced by the mind is called "standing." The mind "I will sit" arises; that mind produces the air element; the air element produces intimation. The bending of the lower body and the erect state of the upper body through the diffusion of the air element produced by the mind is called "sitting." The mind "I will lie down" arises; that mind produces the air element; the air element produces intimation. The stretching out of the whole body horizontally through the diffusion of the air element produced by the mind is called "lying down."

To one who understands thus, this thought occurs: "It is said 'a being goes, a being stands,' but in reality, there is no being who is going or standing." Just as it is said "the cart goes, the cart stands," yet there is no such thing as a "cart" that goes or stands independently; rather, when four oxen are yoked and a skilled driver drives them, it is merely a conventional expression to say "the cart goes, the cart stands." In the same way, the body is like the cart because it lacks volition. The winds born of the mind are like the oxen. The mind is like the driver. When the mind "I will go, I will stand" arises, the air element arises, producing intimation. Through the diffusion of the air element produced by the mind, going and so forth proceed. Then, "a being goes..."
257:
“A being stands, I go, I stand” is merely a conventional expression. Therefore, it is said:
“As a boat goes by the force of the wind, and an arrow goes by the force of the bowstring, so this body goes, impelled by the wind (vāyodhātu).
Just as a machine moves only by the power of a string, so this machine of a body, yoked by the power of the string of the mind, goes, stands, and sits.
Where is that being in this world who, apart from causes and conditions, could stand or go by its own power?”

Therefore, this practitioner, clearly noting going and so forth which occur only by the power of causes and conditions, understands “I go” when going, or understands “I am lying down” when standing, sitting, or lying down.

Alternatively, “in whatever way his body is disposed, he understands it in that way” is a comprehensive statement. The meaning is: in whatever manner the monk's body is positioned, he understands it in that manner. When it is positioned in the manner of going, he understands “he goes.” When it is positioned in the manner of standing, sitting, or lying down, he understands “he is lying down.”

“Thus, internally...” means he dwells contemplating the body in the body by defining his own four postures. “Or externally...” means by defining the four postures of another. “Or both internally and externally...” means he dwells contemplating the body in the body by defining his own four postures at one time and another's four postures at another time. In the phrases “contemplating the nature of arising,” etc., the arising and passing away of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) should be extracted in five ways, such as “with the arising of ignorance, form arises.” With reference to that meaning, “contemplating the nature of arising,” etc., is said here. “Or else mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ is established before him” and so forth are the same as previously explained.

In this context, the mindfulness that defines the four postures is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The preceding craving that causes that mindfulness to arise is the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca). The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The Noble Path (ariya-magga) which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and takes cessation as its object is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca).
258:
In this way, by making an effort through the power of the Four Noble Truths, one reaches Nibbāna. This teaching is the gateway to liberation leading up to Arahantship for a bhikkhu who discerns the four postures.

## The Explanation of the Section on Postures is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of postures, the Teacher now said "Puna caparaṃ" and so forth, in order to analyze it by way of the fourfold clear comprehension. Among those terms, in "abhikkante paṭikkante" (in going forward and returning), first, "abhikkanta" refers to going forward. "Paṭikkanta" refers to returning. Both of these are found in all four postures. In the case of walking, moving the body forward is called "abhikkamati" (going forward). Turning back is called "paṭikkamati" (returning). In the case of standing, even while standing, leaning the body forward is called "abhikkamati". Drawing back is called "paṭikkamati". In the case of sitting, even while sitting, moving toward the front part of the seat is called "abhikkamati". Moving back toward the rear part is called "paṭikkamati". In the case of lying down, the same method applies.

"Sampajānākārī hoti" means one who habitually performs all actions with clear comprehension, or one who habitually practices clear comprehension itself. That bhikkhu indeed practices clear comprehension in going forward and so on; he is never without clear comprehension at any time. That clear comprehension is of four kinds: clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña), clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). Among these four kinds of clear comprehension, when the thought of going forward arises, instead of going according to the whim of the mind, one discerns whether there is a purpose or not, thinking, "Is there any benefit for me in going like this?" and then grasping what is purposeful; this is called clear comprehension of purpose.

In that context, "purpose" means growth in accordance with the Dhamma by way of seeing a cetiya, seeing a Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing elder monks, or seeing a foul object (asubha), and so forth. Indeed, having seen a cetiya or a Bodhi tree and having aroused joy (pīti) with the Buddha as the object, or having seen the Saṅgha and having aroused joy with the Saṅgha as the object, one who contemplates that very joy as subject to destruction and vanishing reaches Arahantship. Having seen elder monks and established oneself in their advice, or having seen a foul object and having produced the first jhāna therein, one who contemplates that very jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing reaches Arahantship. Therefore, seeing these things is purposeful. Some teachers, however, say, "Growth in terms of material requisites (āmisa) is also a purpose, because one practices in dependence on those requisites for the support of the holy life (brahmacariya)."

In that going, discerning what is suitable and unsuitable and grasping what is suitable is called clear comprehension of suitability. For example, seeing a cetiya is first of all purposeful. However, if...
259:
At a great festival of a cetiya, crowds within ten or twelve yojanas gather. Women and men, decorated and prepared according to their wealth, move about like colorful paintings. In such a place, greed (lobha) may arise in that bhikkhu toward a pleasant object, hatred (paṭigha) toward an unpleasant object, or delusion (moha) in looking improperly. Or he may fall into an offense of physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggi), or there may be danger to his life and the holy life (brahmacariya). If this is the case, that place is unsuitable (asappāya). If the aforementioned dangers are absent, it is suitable (sappāya). The same method applies to seeing a Bodhi tree. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful. However, if people have a large pavilion built in a village and hold an all-night Dhamma talk, and if there is a crowd and danger in the same way as mentioned before, that place is unsuitable. If there is no danger, it is suitable. The same method applies to seeing elder monks who have a large following.

Seeing a foul object (asubha) is also purposeful. To illustrate this purpose, there is this story: It is said that a young bhikkhu took a novice (sāmaṇera) and went for tooth-sticks. The novice, stepping off the path and going ahead, saw a foul object, produced the first jhāna, and using that very jhāna as a basis, contemplated the formations (saṅkhāra). Having realized the three lower fruits, he stood there grasping the meditation subject for the higher path. The young monk, not seeing the novice, called out, "Sāmaṇera!" The novice thought, "Since the day I was ordained, I have never spoken even two words with a bhikkhu. On another day, I will produce the higher distinction," and replied, "What is it, Bhante?" When told "Come here," he came with just that one word and said, "Bhante, please go along this path, stand for a moment at the place where I stood, face the east, and look." The monk did so and attained the very same distinction that the novice had attained. Thus, one foul object became beneficial for two people. Although it is purposeful in this way, for a man, a female foul object is unsuitable; for a woman, a male foul object is unsuitable. Only a foul object of the same sex (sabhāga) is suitable. Grasping what is suitable in this way is called clear comprehension of suitability.

For one who has thus grasped what is purposeful and suitable, taking up the resort (gocara) known as one's preferred meditation subject among the thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), and carrying that meditation subject to the place of alms-round is called clear comprehension of the resort. To clarify this clear comprehension of the resort, this fourfold set should be understood: In this Dispensation, a certain bhikkhu carries (the meditation subject) out but does not carry it back; a certain one does not carry it out...
260:
...on the return, he carries [the meditation subject]; some monks carry it neither when going nor when returning; some monks carry it both when going and when returning. Among these four types of monks, the one who, during the day, purifies his mind from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) through walking and sitting meditation, and likewise during the first watch of the night, sleeps during the middle watch, and spends the last watch in sitting and walking meditation, performs the duties of the shrine terrace (cetiyaṅgaṇa) and the Bodhi terrace (bodhiyaṅgaṇa) early in the morning. He waters the Bodhi tree, sets out drinking water and water for use, and undertakes and practices all the Khandhaka duties, such as the duties toward teachers and preceptors (ācariya-upajjhāya).

Having performed the bodily cleansing, he enters the monastery, sits for two or three turns of the cross-legged posture to absorb the warmth, and practices his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). At the time for alms-round, he rises and, keeping the meditation subject as his priority, takes his bowl and robes and leaves the monastery. While reflecting on the meditation subject, he goes to the shrine terrace. If his meditation is the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), he enters the shrine terrace without letting go of that meditation. If it is another meditation subject, he stands at the foot of the stairs and leaves that meditation subject there, as if it were an object held in the hand. Then, taking up the joy that has the Buddha as its object, he ascends the shrine terrace. If it is a large shrine, he should circumambulate it three times and pay homage at the four sides. If it is a small shrine, he should likewise circumambulate it and pay homage at the eight directions.

After worshipping the shrine, when he reaches the Bodhi terrace, he should worship the Bodhi tree, showing deep respect as if he were in the presence of the Blessed One. Having thus worshipped the shrine and the Bodhi tree, he goes to the place where he left his meditation subject and, as if picking up an object stored by hand, he takes back the meditation subject he had set down. Then, keeping the meditation subject as his priority, he puts on his robes near the village and enters for alms. At that time, when people see him, they say, 'Our noble one has come,' and they go out to meet him, take his bowl, and have him sit in the rest house or a house. They offer rice gruel (yāgu) and, until the meal is finished, they wash his feet, anoint them with oil, and sit before him, asking questions or wishing to hear the Dhamma.

Even if they do not ask him to speak, the teachers of the Commentaries say that a Dhamma talk should indeed be given out of compassion for the people. Indeed, there is no such thing as a Dhamma talk that is separate from the meditation subject. Therefore, he preaches the Dhamma based on the meditation subject, partakes of the meal based on the meditation subject, and after performing the thanksgiving (anumodanā), he leaves the village followed by the people who are seeing him off. Having sent the people back right there [at the edge of the village], he continues on his way. Then, having left earlier than that monk...
261:
When the meal-time duties outside the village are finished, the novices and young monks, seeing [the elder], go out to meet him and take his bowl and robes. It is said that ancient monks did not perform duties by looking at faces, thinking, 'This is our preceptor or teacher.' They performed duties according to the order of arrival. They would ask him, 'Venerable sir, how are these people related to you? Are they relatives from the mother's side or the father's side?' When asked, 'What did you see that makes you ask?', they reply, 'We ask because we see their love and great respect for you, venerable sir.' The elder says, 'Friends, these people do for us what even parents find difficult to do. Our bowls and robes actually belong to them. Because of their power, we do not know fear when there is danger, nor do we know hunger when there is famine. There are no others who are as helpful to us as these people.' Thus, he proceeds while speaking of their virtues. This monk is called one who carries [the meditation subject] when going but not when returning.

However, for a monk who, while performing the aforementioned duties early in the morning, finds that the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo) burns strongly—this fire element releases the unacquired (anupādinna) [new food] and takes the acquired (upādinna) [old matter/digestion]. Sweat pours from his body, and he cannot ascend the path of meditation. That monk takes his bowl and robes early, quickly worships the shrine, and enters the village for rice gruel at the very time the cattle are let out. Having received the gruel, he goes to the rest house and drinks it. Then, with just two or three swallows, the fire element born of kamma releases the acquired and takes the unacquired (the gruel). Having attained the cooling of the burning of the fire element, as if bathed with a hundred jars of water, he partakes of the gruel with the meditation subject as his priority. After washing his bowl and face, he reflects on the meditation subject during the interval before the main meal, wanders for alms in the remaining places, and partakes of the food with the meditation subject as his priority. From then on, he returns while holding the meditation subject that appears in constant succession. This monk is called one who does not carry it when going but carries it when returning. Such monks, having drunk gruel and undertaken insight meditation (vipassanā), have reached Arahantship in the Buddha's Dispensation in numbers beyond counting. In the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka), in the rest houses of various villages, there is almost no seat where a monk has not reached Arahantship after drinking gruel.

But the monk who lives negligently, who has laid down the burden [of practice], who lives having broken all duties and being possessed of the five mental barrennesses (cetokhila) and the mental shackles (vinibandha)—he enters the village for alms without even the perception that 'there is such a thing as a meditation subject.' Having wandered and eaten while mingling inappropriately with laypeople, he returns empty. This monk is called one who carries it neither when going nor when returning.
262:
The monk who is described as 'one who goes and returns' should be understood by way of the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgatikavatta). To explain in detail: sons of good family, desiring their own welfare, having ordained in the Dispensation, living together in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred, dwell having made a pact: 'Friends, you did not ordain because of debt, nor out of fear, nor for a livelihood; rather, you ordained here desiring to be free from the suffering of the round of rebirths. Therefore, suppress the defilements that arise while walking, even while walking; suppress the defilements that arise while standing, sitting, or lying down, in those very postures.'

Having made such a pact, when they go for alms, there are stones (markers) at intervals of half a usabha, one usabha, half a gāvuta, and one gāvuta. They go while attending to their meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) with that recognition. If defilement arises in any monk while walking, he suppresses it right there. If he cannot suppress it while walking, he stops. Then the monk coming behind him also stops. That monk reproaches himself, thinking, 'This monk knows the thought that has arisen in me; this is not suitable for me,' and having developed insight (vipassanā), he reaches the stage of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi) right there. If he cannot suppress it while standing, he sits down. Then the monk coming behind him also sits down; the method is the same.

Even if he is unable to reach the stage of the Noble Ones, he goes on only after removing that defilement and attending to his meditation subject. He does not lift a foot with a mind devoid of the meditation subject. If he does lift it, he turns back and returns to the previous spot, like the Elder Mahāphussadeva who dwelt at Āḷindaka.

It is said that that Elder lived for nineteen years fulfilling the duty of going and returning. People plowing, sowing, and threshing along the way, seeing the Elder going in that manner, would say, 'This Elder turns back again and again and goes. Is he perhaps lost, or has he forgotten something?' Without paying attention to them, practicing the recluse's Dhamma with a mind joined with the meditation subject, he attained Arahantship within twenty years. On the very day he attained Arahantship, a deity dwelling at the end of his walking path stood lighting a lamp with her fingers. The four Great Kings, Sakka the lord of devas, and Sahampati Brahma also came to attend on him. Seeing that light, the Elder Vanavāsī Mahātissa asked him the next day, 'There was a light in the presence of the venerable one during the night; what was that light?' The Elder, wishing to conceal his attainment, said, 'A light can be the light of a lamp or the light of a gem,' and so on.
263:
Furthermore, when repeatedly urged, 'You should conceal your attainments within,' he acknowledged it, saying, 'Yes,' and informed them. It is also like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt at Kālavallimaṇḍapa.

That Elder Mahānāga, while fulfilling the duty of going and returning, first resolved, 'I will honor the Great Striving (mahāpadhāna) of the Blessed One,' and for seven years he undertook only standing and walking. Then, having fulfilled the duty of going and returning for sixteen years, he attained Arahantship. That Elder would lift his foot only with a mind joined with the meditation subject; if he lifted it while devoid of it, he would turn back (and start again from the original spot). When he reached the vicinity of a village, at a place where one might wonder, 'Is it a cow or a monk?', he would stand, put on his robe, wash his bowl with water from under his armpit, and take a mouthful of water.

Why did he do so? Thinking, 'Let there not be a distraction from my meditation subject even by the mere words "May you live long" to the people who come to give alms or to pay homage.' If he was asked about the date, the number of monks, or a question, he would swallow the water and then answer. If there was no one asking about the date and so on, he would spit out the water at the village gate when leaving and go his way. This is just like the fifty monks who entered the rains-retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery.

It is said that on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, they made a pact: 'We will not speak to one another until we have attained Arahantship.' When entering the village for alms, they also entered with a mouthful of water. When asked about the date and so on, they practiced in the same manner as mentioned before. The people there, seeing them spit out the water, knew, 'Today one has come, today two have come.'

Those people thought: 'Do these monks not speak only with us, or do they not speak with each other either? If they do not speak with each other, they must surely be quarreling. Come, let us make them ask for forgiveness from one another.' So saying, they all went to the monastery, but among the fifty monks, they did not see even two monks in one place. Then, a man of vision among them said, 'Friends, the place of those who quarrel is not like this. The courtyard of the shrine and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree are well-swept. The brooms are well-stored. The drinking water and washing water are well-placed.' Those people then turned back from there. Those monks attained Arahantship within the three months of the rains-retreat and performed the Pure Pavāraṇā (visuddhipavāraṇā) on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā.

Thus, like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt at Kālavallimaṇḍapa and like the monks who entered the rains-retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery, lifting the foot only with a mind joined with the meditation subject...
264:
Upon reaching the vicinity of the village, he should rinse his mouth, observe the streets, and enter a street where there are no drunkards, brawlers, wild elephants, horses, and the like. While wandering for alms in that street, he should not go with speed as if in a great hurry. For there is no such thing as a "speedy" ascetic practice of alms-gathering. He should go steadily, like a water-cart that has reached uneven ground. When entering houses in order, he should wait for a suitable time to discern whether the householder wishes to give or not. After receiving the alms-food, he should sit in a suitable and comfortable place—whether inside the village, outside the village, or in the monastery—and while attending to his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he should establish the perception of the repulsiveness of food. Reflecting on that food through the similes of greasing an axle, medicating a wound, or eating the flesh of one's own son, he partakes of the food endowed with the eight factors: not for fun, not for intoxication, not for adornment, and not for beautification.

After eating, having attended to the matter of water and rested for a moment to relieve the fatigue of the meal, he attends to his meditation subject just as before the meal, so also after the meal; just as in the first watch of the night, so also in the last watch. This monk is said to "carry [the meditation] and carry it back."

One who fulfills this duty of going and returning (gata-paccāgatika-vatta), if endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya), attains Arahantship even in the first stage of life. If he does not attain it in the first stage, then in the middle stage. If not in the middle stage, then in the last stage. If not in the last stage, then at the time of death. If not at the time of death, then after becoming a young deva. If he does not attain it as a deva, then being born when a Buddha has not appeared, he realizes Paccekabodhi (Enlightenment of a Private Buddha). If he does not realize Paccekabodhi, then in the presence of the Buddhas, he becomes one of swift direct knowledge (khippābhiññā) like the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya, or one of great wisdom like the Elder Sāriputta, or one of great psychic power like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, or a bearer of ascetic practices like the Elder Mahākassapa, or one with the divine eye like the Elder Anuruddha, or a bearer of the Vinaya like the Elder Upāli, or an eloquent preacher of the Dhamma like the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, or a forest-dweller like the Elder Revata, or one of great learning like the Elder Ānanda, or one who is desirous of training like the Buddha’s son, the Elder Rāhula. Thus, among these four groups, for the monk who "carries and carries back," his clear comprehension of the resort (gocarasampajañña) reaches its pinnacle.
265:
Non-delusion regarding moving forward and so forth is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammohasampajañña). This clear comprehension of non-delusion is to be understood thus: In this Dispensation, a monk, when moving forward or moving backward, does not get deluded like blind worldlings (andhaputhujjana) who, regarding moving forward and so forth, are deluded thinking, "The self moves forward," or "Moving forward is produced by the self," or "I move forward," or "Moving forward is produced by me." Instead, without being deluded, when the thought "I will move forward" arises, the air element (vāyodhātu) born of that mind arises, producing intimation (viññatti). Thus, by the power of the diffusion of the air element born of mental activity, this skeleton, which is conventionally called a "body," moves forward.

In each and every lifting of the foot of that skeleton as it moves forward, the two elements of earth (pathavīdhātu) and water (āpodhātu) are inferior and weak, while the other two elements of fire (tejodhātu) and air (vāyodhātu) are superior and strong. It is the same in carrying forward and extending forward. In releasing the foot (lowering it), the fire and air elements are inferior and weak, while the other two (earth and water) are superior and strong. It is the same in placing the foot down and pressing it.

The material and immaterial phenomena (rūpārūpadhamma) that arise in that lifting of the foot do not reach the stage of carrying forward. Likewise, those that arise in carrying forward do not reach the stage of extending forward; those in extending forward do not reach the stage of releasing; those in releasing do not reach the stage of placing; and those in placing do not reach the stage of pressing. Those phenomena, having become joint by joint, part by part, and limit by limit in those very places, break up with a "pata-pata" sound like sesame seeds thrown onto a hot pan.

In such a process, who is the one person that moves forward? Or whose moving forward is it? In the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is only the going of elements, the standing of elements, the sitting of elements, and the lying down of elements. In each and every part, together with matter—
"One mind arises, another mind ceases; it proceeds in an uninterrupted connection like the current of a river."

Thus, non-delusion in moving forward and so forth is called clear comprehension of non-delusion.

## The explanation of the phrase "He is one who acts with clear comprehension in moving forward and moving backward" is finished.

## Looking Ahead and Looking Around (Ālokite Vilokite)

In the phrase "ālokite vilokite," "ālokita" means looking straight ahead. "Vilokita" means looking towards the directions. There are also others such as "olokita" (looking down), "ullokita" (looking up), and "apalokita" (looking behind) by way of looking downwards, upwards, and backwards.
266:
Although there are other names for looking, they are not taken here. Only these two (ālokita and vilokita) are taken appropriately. Or rather, by taking these two as the primary ones, all types of looking are included.

Among these, when the thought 'I will look' arises, the discernment of whether it is purposeful or not, without looking merely according to the mind's whim, is called clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña). This clear comprehension of purpose should be understood by taking the Venerable Nanda as a personal witness. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, if Nanda has to look to the eastern direction, he looks to the eastern direction having applied his whole mind. Thus, while I am looking to the eastern direction, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief will not flow in—in this way, he is one who possesses clear comprehension therein. Monks, if Nanda has to look to the western direction, northern direction, southern direction, above, below, or the intermediate directions, he looks to that direction having applied his whole mind. Thus, while I am looking... he is one who possesses clear comprehension.'

Furthermore, here too, the states of being purposeful and suitable should be understood by way of seeing a stupa, etc., as mentioned before. Not abandoning one's meditation subject is indeed clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña). Therefore, those who have the meditation subjects of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) should perform looking and looking around by way of their own meditation subject; or those who have meditation subjects such as kasiṇa should do so by making the meditation subject the priority.

Internally, there is no 'self' (attā) that is the looker or the looker-around. When the thought 'I will look' arises, the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the mind arises together with that mind, generating intimation (viññatti). Thus, by the power of the mental action and the diffusion of the air element, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper eyelid rises up. There is no one opening them with a mechanical device. From that, eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) arises, performing the function of seeing. Such clear understanding here is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña).

Moreover, clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood here by way of full understanding of the root (mūlapariññā), the state of being a guest (āgantukatā), and the temporary nature (tāvakālikabhāva). First, by way of full understanding of the root:

Life-continuum (bhavaṅga), adverting (āvajjana),
Seeing (dassana), receiving (sampaṭicchana),
Investigating (santīraṇa), determining (voṭṭhabbana),
The seventh is the impulsion (javana).

In that process, the life-continuum occurs, performing the function of a factor of the rebirth-existence. Having turned that life-continuum, the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) occurs, performing the function of adverting. When that mind ceases...
267:
Eye-consciousness occurs, performing the function of seeing. Due to the cessation of that eye-consciousness, the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu) occurs, performing the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana). Due to the cessation of that resultant mind-element, the resultant mind-consciousness element (vipāka-manoviññāṇadhātu) occurs, performing the function of investigating (santīraṇa). Due to the cessation of that resultant mind-consciousness element, the functional mind-consciousness element (kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) occurs, performing the function of determining (voṭṭhabbana). Due to the cessation of that functional mind-consciousness element, the impulsions (javana) run for seven times. Among those seven impulsions, even in the first impulsion, and from the second up to the seventh impulsion, looking forward or looking aside by way of lusting, hating, or being deluded with the thought 'This is a woman, this is a man' does not occur. However, only when they break down and fall like soldiers on a battlefield in a reciprocal manner (above and below), does looking forward or looking aside by way of lusting, etc., with the thought 'This is a woman, this is a man' occur. Thus, here, clear comprehension of non-delusion should first be understood by way of full understanding of the root (mūlapariññā).

When a visible form comes into the range of the eye-door, after the vibration of the life-continuum, the mind-states such as adverting arise and cease by way of performing their respective functions, and finally, the impulsion (javana) arises. That impulsion is like a guest man in the eye-door, which is the 'house' of the previously arisen adverting and so on. Just as it is not proper for a guest man who has entered another's house to ask for something or to give orders while the house-owners are sitting silently, so too, while the adverting and other mind-states, which are like the owners of the eye-door house, do not lust, hate, or become deluded, it is not proper for the impulsion (the guest) to lust, hate, or be deluded. Thus, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of the state of being a guest (āgantukabhāva).

Those mind-states that arise in the eye-door ending with determining (voṭṭhabbana) break up right there along with their associated states. Because they do not see one another, they are very brief and temporary. In that regard, for example, when all the people in a house have died, it is not proper for the one remaining person, who is also of the nature to die at that very moment, to delight in dancing and singing. Similarly, when the adverting and other mind-states, along with their associated states, have died (ceased) right there in the single eye-door, it is not proper for the remaining impulsion, which is also of the nature to die at that very moment, to delight by way of lusting, hating, or being deluded. Thus, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of the temporary nature (tāvakālikabhāva).

Furthermore, this clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditions (paccaya). Here, the eye and the visible form are the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). The act of seeing is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). The feeling associated with that consciousness is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). Perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha). States such as contact (phassa) are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
268:
In this way, through the combination of these five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā), looking straight (ālokana) and looking aside (vilokana) become manifest. In that manifestation, what single thing looks straight, and who looks aside? Similarly, the eye is the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), form is the form-base (rūpāyatana), seeing (eye-consciousness) is the mind-base (manāyatana), and associated states such as feeling are the Dhamma-base (dhammāyatana). Through the combination of these four bases, looking straight and looking aside become manifest. In that manifestation, what single thing looks straight, and who looks aside? Similarly, the eye is the eye-element (cakkhudhātu), form is the form-element (rūpadhātu), seeing is the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu), and associated states such as feeling are the Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu). Through the combination of these four elements, looking straight and looking aside become manifest. In that manifestation, what single thing looks straight, and who looks aside?
