Similarly, the eye is the support condition (nissaya-paccaya), form is the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), adverting (āvajjana) is the proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), decisive support (upanissaya), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata) conditions, light is the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), and associated states such as feeling are the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya). Through the combination of these conditions, looking straight and looking aside become manifest. In that manifestation, what single thing looks straight, and who looks aside? Thus, in this looking, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions.

Regarding 'bending and stretching' (samiñjite pasārite), this occurs in the bending and stretching of the limbs. In that bending and stretching, not doing so merely according to the mind's desire, but discerning the benefit and non-benefit of bending and stretching the hands and feet, and discerning only what is beneficial, is called clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña). In that discernment, for one who remains with hands and feet bent or stretched for a very long time, painful feelings arise at every moment, the mind cannot attain one-pointedness, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) falls away and is ruined, and one cannot attain any special distinction. However, for one who bends at the proper time and stretches at the proper time, those painful feelings do not arise, the mind is one-pointed, the meditation subject increases, and one can attain special distinction; thus, the discernment of benefit and non-benefit should be understood.

Even when there is a benefit, discerning the suitability and unsuitability and discerning only what is suitable is called clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña). In this regard, there is this method: It is said that on the grounds of the Mahācetiya, young monks were reciting their studies. Behind them, young nuns were listening to the Dhamma. Then, a young monk, while stretching out his hand, came into bodily contact [with a nun] and for that reason, he ended up returning to lay life. Another monk, while stretching out his foot, stretched it into a fire, and his foot was burnt to the bone. Another stretched [his hand] into a termite mound and was bitten by a viper. Another stretched [his hand] against a robe-pole, and it...
269:
...a cobra bit him. Therefore, one should not stretch out in such unsuitable places, but only in suitable places. This is called clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) in this context of bending and stretching.

Clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña) should be illustrated by the story of the Great Elder (Mahāthera). It is said that the Great Elder, while sitting in his daytime quarters and conversing with his pupils, suddenly bent his hand. Then, having placed it back in its original position, he bent it again slowly. His pupils asked, "Venerable sir, why did you suddenly bend your hand, then place it back in its original position and bend it again slowly?" The Great Elder replied, "Friends, from the time I began to apply my mind to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), I have never bent my hand while letting go of the meditation subject. But now, while conversing with you, I bent it while letting go of the meditation subject; therefore, I placed it back in its original position and bent it again (with the meditation subject)." The pupils said, "Excellent, venerable sir! One who is called a monk should be of such a nature." Thus, in this context of bending and stretching, not abandoning the meditation subject is to be understood as clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña).

Inside, there is no such thing as a 'self' (attā) who bends or stretches. Just as the hands and feet of a wooden puppet moved by strings move due to the spreading of the functional wind element (kiriyā-vāyodhātu) produced by the mind as previously described, so too do bending and stretching occur. Discerning in this way is to be understood as clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) in this context.

In the phrase "saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe," the term 'dhāraṇa' (wearing/carrying) refers to the wearing of the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) and other robes, and the use of the bowl (patta) for receiving alms-food and so on. In that wearing of robes, for a monk who first puts them on and then wanders for alms, the gain of material requisites (āmisalābha) and the purpose stated by the Blessed One such as "for the warding off of cold" is what is called 'attha' (purpose). Clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood by way of reflecting on that purpose.

For one who is of a hot nature or who is weak, a thin robe is suitable. For one who is sensitive to cold, a thick double-layered robe is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is unsuitable, for it becomes an obstacle to exertion as one has to perform patching and so on. Similarly, robes that are attractive, such as those made of silk or wool, are unsuitable. Such a robe can be a danger to the clothing or even a danger to the life of a monk living alone in the forest. Specifically, a robe obtained through wrong livelihood (micchājīva) such as giving a sign (nimittakamma) and so on, or a robe by the use of which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, is unsuitable. A robe that is the opposite of this is...
270:
If it is a suitable robe, through that suitability, sappāya-sampajañña (clear comprehension of suitability) should be understood here; and through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject, gocara-sampajañña (clear comprehension of the domain) should be understood.

Inside the body, there is no such thing as a 'self' (attā) who wears the robe. In fact, the wearing of the robe occurs only through the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the aforementioned types of consciousness. In that act of wearing the robe, the robe is insentient, and the body is also without volition. The robe does not know, 'I am worn by the body.' The body also does not know, 'I am covered by the robe.' Only elements cover a collection of elements, just as a statue is covered with an old cloth. Therefore, one should not feel joy upon receiving a good robe, nor should one feel dejection upon receiving a poor robe. Just as some people pay respect to the Nāgavammika Cetiya tree and others with flowers, scents, incense, and cloths, while some show disrespect with excrement, urine, mud, or by striking and cutting it with sticks and weapons—yet those Nāgavammika trees and others do not feel joy or dejection—in the same way, one should not feel joy upon receiving a good robe, nor dejection upon receiving a poor robe. Through the power of such reflection, asammoha-sampajañña (clear comprehension of non-delusion) should be understood in this wearing of the robe.

In carrying the bowl as well, one should not take the bowl hastily, but think, 'By taking this bowl and wandering for alms, I shall receive food.' Thus, through the power of the benefit to be obtained by the reason of taking the bowl, sātthaka-sampajañña (clear comprehension of purpose) should be understood.

For one with a lean and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable. For anyone, a bowl that has been struck in four or five places and is difficult to clean is indeed unsuitable. A bowl that is not washed cleanly is not allowable; for the monk who washes that bowl, it becomes an impediment (palibodha). A bowl with the color of a gem is unsuitable because it is desirable, following the same method mentioned regarding the robe. As for a bowl obtained through means such as making a sign (nimittakamma), if unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline for the monk who uses it, this bowl is definitely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. Through that suitability, sappāya-sampajañña should be understood here; and through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject, gocara-sampajañña should be understood.

Inside the body, there is no such thing as a 'self' (attā) who takes the bowl. In fact, what is called taking the bowl occurs only through the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the aforementioned types of consciousness. In that taking of the bowl, the bowl is insentient, and the hands are also without volition. The bowl does not know, 'I am taken by the hands.' The hands also do not know, 'The bowl is taken by us.'
271:
Just as elements grasp a collection of elements, like grasping a red-hot metal plate with tongs, through the power of such reflection, asammoha-sampajañña (clear comprehension of non-delusion) should be understood here.

Furthermore, it is like seeing helpless people lying in a hospice (anāthasālā) with severed hands and feet, with pus and blood oozing from their wounds, infested with worms and surrounded by bluebottles. Compassionate men, seeing them, offer wound-covering rags and medicines in potsherds and the like. Among those sick people, some receive fine rags while others receive coarse ones. The potsherds for medicine also reach some in good shape and others in poor shape. They do not become happy or sad over those cloths and potsherds. Just as those rags are useful to them merely for covering the wounds, and the potsherds merely for receiving the medicine, in the same way, the monk who reflects on the robe as a wound-covering rag, the bowl as a medicine potsherd, and the alms-food received in the bowl as the medicine in the potsherd—this monk should be known as one who acts with supreme clear comprehension through asammoha-sampajañña in carrying the outer robe, the bowl, and the inner robe.

Among the terms beginning with asita: asita means eating alms-food. pīta means drinking beverages such as gruel. khāyita means chewing hard food such as cakes. sāyita means tasting lickables such as honey and molasses. In that eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, the eightfold purpose mentioned by the method 'not for fun,' etc., is called 'purpose' (attha). Through the power of that purpose, sātthaka-sampajañña should be understood. Among foods that are coarse, fine, bitter, sweet, etc., if a certain food causes discomfort to a certain monk, that food is unsuitable (asappāya) for him. If a certain food is obtained through means such as making a sign (nimittakamma), and for the one who eats it, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, that food is definitely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable (sappāya). Through that suitability, sappāya-sampajañña should be understood here. Through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject, gocara-sampajañña should be understood.

Inside the body, there is no such thing as a 'self' (attā) who eats. Only through the power of the diffusion of the air element produced by mental activity (cittakiriya-vāyodhātu) as described, does what is called taking the bowl occur. Only through the diffusion of the air element produced by mental activity does the lowering of the hand into the bowl occur. Only through the diffusion of the air element produced by mental activity do the making of the morsel, the raising of the morsel, and the opening of the mouth occur. No one opens the jawbones with a key or a mechanism. Only through the diffusion of the air element produced by mental activity do the placing of the morsel in the mouth, the upper teeth performing the function of a pestle, the lower teeth performing the function of a mortar, and the tongue performing the function of a hand occur.
272:
In this way, in that mouth, the thin saliva at the tip of the tongue and the thick saliva at the root of the tongue smear the food. There is no one who, with a spoon or a ladle, pushes into the stomach that food which is turned by the hand of the tongue in the mortar of the lower teeth, moistened by the water of saliva, and crushed by the pestle of the upper teeth; it enters only by the wind element (vāyo-dhātu). There is no one who, having spread a bed of straw, holds up each portion of food as it enters; it remains only by the power of the wind element. There is no one who, having made a tripod and lit a fire, cooks each portion of food as it stays; it is cooked only by the fire element (tejo-dhātu). There is no one who, with a stick or a staff, brings out each portion of food as it is cooked; only the wind element brings it out.

Thus, the wind element carries, brings in, holds, turns, crushes, dries, and brings out (the food). The earth element (pathavī-dhātu) holds, turns, crushes, and dries. The water element (āpo-dhātu) provides cohesion and maintains moisture. The fire element cooks the food that has entered within. The space element (ākāsa-dhātu) provides the passage. The consciousness element (viññāṇa-dhātu), depending on appropriate effort in various places, takes hold (of the food). In this way, through the power of reflecting on the process, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood here.

Furthermore, clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood here by reflecting on the tenfold foulness: through going, seeking, consuming, the stomach (āsaya), storage, the uncooked, the cooked, the result, the discharge (nissanda), and the smearing. The detailed explanation of this should be taken from the 'Description of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Food' (Āhārepāṭikūlasaññā-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga.

In the act of defecating and urinating: in the performing of defecation and urination. There, for one who does not defecate or urinate when it is time, sweat is released from the whole body, the eyes roll, the mind is not concentrated, and other diseases arise. But for one who does, these do not occur. This is the meaning here. Through the power of that benefit, clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood. For one who defecates or urinates in an unsuitable place, there is an offense, loss of reputation, and danger to life. For one who does so in a suitable place, these do not occur. This is suitability (sappāya) here. Through the power of that suitability, clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) should be understood, and through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject, clear comprehension of resort (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood.
273:
Inside the body, there is no such thing as a 'self' (atta) that performs defecation and urination. Rather, the act of defecating and urinating occurs only through the diffusion of the wind element caused by the mind. Just as pus and blood exit involuntarily from a ripe boil when it bursts, and just as water exits involuntarily from an overfilled water pot, so too, the feces and urine accumulated in the rectum and bladder, being pressed by the force of the wind, exit even if one does not wish it. This feces and urine exiting in such a way belongs neither to that monk himself nor to others. It is merely the discharge of bodily impurities. How? Just as for one who pours out old water from a water pot, that water belongs neither to himself nor to others, but is merely a cleaning; even so is this. Through the power of reflecting on the process in this way, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood here in the act of defecating and urinating.

In the words 'in going' (gatādisu) and so on: 'in going' (gate) means in the act of walking; 'in standing' (ṭhite) means in the act of standing; 'in sitting' (nisinne) means in the act of sitting; 'in sleeping' (sutte) means in the act of lying down; 'in waking' (jāgarite) means in the act of being awake; 'in speaking' (bhāsite) means in the act of talking; 'in keeping silence' (tuṇhībhāve) means in the act of not talking. In the passage, "When going, he knows 'I am going'; when standing, he knows 'I am standing'; when sitting, he knows 'I am sitting'; when lying down, he knows 'I am lying down,'" the long postures are spoken of. In the passage, "In going forward and returning, in looking ahead and looking aside, in bending and stretching," the middle postures are spoken of. But here, in "going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking," the minor postures are spoken of. Therefore, in these as well, the state of acting with clear comprehension (sampajāna-kārī) should be understood in the manner already stated.

The Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva, however, said: 'If a person, after walking for a long time or practicing walking meditation, stands and subsequently reflects, "The material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) and mental phenomena (nāma-dhamma) that occurred during the time of walking have ceased right here," such a person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in going. If a person, while teaching, answering questions, or attending to a meditation subject, stands for a long time and subsequently sits and reflects, "The material and mental phenomena that occurred during the time of standing have ceased right here," such a person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in standing. If a person, due to teaching and so on, sits for a long time and subsequently lies down and reflects, "The material and mental phenomena that occurred during the time of sitting have ceased right here," such a person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sitting. If a person, while lying down, teaching or attending to a meditation subject, falls asleep and subsequently...'
274: Upon waking from sleep, one reflects: 'The mental and material phenomena that occurred during sleep have ceased right here.' One who reflects in this way is called one who acts with clear comprehension (sampajāna-kārī) in sleeping and waking. This is because the non-occurrence of functional consciousness (kiriya-citta) is called sleep, and its occurrence is called waking. When speaking, one speaks with mindfulness and clear comprehension, reflecting: 'This sound arises depending on the lips, teeth, tongue, and palate, and depending on the mental effort appropriate for that sound.' Or, after chanting, preaching the Dhamma, contemplating a meditation subject, or answering questions for a long time, one later remains silent and reflects: 'The mental and material phenomena that occurred while speaking have ceased right here.' This person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking. One who remains silent, having attended to the Dhamma or a meditation subject for a long time, later reflects: 'The mental and material phenomena that occurred while being silent have ceased right here. When there is the occurrence of derived matter (upādā-rūpa), it is called speaking; when there is not, it is called being silent.' This person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in being silent. In this Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, it is specifically the clear comprehension without delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) mentioned by the Elder Mahāsīva that is intended. In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, however, all four types of clear comprehension are obtained. Therefore, in this sutta, acting with clear comprehension should be understood specifically by way of clear comprehension without delusion. In all instances of the term 'acting with clear comprehension' (sampajāna-kārī), the meaning should be understood by way of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness. In the Vibhaṅga, however, these terms are analyzed thus: 'Mindful and clearly comprehending, he goes forward; mindful and clearly comprehending, he goes back.' 'Thus, in his own body' means that by grasping the four types of clear comprehension in this way, he dwells contemplating the body in the body, either in his own body, or in another's body, or at times in his own and at times in another's. In this sutta, in the phrases such as 'contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing,' only the arising and vanishing of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) should be shown. The remaining phrases are just as previously stated. In this sutta, the mindfulness that grasps the four types of clear comprehension is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The prior craving that causes that mindfulness to arise is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The Noble Eightfold Path of the kind described is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Thus, having made an effort by way of the Four Noble Truths, one reaches Nibbāna, the state of peace.
275:
By the power of a single monk who grasps these four types of clear comprehension, it becomes the gateway to escape from the round of rebirth up to the Fruition of Arahantship.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Attention to Repulsiveness

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of the fourfold clear comprehension, he now said "Puna caparaṃ" and so forth to analyze it by way of attention to repulsiveness (paṭikūlamanasikāra). In those words "imam-eva kāyaṃ" and so forth, everything that should be said has been explained in detail in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the meditation subject of mindfulness occupied with the body (kāyagatāsati). "With two openings" (ubhatomukhā) means being endowed with two openings, at the bottom and at the top. "Of various sorts" (nānāvihitassa) means of various kinds.

Here is the comparison with the metaphor: This body made of the four great elements is like a bag with two openings. The thirty-two parts, such as hair and so on, are like the various grains mixed and put into that bag. The practitioner (yogāvacara) is like a man with good eyesight. When that man loosens the bag and examines it, the time when the various grains become clear should be understood as the time when the thirty-two parts become manifest to the yogi.

"Thus, internally..." (iti ajjhattaṃ vā) means that by grasping the hair and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in one’s own body, or in the body of another, or at times in one’s own and at times in another’s body. From here on, it is the same as the method already stated. Specifically, here, the mindfulness that grasps the thirty-two parts is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); by applying it in this way, the gateway to escape from the round should be understood. The rest is just the same as what was said before.

## The Explanation of the Section on Attention to Repulsiveness is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Attention to the Elements

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of attention to repulsiveness, he now said "Puna caparaṃ" and so forth to analyze it by way of attention to the elements (dhātumanasikāra). Therein, this is...
276:
The explanation of the meaning, along with the correlation of the simile with the subject, is as follows: Just as a certain butcher or his apprentice, who serves for food and wages, having slaughtered a cow and carved it, might sit at a four-way crossroads—which is the middle of the great roads going in the four directions—having divided it into portions; in the same way, a monk, because of the fact that he is positioned in any one of the four postures, contemplates this body just as it is positioned, just as it is placed: "In this body there is the earth element... the air element."

What is the intended meaning? For example, as long as the butcher is raising the cow, bringing it to the slaughterhouse, tying it up there, slaughtering it, or looking at the slaughtered dead cow, the perception of "cow" does not disappear until he has carved it into pieces. However, for the butcher who sits having divided it into parts, the perception of "cow" disappears and the perception of "meat" arises. To that butcher, the thought does not occur: "I am selling a cow, these people are taking away a cow."

Rather, it occurs to him only as: "I am selling meat, these people are taking away meat." In the same way, for this monk, whether as a foolish worldling in the past, as a layman, or even after ordaining as a monk, the perception of a "being" or a "person" does not disappear as long as he does not contemplate this very body, just as it is positioned and placed, by dividing the mass and seeing it in terms of elements. But for the monk who contemplates it in terms of elements, the perception of a "being" disappears, and the mind becomes established through the power of the elements alone. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "He contemplates this very body, just as it is positioned and placed, in terms of elements: 'In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.' Just as, monks, a skilled butcher or... the air element."

The yogi should be understood as the butcher; the perception of a being as the perception of a cow; the four postures as the four-way crossroads; and the contemplation in terms of elements as the state of sitting after dividing into pieces. This is the explanation of the Pali text here. The discussion on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), however, is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus, internally" means that by thus grasping the four elements, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in the body of another, or at times in his own and at times in the body of another...
277:
He dwells contemplating the body in the body. What follows is exactly as previously described. However, in this section on attention to the elements, it should be understood that mindfulness which discerns the four elements is the Truth of Suffering; thus, the connection is made to show the way of liberation. The rest is the same as what was said before.

## The Explanation of the Section on Attention to the Elements is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Nine Cemetery Contemplations

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of attention to the elements, the Blessed One now said "Again, another..." and so forth, in order to analyze it by way of the nine cemetery contemplations. In that passage, "seyyathāpi passeyya" means just as one might see. "Sarīraṃ" means a dead corpse. "Sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ" means a corpse cast away in a cemetery. A corpse dead for one day is called "ekāhamata." A corpse dead for two days is called "dvīhamata." A corpse dead for three days is called "tīhamata." Like a smith's bellows, because of the air that rises upwards in succession due to the exhaustion of life, it is bloated, and thus called "uddhumātaka." A corpse with a discolored appearance is called "vinīla." Because it is simply of a bluish color, it is called "vinīlaka." Or, because it is loathsome, it is called "vinīlaka" meaning a loathsome bluish color. This is a designation for a corpse that is reddish in places where flesh is thick, whitish in places where pus collects, and generally bluish, appearing like a bluish cloth wrapped around it in the blue areas. A corpse with pus trickling from the nine wounds or from the ruptured parts is called "vipubba." "Vipubba" itself is "vipubbaka." Or, because it is loathsome, it is called "vipubbaka" meaning loathsome pus. A corpse that has become "vipubbaka" or has reached such a state is called "vipubbakajāta."

That monk compares his own body with that dead corpse by means of wisdom; he applies it. How? "This body too is of such a nature, will become like that, and cannot escape it." The meaning is: because of the presence of these three things—life, heat, and consciousness—this body is able to endure standing, walking, and so forth. But when these things are gone, this body too is of such a nature that it is simply of a rotting nature; it will become like that, meaning it will have the various states such as being bloated; and it cannot escape it, meaning it cannot avoid becoming bloated and so forth.

"Thus, internally" means that by thus grasping the states of being bloated and so forth, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in the body of another, or at times in his own and at times in the body of another.
278:
‘Being eaten’ (khajjamānaṃ) means being eaten by [animals] such as crows, etc., which sit on the belly and other parts, and pluck out the flesh of the belly, the lips, the eye-sockets, and so forth. ‘With flesh and blood’ (samaṃsalohitaṃ) means being joined with the remaining flesh and blood. ‘Fleshless but smeared with blood’ (nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ) is said in reference to the state where the flesh is exhausted but the blood has not yet dried up. ‘In another [direction]’ (aññena) means in another quarter or direction. ‘Hand-bones’ (hatthaṭṭhikaṃ) refers to the sixty-four types of hand-bones scattered separately. The same method applies to the foot-bones and so on. ‘More than a year old’ (terovassikāni) refers to bones that have passed beyond a year. ‘Rotten’ (pūtīni) refers to bones that, being in the open, have become rotten after more than a year due to contact with wind, sun, and rain. However, bones that are underground remain for a much longer time. ‘Reduced to powder’ (cuṇṇakajātāni) means bones that have become fine powder and are scattered. In all instances, one should apply this to this very body by way of the aforementioned method, such as ‘being eaten’ and so forth.

‘Thus, internally...’ (iti ajjhattaṃ vā) means that by such comprehension, from the stage of being eaten up to the state of being reduced to powder, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body, or in another's body, or at times in one's own and at times in another's body.

At this point, the nine charnel grounds (corpses discarded in a cemetery) should be combined. All corpses described by the method ‘a corpse dead for one day’ and so forth constitute one; ‘a corpse being eaten by crows’ and so forth is one; ‘a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews’ is one; ‘a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews’ is one; ‘a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by sinews’ is one; ‘bones disconnected and scattered in all directions’ is one; ‘bones bleached white, like the color of a conch’ is one; ‘bones heaped up, more than a year old’ is one; and ‘bones rotten and reduced to powder’ is one.

‘Thus, monks...’—the Blessed One said this, concluding the contemplation of the body after showing the nine charnel grounds. Therein, the mindfulness that grasps the nine charnel grounds is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); the prior craving that originates that mindfulness is the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca); the non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca); and the Noble Path that fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Thus, having ascended by way of the Four Noble Truths, one reaches Nibbāna. This is the gateway to liberation (niyyānamukha) up to Arahantship for monks who grasp the nine charnel grounds.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Nine Charnel Grounds is Finished.

With this much, the contemplation of the body is finished in fourteen sections: the section on mindfulness of breathing, the section on postures, the section on fourfold clear comprehension, the section on the reflection on repulsiveness, the section on the reflection on the elements, and the nine sections on the charnel grounds.
279:
Among those fourteen sections, only these two—the section on mindfulness of breathing and the section on the reflection on repulsiveness—are meditation subjects of absorption (appanā-kammaṭṭhāna). The remaining twelve are meditation subjects of access (upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna) only, because they are taught by way of the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā) regarding the charnel grounds and so forth.

## The Contemplation of the Body is Finished.

## Explanation of the Contemplation of Feelings

Having thus taught the contemplation of the body in its fourteen modes, the Blessed One now said, “And how, monks...” and so forth, in order to teach the contemplation of feelings in its nine modes. Therein, ‘a pleasant feeling’ (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ) means that when experiencing a pleasant bodily or mental feeling, one understands, “I feel a pleasant feeling.” In that regard, indeed, even infants lying on their backs understand, “We feel pleasure,” at such times as when they are nursing; however, this [teaching] is not said in reference to such kind of knowing. For such knowing does not abandon the assumption of a being (sattūpalabdhi), does not remove the perception of a being (satta-saññā), and is neither a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) nor the development of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā). But the knowing of this monk abandons the assumption of a being, removes the perception of a being, and is both a meditation subject and the development of mindfulness. For this was said in reference to experiencing with clear comprehension (sampajāna-vediyana) thus: “Who feels? Whose is the feeling? For what reason does the feeling arise?”

Among those questions, “Who feels?”—no being or person feels. “Whose is the feeling?”—the feeling does not belong to any being or person. “For what reason does the feeling arise?”—this feeling arises only because of a physical basis (vatthu) and an object (ārammaṇa). Therefore, he understands thus: “Having made this or that basis and object for pleasant feelings and so forth, it is feeling itself that feels. Based on that occurrence of feeling, it is a mere conventional expression (vohāramatta) to say ‘I feel.’” Thus, one who notes that feeling itself feels, having made the basis and object its cause, should be understood as one who “understands that he feels a pleasant feeling.” He is like a certain elder on Cittalapabbata. It is said that the elder, when he was unwell, was tossing to and fro, groaning due to intense pain. Then a young monk asked, “Venerable sir, which part of you hurts?” [The elder replied,] “Friend, there is no such thing as a specific place that hurts; it is just feeling that feels, having made a basis and an object its cause.” Thus—
280:
"Venerable Sir, is it not proper to endure from the moment you know?" he asked. "Friend, I shall endure," the Elder replied. "Venerable Sir, endurance is noble," he said again, and the Elder endured. Then, the wind element pierced through to his heart, and his intestines lay in a heap on the couch. The Elder showed the young monk, saying, "Friend, endurance is proper only when it is to this extent." The young monk remained silent. The Elder, balancing his energy, attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and being a samasīsī (one who attains the end of defilements and life simultaneously), he attained Parinibbāna.

Just as with pleasure, so with pain... [etc.] ...when experiencing a neutral feeling (neither-painful-nor-pleasant) detached from sensual pleasures, he understands, "I experience a neutral feeling detached from sensual pleasures." Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the meditation on materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), taught the meditation on mentality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by way of feeling when He taught the meditation on mentality. Indeed, meditation is twofold: meditation on materiality and meditation on mentality. These are also called the grasping of materiality (rūpa-pariggaha) and the grasping of mentality (arūpa-pariggaha). Among these, when the Blessed One taught the meditation on materiality, He taught the definition of the four elements (catu-dhātu-vavatthāna) by way of brief attention or detailed attention. Both methods are shown in all their aspects in the Visuddhimagga.

However, when teaching the meditation on mentality, He usually teaches by way of feeling. In the meditation on mentality, there are three ways of immersion: by way of contact (phassa), by way of feeling (vedanā), and by way of consciousness (citta). How? For some, after grasping the meditation on materiality in brief or in detail, contact—which is the first impact of the mind and mental factors on that object, arising while touching that object—becomes clear. For some, feeling—arising while experiencing that object—becomes clear. For some, consciousness—arising while knowing and grasping that object—becomes clear. Among those three, for the one to whom contact is clear, he grasps the group of five starting with contact (phassa-pañcamaka), thinking: "Not only contact arises; together with it, feeling which experiences that same object also arises, perception (saññā) which marks it also arises, volition (cetanā) which urges also arises, and consciousness (viññāṇa) which cognizes also arises." For the one to whom feeling is clear, he also grasps the group of five starting with contact, thinking: "Not only feeling arises; together with it, contact which touches that same object also arises, perception which marks it also arises, volition which urges also arises, and consciousness which cognizes also arises." For the one to whom consciousness is clear, he thinks: "Not only consciousness arises; together with it, contact which touches that same object..."
281:
...contact also arises, feeling which experiences also arises, perception which marks also arises, and volition which urges also arises." Thus, he grasps only those states that form the group of five starting with contact.

That yogi, investigating "On what do these five states starting with contact depend?", understands clearly: "They depend on the base (vatthu)." The "base" refers to the physical body (karaja-kāya). With reference to this physical body, it was said: "This consciousness of mine is supported here, bound up here." In essence, that body consists of the great primary elements (mahābhūta) and the remaining derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) born of kamma. Thus, between this base and the five states starting with contact, he sees only mentality and materiality: "The materiality called the base is 'materiality' (rūpa); the states starting with contact are 'mentality' (nāma)." Within this mentality and materiality, materiality is the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), and mentality consists of the four mental aggregates; thus, there are only the five aggregates. There are no five aggregates separate from mentality and materiality, and no mentality and materiality separate from the five aggregates.

That yogi, investigating "What is the cause of these five aggregates?", sees that "They have causes such as ignorance (avijjā), etc." Then he realizes: "This is merely cause and effect; there is no other being or person; it is just a heap of pure formations (saṅkhāra)." By means of mentality and materiality together with their causes, he applies the three characteristics and dwells contemplating "impermanence, suffering, and non-self" (anicca, dukkha, anatta) according to the sequence of insight (vipassanā).

That yogi, aspiring "May I reach penetration this very day," obtains suitable weather (utu-sappāya), a suitable person (puggala-sappāya), suitable food (bhojana-sappāya), and suitable hearing of the Dhamma (dhammassavana-sappāya). Sitting in a single cross-legged posture, he brings insight to its peak and is established in the fruit of Arahantship. Thus, the meditation was taught to these three persons up to the attainment of Arahantship.

In this Sutta, however, when the Blessed One taught the meditation on mentality, He taught it by way of feeling. If taught by way of contact or by way of consciousness, it is not clear and appears like a mass of darkness. But by way of feeling, it is clear. Why? Because the arising of feelings is distinct. The arising of pleasant feeling and painful feeling is very distinct. When pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) arises, it arises while moving the whole body, as if kneading it, pervading it, and moistening it—like making one eat butter washed a hundred times, or like anointing with oil cooked a hundred times, or like extinguishing heat with a thousand jars of water—causing one to exclaim, "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!" When painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) arises, it arises while moving the whole body, as if kneading it, pervading it, and moistening it—like inserting a heated iron plate, or like pouring molten copper, or like throwing a bundle of torches into a forest of dry grass and trees...
282:
...like one crying out, "Oh, what suffering! Oh, what suffering!" Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is obvious.

However, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā) is not obvious, like darkness which is difficult to see. It becomes clear to one who grasps it by way of the neutral mode, which rejects both the agreeable and the disagreeable when pleasant and painful feelings have subsided. For example, a deer hunter following the tracks of a deer that has run up onto a rock plateau sees the tracks on this side and that side of the rock. Even though he does not see them in the middle, he knows by way of inference: "It ascended here, it descended there; it must have passed through this area on the rock plateau in the middle." Similarly, the arising of pleasant feeling is obvious like the tracks at the place of ascent. The arising of painful feeling is obvious like the tracks at the place of descent. Just as the inference is made that "it ascended here, descended there, and went thus in the middle," neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling becomes clear to one who grasps it by way of the neutral mode, rejecting the agreeable and disagreeable when pleasant and painful feelings have subsided. In this way, the Blessed One first taught the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) and afterwards showed the meditation subject of immateriality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by bringing it forth through the power of feeling.

Not only here did He show it thus, but also in many suttas of various meanings such as the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, Āneñjasappāya Sutta, and in the Dīgha Nikāya: the Mahānidāna Sutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta; in the Saṃyutta Nikāya: the Cūḷanidāna Sutta, Rukkūpama Sutta, Parivīmaṃsana Sutta, and the entire Vedanā Saṃyutta. In these various suttas, He first taught the meditation subject of materiality and afterwards showed the meditation subject of immateriality by bringing it forth through the power of feeling. Just as in those suttas, in this Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta as well, He first taught the meditation subject of materiality and afterwards showed the meditation subject of immateriality by bringing it forth through the power of feeling.

Therein, among the words "a pleasant feeling" (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ) and so forth, this is another method of understanding: "He understands: I feel a pleasant feeling." This means that at the moment of pleasant feeling, because painful feeling is absent, one who is experiencing a pleasant feeling understands, "I feel a pleasant feeling." By such understanding, because the painful feeling previously experienced is now absent, and because this pleasant feeling, prior to this...
283:
...was absent, feeling is called impermanent (anicca), unstable, and subject to change. Thus, one becomes one who clearly understands that feeling in due order.

The Blessed One also said this:

"Aggivessana, at the time when one feels a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a painful feeling, nor does one feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one feels only a pleasant feeling. Aggivessana, at the time when one feels a painful feeling... (p) ...a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a pleasant feeling, nor does one feel a painful feeling; at that time one feels only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Aggivessana, pleasant feeling is also impermanent, conditioned (saṅkhata), dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna), subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Painful feeling is also... (p) ...Aggivessana, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is also impermanent... (p) ...subject to cessation. Aggivessana, seeing thus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, disenchanted with painful feeling, and disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state to come'" (M. Ni. 2.205).

In the phrases "or a carnal pleasant [feeling]" (sāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ) and so forth: carnal pleasant feelings (sāmisa-sukha-vedanā) are the six types of joy based on the household life (gehasita-somanassa) which depend on the five cords of sensual pleasure. Spiritual pleasant feelings (nirāmisa-sukha-vedanā) are the six types of joy based on renunciation (nekkhammasita-somanassa). Carnal painful feelings are the six types of grief based on the household life (gehasita-domanassa). Spiritual painful feelings are the six types of grief based on renunciation (nekkhammasita-domanassa). Carnal neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are the six types of equanimity based on the household life (gehasita-upekkhā). Spiritual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are the six types of equanimity based on renunciation (nekkhammasita-upekkhā). The classification of these feelings has already appeared in the text of the Uparipaṇṇāsa.

"Thus internally" (iti ajjhattaṃ vā) means that by defining pleasant feelings and so forth in this way, one dwells contemplating feelings in one's own feelings, or in the feelings of others, or at times in one's own and at times in the feelings of others. In the phrase "or contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing" (samudayavayadhammānupassī vā), one dwells contemplating the nature of arising by seeing the arising and vanishing of feelings through five modes each, such as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling"...
284:
Or he dwells in feelings; or he dwells in feelings contemplating the nature of vanishing; or he dwells in feelings contemplating sometimes the nature of arising and sometimes the nature of vanishing—thus it should be understood. From here on, it is the same method as described in the Contemplation of the Body (Kāyānupassanā).

In truth, in this Contemplation of Feeling, the mindfulness that grasps feeling is the Truth of Suffering (Dukkha Sacca). By making this connection, the path of exit for the monk who grasps feeling should be understood. The rest is the same.

## The Contemplation of Feeling is finished.

## Explanation of the Contemplation of Mind

Having taught the Contemplation of Feeling (Vedanānupassanā) in nine ways, he now speaks the words beginning with "And how, bhikkhus" to teach the Contemplation of Mind (Cittānupassanā) in sixteen ways. In those words, "mind with lust" (sarāgaṃ) refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. "Mind without lust" (vītarāgaṃ) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate (avyākata) consciousness. However, because this Contemplation of Mind is only an investigation (sammasana) and not a synthesis of dhammas (dhamma-samodhāna), not even a single supramundane (lokuttara) consciousness is obtained here. The remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses belong neither to the former term nor to the latter term.

"Mind with hate" (sadosaṃ) refers to the two types of consciousness accompanied by hate. "Mind without hate" (vītadosaṃ) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses belong neither to the former term nor to the latter term. "Mind with delusion" (samohaṃ) refers to two types: consciousness accompanied by doubt (vicikicchā) and consciousness accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca). However, since delusion arises in all unwholesome states, all those unwholesome consciousnesses are also included here. Indeed, in this very dyad, all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are fully included. "Mind without delusion" (vītamohaṃ) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. "Contracted mind" (saṅkhittaṃ) refers to mind fallen into sloth and torpor (thina-middha); this is called a shrunken mind. "Distracted mind" (vikkhittaṃ) refers to mind accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca); this is called a scattered mind.

"Exalted mind" (mahaggataṃ) refers to fine-material sphere and immaterial sphere consciousness. "Unexalted mind" (amahaggataṃ) refers to sense-sphere consciousness. "Surpassable mind" (sauttaraṃ) refers to sense-sphere consciousness. "Unsurpassable mind" (anuttaraṃ) refers to fine-material sphere and immaterial sphere consciousness. Even among those two, the fine-material sphere is surpassable, and only the immaterial sphere is unsurpassable. "Concentrated mind" (samāhitaṃ) refers to a mind that has either absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). "Unconcentrated mind" (asamāhitaṃ) refers to a mind devoid of both types of concentration. "Liberated mind" (vimuttaṃ) refers to a mind liberated through temporary liberation (tadaṅga-vimutti) or liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti). "Unliberated mind" (avimuttaṃ) refers to a mind devoid of both types of liberation. As for liberation by eradication (samuccheda), tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi), and escape (nissaraṇa), there is no occasion for them here.
285:
Thus, internally... by grasping the mind with lust and so forth, at whatever moment whatever mind arises, noting that mind, he dwells contemplating the mind in his own mind, or in another's mind, or sometimes in his own and sometimes in another's. In the phrase "contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing" (samudayawayadhammānupassī), the arising and vanishing of consciousness should be extracted through five aspects, such as "with the arising of ignorance, consciousness arises." From here on, it is the same method as previously described.

In truth, in this Contemplation of Mind, the mindfulness that grasps the mind is called the Truth of Suffering. By making this connection, the path of exit from the round of suffering for the monk who grasps the mind should be understood. The rest of the text is the same.

## The Explanation of the Contemplation of Mind is finished.
## Explanation of the Contemplation of Phenomena: Section on the Hindrances

Having taught the Contemplation of Mind in sixteen ways, he now speaks the words beginning with "And how, bhikkhus" to teach the Contemplation of Phenomena (Dhammānupassanā) in five ways. Alternatively, the Blessed One taught the grasping of pure matter (rūpa) through the Contemplation of the Body. He taught the grasping of pure mentality (nāma) through the Contemplation of Feeling and the Contemplation of Mind. Now, to teach the grasping of a mixture of matter and mentality, he says "And how, bhikkhus" and so forth. Or, he taught only the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) through the Contemplation of the Body; only the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) through the Contemplation of Feeling; and only the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) through the Contemplation of Mind. Now, to also teach the grasping of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), he says "And how, bhikkhus" and so forth.

In that text, "present" (santaṃ) means existing by way of frequent occurrence. "Absent" (asantaṃ) means not existing, either because of non-occurrence or because of having been abandoned. "And how" (yathā ca) means he knows the reason why sensual desire (kāmacchanda) arises. In this manner, the meaning in all terms should be understood.

That sensual desire arises due to unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) toward a beautiful object (subha-nimitta). "Beautiful object" (subha-nimitta) refers to either a beautiful appearance or a beautiful object of sense. "Unwise attention" (ayoniso manasikāra) refers to attention that is not the right means, attention on the wrong path, such as taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, or the non-self as self, or—
286:
Attention to the unattractive as beautiful, and the frequent occurrence of such attention towards that object, gives rise to sensual desire. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is the sign of the beautiful (subha-nimitta); frequent unwise attention therein is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and abundance of arisen sensual desire."

However, through wise attention to the sign of the unattractive (asubha-nimitta), that sensual desire is abandoned. The sign of the unattractive refers to both the unattractive itself and the object of the unattractive. Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) means attention by way of means, attention in the right way, or attention to the impermanent as impermanent, the suffering as suffering, the non-self as non-self, or the unattractive as unattractive. To one who frequently applies such attention to that object, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is the sign of the unattractive; frequent wise attention therein is the non-nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the abandonment of arisen sensual desire."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of sensual desire: learning the sign of the unattractive, devotion to the meditation on the unattractive, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, noble friendship, and suitable talk. For one who learns the ten kinds of unattractive signs, for one who develops them, for one who has the doors of the sense faculties closed, and for one who is moderate in eating by having the habit of drinking water to sustain oneself when there is space for four or five mouthfuls of food remaining, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore, it is said:

"When there is space for four or five mouthfuls remaining,
One should drink water instead of eating;
This is sufficient for the comfortable living
Of a bhikkhu who is resolute."

Sensual desire is also abandoned for one who associates with noble friends who delight in the meditation on the unattractive, such as the Elder Tissa who practiced the unattractive meditation, and through suitable talk related to the ten kinds of unattractive things while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of sensual desire." He understands that sensual desire abandoned by these six things will not arise again in the future through the Path of Arahantship.

Through unwise attention to the sign of irritation (paṭigha-nimitta), ill-will (byāpāda) arises. In this context, irritation itself is the sign of irritation, and the object of irritation is also the sign of irritation. Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) has the same single characteristic in all instances. To one who frequently applies that unwise attention to that sign...
287:
...to one who brings about (unwise attention to the sign of irritation), ill-will arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is the sign of irritation; frequent unwise attention therein is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill-will, and for the growth and abundance of arisen ill-will."

Through wise attention to the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti), that ill-will is abandoned. In that context, when "loving-kindness" (mettā) is mentioned, both absorption (appanā) and access (upacāra) are applicable. However, when "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti) is mentioned, only absorption is applicable. Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) has the characteristic already described. To one who frequently applies that attention to that liberation of mind through loving-kindness, ill-will is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness; frequent wise attention therein is the non-nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen ill-will, and for the abandonment of arisen ill-will."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of ill-will: learning the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the meditation on loving-kindness, reflection on the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā), abundance of reflection, noble friendship, and suitable talk. Ill-will is abandoned for one who learns loving-kindness by way of any of the methods: specified pervasion (odhissaka), unspecified pervasion (anodhissaka), or pervasion by direction (disā-pharaṇa), and for one who develops the meditation on loving-kindness through those methods. 

Reflection on the ownership of kamma for oneself and others is as follows: "What will you do by being angry with this person? Will you be able to destroy his virtue and so on? Have you not come here by your own kamma and will you not depart by your own kamma? Being angry with another is like wanting to hit another after picking up glowing coals, a heated iron rod, or excrement. What will this person do by being angry with you? Will he be able to destroy your virtue and so on? He has come by his own kamma and will depart by his own kamma; like a gift that is not accepted, or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger of his will fall back upon his own head."

Ill-will is abandoned for one who reflects on the ownership of kamma in this way, for one who stands firm in reflection after considering the ownership of kamma of both parties, for one who associates with noble friends who delight in the meditation on loving-kindness like the Elder Assagutta, and through suitable talk related to loving-kindness while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of ill-will." He understands that ill-will abandoned by these six things will not arise again in the future through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga).
288:
Due to unwise attention toward discontent and so forth, sloth and torpor (thina-middha) arise. Discontent (arati) means being weary or dissatisfied. Laziness (tandī) means physical sluggishness. Stretching (vijambhitā) means the bending or twisting of the body in various ways (yawning and stretching). Food-drunkenness (bhattasammada) means the confusion or distress caused by food. Sluggishness of mind (cetaso līnatta) means the state of the mind being withdrawn or limp. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to these things such as discontent, sloth and torpor arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there are discontent, laziness, stretching, food-drunkenness, and sluggishness of mind; frequently applying unwise attention therein is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the growth and increase of arisen sloth and torpor."

However, the abandonment of that sloth and torpor occurs through wise attention toward the element of arousal and so forth. The element of arousal (ārambha-dhātu) is the energy (vīriya) characterized by the initial effort. The element of exertion (nikkama-dhātu) is energy stronger than the element of arousal because it has emerged from indolence. The element of striving (parakkama-dhātu) is energy even stronger than the element of exertion because it advances to successive stages. For one who frequently applies wise attention to this threefold energy, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there are the element of arousal, the element of exertion, and the element of striving; frequently applying wise attention therein is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the abandonment of arisen sloth and torpor."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of sloth and torpor: perceiving the cause of sloth and torpor in overeating, changing the postures, attending to the perception of light, living in the open air, having noble friends, and suitable conversation. For one who has eaten excessively—such as the 'hand-feeder' (āharahatthaka), 'staying-until-finished' (tatravaṭṭaka), 'clothing-unfitter' (alaṃsāṭaka), 'crow-swallower' (kākamāsaka), or 'vomit-eater' (bhuttavami-taka) styles of gluttony—and sits to practice the recluse's Dhamma by night or by day, sloth and torpor come overwhelming him like a great elephant. But for a bhikkhu who has the habit of moderation, stopping when there is space for four or five more morsels and drinking water instead, that sloth and torpor does not occur. Thus, for one who perceives the cause in overeating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. For one who changes to another posture from the one in which sloth and torpor descended; for one who attends to the light of the moon, lamps, or torches at night, or the light of the sun by day; for one who lives in the open air; and for one who associates with noble friends like the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera who have abandoned sloth and torpor—for such a person, sloth and torpor are abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable conversation connected to the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) while standing or sitting. Therefore, it is said: "Six things [lead to the abandonment] of sloth and torpor..."
289:
"...lead to the abandonment" (it is said). He understands that sloth and torpor, abandoned by these six things, will not arise again in the future through the Path of Arahantship.

Restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) arise due to unwise attention to the unpeacefulness of mind. Unpeacefulness (avūpasama) means the state of being unpeaceful. In terms of ultimate reality, this unpeaceful state is restlessness and remorse itself. For a person who frequently applies unwise attention to that unpeacefulness of mind, restlessness and remorse arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is unpeacefulness of mind. Frequently applying unwise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the growth and abundance of arisen restlessness and remorse."

However, the abandonment of restlessness and remorse occurs through wise attention to the peace of mind known as concentration (samādhi). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is peace of mind. Frequently applying wise attention to that is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the abandonment of arisen restlessness and remorse."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse: great learning, inquiry, knowledge of the disciplinary rules (Vinaya), associating with elders, good friendship, and suitable talk. Through great learning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned for one who learns one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas both in terms of the Pali text and the meaning. They are also abandoned for one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and unallowable (kappiyākappiya); for one who is knowledgeable (pakataññū) through mastery of the Vinaya injunctions; for one who approaches senior elders; and for one who associates with good friends who are experts in the Vinaya, such as the Elder Upāli. Restlessness and remorse are also abandoned by suitable talk concerning what is allowable and unallowable while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse." He understands that when restlessness and remorse are abandoned by these six things, restlessness will not arise again in the future through the Path of Arahantship, and remorse will not arise again through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga).

Doubt (vicikicchā) arises due to unwise attention to things that are grounds for doubt. Things that are grounds for doubt are doubt itself, because they are the cause of repeated doubt. For a person who frequently applies unwise attention to those things, doubt arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are things that are grounds for doubt..."
290:
...phenomena exist; in those phenomena, there is the frequent practice of unwise attention. This cause, namely the frequent practice of unwise attention, leads to the arising of unarisen doubt, or to the increase and expansion of arisen doubt," thus it is said (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).

However, through wise attention to phenomena such as the wholesome and so forth, there is the abandoning of that doubt. Therefore, He said: "Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, blameable and blameless phenomena, phenomena to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, inferior and superior phenomena, and phenomena that are counterparts of the dark and the bright. In those phenomena, there is the frequent practice of wise attention. This cause, namely the frequent practice of wise attention, leads to the non-arising of unarisen doubt, or to the abandoning of arisen doubt."

In another way, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt: great learning, inquiry, understanding the nature of the Vinaya, abundance of resolution, good friendship, and suitable talk. Through great learning, doubt is abandoned for one who learns even one... or all five Nikāyas, both in terms of the text (Pāḷi) and the meaning. Doubt is also abandoned for one who is frequent in inquiry concerning the Triple Gem, for one who has achieved mastery through practice in the Vinaya, for one who is abundant in resolution characterized by confirming faith in the Triple Gem, and for one who associates with good friends such as the Elder Vakkali, who was foremost among those liberated by faith. Doubt is also abandoned by suitable talk based on the virtues of the Triple Gem during activities such as standing or sitting. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt." One understands that doubt abandoned by these six things will not arise again in the future through the Path of Stream-entry.

"Thus internally," and so forth, means that by thus defining the five hindrances, one dwells contemplating phenomena in one's own phenomena, or in the phenomena of others, or at times in one's own and at times in the phenomena of others. Here, the arising and vanishing should be extracted according to the method mentioned for the five hindrances by way of unwise attention and wise attention regarding the sign of the beautiful (subhanimitta), the sign of the foul (asubhanimitta), and so forth. What follows is according to the method already mentioned.

Indeed, in this context, it should be understood that the mindfulness that defines the hindrances is the Truth of Suffering; by making such a connection, the door to liberation for the bhikkhu who defines the hindrances is known. The rest of the sequence of words is just the same as the method already mentioned.

## The Explanation of the Section on Hindrances is Finished.
291:
## Explanation of the Section on Aggregates
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the five hindrances, He now said "Again, and further," and so forth, to analyze it by way of the five aggregates. There, "in the five aggregates of clinging" (pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu) means in the aggregates of clinging; it refers to the groups of phenomena or heaps of phenomena that are the causes of clinging. This is the summary here. The detailed discourse on the aggregates is stated in the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus is form" means one understands form according to its nature as: "This is form, this much is form, there is no form beyond this." The same method applies to feeling and the others. This is the summary here. In detail, form and the others are stated in the discourse on the aggregates in the Visuddhimagga itself.

"Thus is the arising of form" means the arising of form in five ways by way of the arising of ignorance and so forth. "Thus is the vanishing of form" means the vanishing of form in five ways by way of the cessation of ignorance and so forth. The same method applies to feeling and the others. This is the summary. The detail is stated in the discourse on the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away (udayabbayañāṇa) in the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus internally," and so forth, means that by thus defining the five aggregates, one dwells contemplating phenomena in one's own phenomena, or in the phenomena of others, or at times in one's own and at times in the phenomena of others. Here, the arising and vanishing (samudaya-vaya) should be extracted by way of the fifty characteristics mentioned regarding the five aggregates, such as "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form."

Indeed, in this section on aggregates, it should be understood that the mindfulness that defines the aggregates is the Truth of Suffering; by making such a connection, the cause of the exit through the Path for the bhikkhu who defines the aggregates is known. The remaining words are just the same as those (in the section on hindrances) mentioned before.

## The Explanation of the Section on Aggregates is Finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Sense Bases
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the five aggregates, He now said "Again, and further," and so forth, to analyze it by way of the sense bases. There, "in the six internal and external sense bases" means in these six internal bases: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and in these [six external bases]: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects...
292:
Regarding the six external sense bases: 'He knows the eye' means he knows the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) as it really is, by way of its own function and characteristic. 'He knows forms' means he knows the external forms produced by the four causes as they really are, by way of their own function and characteristic. The fetter that arises dependent on both the eye and forms refers to the ten types of fetters: the fetter of sensual desire (kāmarāga-saṃyojana), aversion (paṭigha), conceit (māna), views (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rules and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa), desire for existence (bhavarāga), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), and ignorance (avijjā). He knows these fetters as they really are, by way of their own function and characteristic.

How does this fetter arise? Firstly, for one who enjoys and delights in a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) that has come into range at the eye-door by way of sensual gratification, the fetter of sensual desire arises. For one who is angry at an undesirable object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa), the fetter of aversion arises. For one who thinks, "Apart from me, no one else is able to make this object clear," the fetter of conceit arises. For one who grasps, "This form-object is permanent and stable," the fetter of views arises. For one who doubts, "Is this form-object a being, or does it belong to a being?" the fetter of doubt arises. For one who longs for existence, thinking, "May we easily obtain this in a prosperous life," the fetter of desire for existence arises. For one who undertakes rules and rituals, thinking, "In the future, one can obtain such an object by undertaking this kind of virtue and practice," the fetter of adherence to rules and rituals arises. For one who is envious, thinking, "May others not get this form-object," the fetter of envy arises. For one who is stingy and does not wish to give the form-object he has obtained to another, the fetter of stinginess arises. Through the power of non-knowing (aññāṇa) that is co-nascent with all these, the fetter of ignorance arises.

'The unarisen fetter' means he knows the cause by which those ten fetters, which have not yet arisen (by way of active manifestation/samudācāra), come to arise. 'The arisen fetter' means he knows the cause by which those ten fetters, which have arisen either because they have not been abandoned or by way of active manifestation, come to be abandoned. 'The abandoned fetter' means he knows the cause by which those ten fetters, which have been abandoned by way of temporary abandonment (tadaṅga-pahāna) or abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), do not arise in the future. By what cause do they not arise in the future? Firstly, for the five types of fetters consisting of views, doubt, adherence to rules and rituals, envy, and stinginess...
294:
The term 'non-existent' (asanta) means not being present in one's own continuity by way of non-attainment. Regarding the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (sati-sambojjhaṅga) in the Pali text beginning with 'unrisen,' it is as follows: "Monks, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unrisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of its development when it has arisen." Therein, mindfulness itself is the thing that is the basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) has the characteristics already mentioned; for one who frequently applies it to those things of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises.

Furthermore, four things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and being inclined towards that enlightenment factor. The enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven instances such as going forward; through avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness who are like crows dropping food; through associating with persons of established mindfulness like Elder Tissadatta and Elder Abhaya; and through having a mind inclined towards establishing mindfulness in postures such as standing and sitting. It should be understood that this enlightenment factor of mindfulness, having arisen through these four causes, reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga): "Monks, there are wholesome and unwholesome states... states that have dark and bright counterparts; frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unrisen enlightenment factor of investigation of states, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of its development when it has arisen." Thus it arises as taught.

Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states: inquiring, making the objects clean, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reflecting on the range of profound knowledge, and being inclined towards that enlightenment factor. Therein, 'inquiring' (paripucchakatā) means the abundance of inquiry concerning the meaning of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), faculties (indriya), powers (bala), enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga), path factors (maggaṅga), jhāna factors (jhānaṅga), serenity (samatha), and insight (vipassanā).

'Making the objects clean' (vatthu-visadakiriyā) means making the internal and external objects clean and pure. If one's hair, nails, and body hair are too long, or if the body is smeared with sweat and dirt and is filthy, then the internal object is not clean.
295:
It is not pure. When the robes are worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling, or when the monastery and lodgings are littered and dirty, then the external object is not clean and pure. Therefore, the internal object should be made clean by shaving the hair and so on, by making the body light through emetics and purgatives, and by anointing and bathing. The external object should be made clean by sewing, washing, dyeing, and bordering [the robes], and so on.

Indeed, if these internal and external objects are not clean, the knowledge in the arising consciousness and mental factors is also not pure, like the light of a lamp flame that arises depending on an impure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. But if the internal and external objects are clean, the knowledge in the arising consciousness and mental factors is also clean and pure, like the light of a lamp flame that arises depending on a pure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. Therefore, it was said: "Making the objects clean leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states."

'Balancing the faculties' (indriya-samatta-paṭipādanā) means making the faculties such as faith and so on equal to one another in their functions, without deficiency or excess. If the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is too strong for that practitioner and the other faculties are weak, then the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) cannot perform the function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) cannot perform the function of establishing [on the object], the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) cannot perform the function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) cannot perform the function of seeing. Therefore, that faculty of faith should be diminished either by reflecting on the nature of things or by not attending to it in the way that caused it to become strong. The story of Elder Vakkali is an illustration here. If the faculty of energy is too strong, then the faculty of faith cannot perform the function of decision, nor can the other faculties perform their respective functions. Therefore, that faculty of energy should be diminished by developing tranquility (passaddhi) and so on. In that case, the story of Elder Soṇa should be shown. Thus, it should be understood that if any one of the remaining faculties is too strong, the others are unable to perform their functions.

Particularly here, they praise the equality of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy. For one with strong faith but weak wisdom is blindly confident; he is confident in things that are not worthy of confidence. One with strong wisdom but weak faith tends towards the side of craftiness. Like a disease caused by medicine, he becomes incurable. Thinking "merit occurs just by the arising of a thought," he overreaches and does not perform acts of giving and so on, and is liable to be reborn in hell. Only when the two are equal is he confident in what is worthy of confidence. If concentration is strong and energy is weak, because concentration tends towards laziness, laziness overcomes him. If energy is strong and concentration is weak, energy...
296:
Because energy has the quality of agitation (if energy is stronger than concentration), agitation tends to overwhelm. If concentration is coupled with energy, one cannot fall into laziness. If energy is coupled with concentration, one cannot fall into agitation. Therefore, both should be balanced. Only when both are balanced can attainment (appanā) occur.

Furthermore, for one practicing serenity (samatha), strong faith (saddhā) is also appropriate. Only by having such faith and conviction can one reach attainment. Between concentration and wisdom, for one practicing serenity, strong one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is appropriate; in this way, one reaches attainment. For one practicing insight (vipassanā), strong wisdom is appropriate; in this way, one can penetrate the three characteristics. However, even when both are balanced, attainment indeed occurs. Mindfulness (sati), however, is appropriate in all places as it should be strong.
