This is because mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation through the power of faith, energy, and wisdom, which are on the side of agitation; and from falling into laziness through the power of concentration, which is on the side of laziness. Therefore, mindfulness is desired in all places, like salt in all dishes, or like a chief minister in all royal affairs. Thus, the Blessed One said: "Mindfulness is said to be useful in all places. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, mindfulness is manifested as protection, and without mindfulness, there can be no exertion or restraint of the mind."

Avoiding unwise persons means avoiding from afar those foolish people who lack the wisdom to penetrate the divisions of the aggregates (khandha) and so on. Associating with wise persons means associating with those endowed with wisdom that perceives the characteristics and the wisdom of rise and fall (udayabbaya). Reflecting on the sphere of deep knowledge means reflecting on the distinctions of deep wisdom occurring in the deep aggregates and so on. Inclination towards that Dhamma means having a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined towards the arising of the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga) while standing, sitting, etc. One knows that for such a person, the fulfillment of development occurs through the path of arahantship (arahattamagga).

The arising of the factor of enlightenment of energy is as follows: "Monks, there is the element of arousal (ārabhadhātu), the element of endeavor (nikkamadhātu), and the element of exertion (parakkamadhātu). Frequent wise attention to these leads to the arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment of energy, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen factor of enlightenment of energy."
297:
Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the factor of enlightenment of energy: (1) reflecting on the fear of the woeful planes, (2) seeing the benefits, (3) reflecting on the path to be traveled, (4) honoring the almsfood, (5) reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, (6) reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, (7) reflecting on the greatness of birth, (8) reflecting on the greatness of fellow practitioners, (9) avoiding lazy persons, (10) associating with energetic persons, and (11) having a mind inclined towards that energy.

Among those eleven, when experiencing great suffering in hells starting from the fivefold binding and torture; or when being captured by nets, traps, etc., in the animal realm; or when being beaten and prodded with goads and spikes to pull carts, etc.; or when being afflicted by hunger and thirst for many thousands of years, even for the interval between two Buddhas, in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta); or when experiencing suffering from wind, heat, etc., with a body sixty or eighty cubits high consisting only of bone and skin among the Kālakañjika asuras—at such times, it is not possible to arouse the factor of enlightenment of energy. "O monk, now is the only time for you to exert energy." Thus, for one reflecting on the fear of the woeful planes, the factor of enlightenment of energy arises.

"A lazy person is unable to attain the nine supramundane states; only an energetic person can. This is the benefit of energy." Thus, for one seeing the benefits, the factor of enlightenment of energy arises. "You must travel the path taken by all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples; a lazy person is unable to travel that path." Thus, for one reflecting on the path to be traveled, the factor of enlightenment of energy arises. "Those people who serve you with almsfood and so on are not your relatives, nor are they your slaves or servants. They do not give these excellent alms thinking, 'We shall live depending on you.' Rather, they give expecting the great fruit of their own deeds. Even the Teacher did not allow these requisites for you thinking, 'This person will live happily with a strong body by using these requisites.' Rather, he allowed them thinking, 'This person, while using these requisites, will practice the recluse's Dhamma and be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha).' If you now live lazily, you do not honor that almsfood. Only the use of almsfood by an energetic person is called honoring the almsfood." Thus, for one reflecting on honoring the almsfood like the Elder Mahāmitta, the factor of enlightenment of energy arises.
298:
The Elder, it is said, resided in the Kassaka Cave. In his alms-resort village, a certain great laywoman looked after the Elder, treating him like a son. One day, as she was about to go to the forest, she said to her daughter: "Dear daughter, in such a place there is old rice, in such a place milk, in such a place ghee, and in such a place molasses. When your brother, the Venerable Ayyamitta, arrives, cook the rice and offer it to him along with the milk, ghee, and molasses. You should also eat. As for me, I have already eaten yesterday's leftover rice with sour gruel."

The daughter asked, "Mother, what will you eat for lunch?" She replied, "Put some leaves in and cook a sour congee with broken rice grains, and keep it for me."

The Elder, while putting on his robe and taking out his bowl from its bag, heard those words and admonished himself: "The great laywoman ate leftover rice with sour gruel, and for lunch, she will eat sour congee made of broken rice and leaves. For your sake, however, she gave instructions for old rice and so on. This laywoman, depending on you, does not hope for fields, property, food, or clothing, but gives while aspiring for the three types of prosperity. Will you be able to give her those prosperities or not? This alms-food should not be accepted by you while you are with lust, hatred, and delusion."

Reflecting thus, he put the bowl back into the bag, untied the strap, and returned to the Kassaka Cave. Then, placing the bowl under the couch and the robe on the robe-rack, he made a firm determination of energy: "I will not go out until I have attained Arahantship," and sat down. That monk, who had lived heedfully for a long time, developed insight and attained Arahantship even before the mealtime. Like a blooming lotus, the great Khīṇāsava (Arahant) Elder, with a smiling face, emerged from the cave. A deity dwelling in a tree at the cave entrance uttered this inspired exclamation:

"Homage to you, O noble man! Homage to you, O supreme man!
Who has exhausted the taints, you are worthy of offerings, dear sir."

Furthermore, the deity said, "Venerable sir, by giving alms to Arahants like you, this old woman will be released from suffering."

The Elder rose, opened the door, and looking at the time, realized it was still early morning. Taking his bowl and robe, he entered the village. The young girl, having prepared the meal, sat looking out the door, thinking, "Now my brother will come, now he will come." When the Elder reached the house door, the girl took the bowl, filled it with milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, and offered it into his hands. The Elder said, "May you be happy," gave the blessing, and departed. That young girl also...
299:
...stood watching (the Elder). Indeed, at that time, the Elder's complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were especially clear, and his face was as beautiful as a ripe palm fruit released from its stalk. The great laywoman returned from the forest and asked, "Dear daughter, did your brother come?" The girl reported the whole matter. The laywoman, realizing "Today my son's task of monkhood has reached its pinnacle," said, "Dear daughter, your brother delights in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is not weary of it."

"The so-called seven noble wealths are the heritage of the Buddha, and this heritage is very great. A lazy person is not able to take that heritage. Just as parents might cast out a wayward son, saying 'This is not our son,' and he does not receive the inheritance after their death; in the same way, a lazy person cannot receive this heritage of noble wealth. Only one who has aroused energy can receive it." Thus, (the enlightenment factor of energy) arises in one who reflects on the greatness of the heritage.

"Your teacher, the Buddha, is truly great. Indeed, when your teacher was conceived in his mother's womb, when he renounced the world, when he attained Buddhahood by realizing the Four Noble Truths, when he turned the Wheel of Dhamma, when he performed the Twin Miracle, when he descended from the deva realm, when he relinquished the life-force, and when he attained Parinibbāna, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. Is it proper for you to be lazy after ordaining in the Dispensation of such a Teacher?" Thus, (the enlightenment factor of energy) arises in one who reflects on the greatness of the Teacher.

By way of birth: "You are not of low birth now. You come from the unbroken lineage of Mahāsammata. You are born in the Okkāka royal dynasty. You are the grandson of King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of Venerable Rāhula. Being such a Son of the Conqueror (Jinaputta), it is not proper for you to live lazily." Thus, (the enlightenment factor of energy) arises in one who reflects on the greatness of birth.

"Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Moggallāna, and the eighty great disciples realized the supramundane Dhamma only through energy. Will you follow the path of these fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) or not?" Thus, (the enlightenment factor of energy) arises in one who reflects on the greatness of fellow practitioners.

It also arises by avoiding lazy persons who are like pythons that have filled their bellies and lie still, lacking physical and mental energy; by associating with persons who have aroused energy and are resolute; and by having a mind inclined, leaning, and slanting towards arousing energy in postures such as standing and sitting. He understands that the enlightenment factor of energy thus arisen reaches fulfillment in development through the Path of Arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of joy (pīti-sambojjhaṅga): "Bhikkhus, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy. Frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of joy..."
300:
“Monks, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture (pītisambojjhaṅga). Frequently giving wise attention to those things is the cause for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture, and for the further growth, increase, and fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture.” Thus, as taught in the Saṃyutta Nikāya (5.232), the enlightenment factor of rapture arises. Among those things, rapture itself is called the thing that is the basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture. The attention that produces that rapture is called wise attention (yoniso manasikāra).

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture: the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), the recollection of the Dhamma (dhammānussati), the recollection of the Saṅgha (saṅghānussati), the recollection of one's own virtue (sīlānussati), the recollection of one's own generosity (cāgānussati), the recollection of deities as witnesses to one's own virtues (devatānussati), the recollection of the peace of Nibbāna (upasamānussati), avoiding coarse persons, associating with refined and gentle persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses (suttantas), and inclining the mind toward that rapture.

For one who recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of rapture arises, pervading the entire body up to the level of access concentration (upacāra samādhi). It also arises for one who recollects the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha; for a monk who reflects on the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) which has been kept unbroken for a long time; for a layperson who reflects on the ten precepts or five precepts; for a monk who, in times of danger such as famine, gives excellent food to his fellow practitioners and reflects on his generosity, thinking, “We have given such a gift”; for a layperson who reflects on the gifts given to virtuous ones at such times; for one who reflects on the existence within oneself of such qualities by which deities reached the state of devas; for one who reflects, “The defilements abandoned through attainment (samāpatti) have not occurred for sixty or seventy years”; for one who avoids coarse persons who are like dust on a donkey's back, who show clear coarseness by acting disrespectfully when visiting a stūpa, a Bodhi tree, or an elder monk, and who lack devotion and affection for the Buddha and so forth; for one who associates with refined persons who have a gentle mind and much devotion to the Buddha and so forth; for one who reflects on inspiring discourses that explain the qualities of the Triple Gem; and for one who has a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined toward the production of rapture while standing, sitting, and so forth. He knows that this arisen enlightenment factor of rapture reaches fulfillment of development through the path of Arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhisambojjhaṅga): “Monks, there are tranquility of body (kāyapassaddhi) and tranquility of mind (cittapassaddhi). Frequently giving wise attention to them is the cause for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, and for the further growth, increase, and fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.” Thus it arises. Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility: using superior food, using a comfortable climate, using a comfortable posture...
301:
...having equanimous application (majjhattapayogatā), avoiding persons with restless bodies, associating with persons with tranquil bodies, and having a mind inclined toward that tranquility.

Indeed, tranquility arises for one who partakes of superior, smooth, and suitable food; and for one who makes use of a suitable climate and suitable postures among the various climates of cold and heat and postures such as standing. This is not said with reference to a person of the nature of a Great Man (mahāpurisajātika) who can endure all climates and postures. For one who has preferences and aversions (regarding climate and posture), tranquility arises when avoiding unsuitable climates and postures and using suitable ones. Equanimous application (majjhattapayoga) is the reflection on the ownership of one's own and others' kamma (kammassakatā); through this equanimous application, tranquility arises. It also arises for one who avoids a person with a restless body who wanders about harming others with clods of earth, sticks, and the like; for one who associates with a person with a tranquil body whose hands and feet are restrained; and for one who has a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined toward the production of tranquility while standing, sitting, and so forth. He knows that for this arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, there is fulfillment of development through the path of Arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of concentration (samādhisambojjhaṅga): “Monks, there are the sign of serenity (samathanimitta) and the sign of non-distraction (abyagganimitta). Frequently giving wise attention to them is the cause for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, and for the further growth, increase, and fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.” Thus it arises. In that context, serenity itself is the sign of serenity, and it is called the sign of non-distraction in the sense of being undistracted.

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration: making the physical basis clean (vatthuvisadakiriyatā), balancing the faculties (indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā), skill in the sign (nimittakusalatā), uplifting the mind at the right time, restraining the mind at the right time, gladdening the mind at the right time, looking on with equanimity at the right time, avoiding unconcentrated persons, associating with concentrated persons, reflecting on the jhānas and liberations (vimokkha), and having a mind inclined toward that concentration. Among these, making the physical basis clean and balancing the faculties should be understood in the manner already stated.

Skill in the sign (nimittakusalatā) means skill in grasping the sign of a kasiṇa. Uplifting the mind at the right time means uplifting the mind by bringing about the enlightenment factors of investigation of states (dhammavicaya), energy (vīriya), and rapture (pīti) at the time when the mind is sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth. Restraining the mind at the right time means at the time when...
302:
## 
Due to factors such as excessively exerted energy, the mind becomes restless. At that time, that restless mind should be restrained by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. "Gladdening the mind at the proper time" means that at the time when the mind is devoid of delight, either due to weak application of wisdom or due to not attaining the bliss of peace, one should inspire that mind with a sense of urgency by reflecting on the eight grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu). The eight grounds for urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death (these four); the suffering of the states of loss as the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present. One should also generate confidence by repeatedly recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem. This practice is called "gladdening the mind at the proper time."

"Equanimity at the proper time" means that at the time when, through right practice, the mind is not sluggish, not restless, not devoid of delight, and proceeds evenly toward the object, having entered the path of serenity (samatha), one then does not take interest in encouraging, restraining, or gladdening that mind, just as a charioteer does not take interest in horses that are running evenly. This practice is called "equanimity at the proper time." "Avoiding persons who are not concentrated" means keeping far away from persons who have a distracted mind and have not attained either access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). "Associating with concentrated persons" means associating with, frequenting, and attending upon persons who have a mind concentrated through access or absorption concentration. "Being inclined toward that concentration" means having a mind that is inclining, leaning, and slanting only toward the arising of concentration in postures such as standing and sitting. For one who practices in this way, this concentration enlightenment factor arises. One understands that for the concentration enlightenment factor that has thus arisen, there is fulfillment of its development through the path of arahantship.

Regarding the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor: "Bhikkhus, there are things that are the basis for the equanimity enlightenment factor; frequently giving wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen equanimity enlightenment factor, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of the development of the arisen equanimity enlightenment factor." Thus it arises. Therein, equanimity itself is called the things that are the basis for the equanimity enlightenment factor.

Furthermore, five things lead to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor: neutrality toward beings (satta-majjhattatā), neutrality toward formations (saṅkhāra-majjhattatā), avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations, associating with persons who are neutral toward beings and formations, and being inclined toward that equanimity.

Among those, one arouses neutrality toward beings in two ways: "You have come by your own kamma and will depart by your own kamma; this person too, by his own kamma..."
303:
"...has come and will depart by his own kamma; whom are you attached to?" Thus, one arouses neutrality through the reflection on the ownership of one's own kamma (kammassakatā). Also, "In the ultimate sense, there is no being at all; so, whom are you attached to?" Thus, one arouses neutrality through the reflection on the absence of a being (nissatta). One arouses neutrality toward formations in two ways: "This robe will gradually reach a state of discolouration and wear, becoming a foot-wiping rag, and will be discarded at the end of a stick; if this robe had an owner, he would not allow it to perish in this way." Thus, one arouses neutrality through the reflection on the state of being ownerless (asāmika). Also, "This robe does not last long; it is only temporary." Thus, one arouses neutrality through the reflection on temporariness (tāvakālika). As with the robe, the same method should be applied to the bowl and other requisites.

In the phrase "avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations," the decision should be understood as follows: A certain person, whether a layperson or a monk, is attached to and fond of his own sons and daughters, or his own pupils and fellow disciples of the same preceptor, etc. For them, he himself performs tasks such as shaving their hair, sewing, washing and dyeing their robes, and firing their bowls. If he does not see them even for a moment, he looks here and there like a frightened deer, asking, "Where is such-and-such a novice? Where is such-and-such a young monk?" Even when requested by another for the purpose of shaving hair, etc., saying, "Please send such-and-such a person for a moment," he does not give them, saying, "We ourselves do not dare to make him do our own work; if you take him, he will be exhausted." Such a person is called one attached to beings (satta-kelāyana). Another person is attached to and fond of requisites such as the bowl, robe, cup, and walking stick, and does not even allow another to touch them with their hand. When asked for a temporary loan, he says, "We ourselves, being so fond of this, do not dare to use it; how can we give it to you?" Such a person is called one attached to formations (saṅkhāra-kelāyana). A person who is neutral and indifferent toward both these types of objects is called one neutral toward beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra-majjhatta). Thus, this equanimity enlightenment factor arises by avoiding far away such persons who are attached to beings and formations, by associating with persons who are neutral toward beings and formations, and by having a mind that is inclining, leaning, and slanting toward the arising of that equanimity enlightenment factor in postures such as standing and sitting. One understands that the equanimity enlightenment factor that has thus arisen reaches fulfillment of development through the path of arahantship.

"Thus internally..." means having thus grasped one's own seven enlightenment factors, or those of another, or at one time one's own and at another time another's enlightenment factors...
304:
Comprehending (the factors of enlightenment), he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. Furthermore, in this section on the factors of enlightenment (Bojjhaṅga-pabba), the arising and vanishing of the factors of enlightenment should be understood by way of their occurrence and cessation. The text following this is to be understood in the same manner as previously described.

To state the distinction: in this section on the factors of enlightenment, the mindfulness that comprehends the factors of enlightenment is called the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). Having made this connection, the way of deliverance from the round of rebirths for the bhikkhu who comprehends the factors of enlightenment should be understood. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Factors of Enlightenment is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Four Truths
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the seven factors of enlightenment, the Blessed One now says, "And again, further..." and so on, in order to analyze it by way of the Four Noble Truths.

In that passage, "he understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'" means that, setting aside craving (taṇhā), he understands the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence as they really are, in their specific nature, as "This collection of phenomena is the truth of suffering." He understands the preceding craving, which is the producer and originator of that very truth of suffering, as "This is the truth of the origin of suffering." He understands Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence of both (suffering and its origin), as "This is the truth of the cessation of suffering." He understands the Noble Path, which is the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of the origin, and the realization of cessation, as "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." This is the meaning of understanding according to the undistorted nature. The remaining discourse on the Noble Truths has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus, internally..." and so on means that he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, having comprehended either his own four truths, or another's four truths, or at times his own and at times another's four truths. In this section on the four truths, the arising and vanishing of the four truths should be understood by way of their occurrence and cessation as appropriate. The text following this is to be understood in the same manner as previously described.

Specifically, in this section on the four truths, the mindfulness that comprehends the four truths is called the truth of suffering. Having made this connection, the way of deliverance from the round of rebirths for the bhikkhu who comprehends the truths should be understood. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Four Truths is Finished.
305:
By this much, twenty-one meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) have been taught: mindfulness of breathing, the four postures, the four kinds of clear comprehension, the thirty-two parts of the body, the determination of the four elements, the nine charnel ground contemplations, the contemplation of feelings, the contemplation of mind, the comprehension of the hindrances, the comprehension of the aggregates, the comprehension of the sense bases, the comprehension of the factors of enlightenment, and the comprehension of the truths. Among these meditation subjects, eleven—mindfulness of breathing, the thirty-two parts of the body, and the nine charnel ground contemplations—are meditation subjects of absorption (appanā). However, the Elder Mahāsīva, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, says: "The nine charnel ground contemplations are taught by way of the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā)." Therefore, according to his view, there are only two absorption meditation subjects, while the rest are access (upacāra) meditation subjects.

Does adherence (abhinivesa) arise in all these meditation subjects? It does not. Adherence does not arise in the postures, clear comprehension, hindrances, and factors of enlightenment; it arises in the remaining meditation subjects. But the Elder Mahāsīva says: "Adherence arises in these as well. For one comprehends thus: 'Do I have the four postures or not? Do I have the four kinds of clear comprehension or not? Do I have the five hindrances or not? Do I have the seven factors of enlightenment or not?' Therefore, adherence arises in all meditation subjects."

"Monks, whoever..." refers to anyone, whether a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman. "Should develop in this way" means developing according to the sequence of meditation described from the beginning. "May expect" means it is to be expected; it means the result will certainly occur. "Final knowledge" (aññā) refers to the fruit of Arahatship. "If there is a trace of clinging left" means if the residue of grasping has not yet been fully exhausted. "Non-returning" (anāgāmitā) means the state of being an Anāgāmī.

Having thus shown the state of the Dispensation as leading to deliverance by way of seven years, the Blessed One said, "Let alone seven years, monks..." and so on, wishing to show a shorter period of time. All this is spoken by way of the person to be led (neyya-puggala) of middle capacity. However, with reference to a person of quick understanding (tikkha-pañña), it is said: "Instructed in the morning, he will attain distinction in the evening; instructed in the evening, he will attain distinction in the morning."
307:
## 2. Sīhanādavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta

"Thus have I heard" and so forth—this is the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta. Since there is an occasion for its origin (atthuppatti), I shall first present that occasion and then provide the word-by-word commentary in due order. For what reason was this sutta taught? It was taught because of the lamentation of the titthiyas (ascetics of other sects) caused by the gain and honor [received by the Buddha]. Indeed, as stated in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One. Truly, the beings living in this world are established in four groups according to the four types of persons: those who measure by form and are satisfied with form, those who measure by sound and are satisfied with sound, those who measure by austerity and are satisfied with austerity, and those who measure by Dhamma and are satisfied with Dhamma.

The distinction between these four is as follows: What kind of person measures by form and is satisfied with form? Here, a certain person, having seen [the Buddha's] height, or his girth, or his proportions, or his physical perfection, takes that as a measure and develops faith. This person is called one who measures by form and is satisfied with form.

What kind of person measures by sound and is satisfied with sound? Here, a certain person, having heard the reports of others' praise, commendation, extolling, and the spreading of his virtues, takes that as a measure and develops faith. This person is called one who measures by sound and is satisfied with sound.

What kind of person measures by austerity and is satisfied with austerity? Here, a certain person, having seen the austerity of [the Buddha's] robes, or the austerity of his bowl, or the austerity of his lodging, or having seen his various difficult austere practices, takes that as a measure and develops faith. This person is called one who measures by austerity and is satisfied with austerity.

What kind of person measures by Dhamma and is satisfied with Dhamma? Here, a certain person, having seen [the Buddha's] virtue, or his concentration, or his wisdom, takes that as a measure and develops faith. This person is called one who measures by Dhamma and is satisfied with Dhamma.
308:
Among these four types of persons, the one who measures by form (rūpappamāṇa) develops faith in the Perfectly Enlightened One upon seeing his glorious and incomparable body—its height, its girth, the perfection of its proportions such as the hands and feet, and the beauty of its complexion; a body adorned with the eighty minor marks like a great golden cloth variegated with various jewels; a body crowded with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man like the sky illuminated by a host of stars; a body like the Pāricchattaka tree, a hundred yojanas high and in full bloom; a body eighteen cubits in height, surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance.

The one who measures by sound (ghosappamāṇa) develops faith in the Perfectly Enlightened One upon hearing the reputation that has arisen, such as: "For four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand cycles, the Blessed One fulfilled the ten perfections, the ten higher perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections; he made the great sacrifices of his limbs, his children and wife, his kingdom, his life, and his eyes."

The one who measures by austerity (lūkhappamāṇa) develops faith in the Perfectly Enlightened One upon seeing the austerity of the Blessed One's robes, thinking: "If the Blessed One had remained in the household life, he would have worn only clothes made in Kāsi; but now, having gone forth, he is content with paṃsukūla robes made of hemp and performs a difficult task." Upon seeing the austerity of his bowl, he develops faith in the Perfectly Enlightened One, thinking: "While living in the household life, this Blessed One enjoyed fragrant sālī rice worthy of a Cakkavatti king from excellent red-gold vessels; but now, carrying a stone bowl, he wanders for alms from door to door among families high and low, and being content with the morsels of alms-food he receives, he performs a difficult task." Upon seeing the austerity of his lodging, he develops faith in the Perfectly Enlightened One, thinking: "While living in the household life, this Blessed One enjoyed royal splendor like celestial bliss, surrounded by various kinds of dancers in three palaces suitable for the three seasons; but now, having gone forth, he is content with lodgings at the foot of trees and the like, using wooden planks, stone slabs, benches, and small couches, and thus performs a difficult task." Upon seeing his difficult austere practices, he develops faith in the Perfectly Enlightened One, thinking: "For six years, he subsisted on a mere handful of mung bean soup, horse gram soup, pea soup, and the like; he practiced breathless meditation (appāṇaka-jhāna); he lived without regard for his body or his life. Oh, how the Blessed One performs such wonderful and difficult tasks!"
309:
A person who measures by the Dhamma also admires only the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, having seen His many wonders such as His perfection in virtue, concentration, wisdom, His attainments in absorption, liberation, and concentration, the fulfillment of His supernormal knowledges, the Twin Miracle, the descent from the celestial realm, and the taming of Pāthikaputta. Those who are thus inspired bring great gains and offerings to the Blessed One. As for the heretics, their gains and offerings declined, just like the crow in the Bāveru Jātaka.

As it is said:
"As long as they had not seen the crested peacock with its sweet song,
The people there worshipped the crow with meat and fruit.
But when the peacock, gifted with a beautiful voice, came to Bāveru,
The gains and offerings of the crow then vanished.
So long as the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, the Light-maker, had not arisen,
The people worshipped many other recluses and brahmins.
But when the Buddha, gifted with a beautiful voice, taught the Dhamma,
The gains and offerings of the heretics then vanished."

The heretics, whose gains and offerings had thus declined, were like fireflies that can shine only an inch or two in the night but lose their radiance when the sun rises.

Indeed, fireflies show their light only in the darkness of the dark fortnight of the month, for that darkness is their domain. But when the sun, endowed with rays, arises, the light of the swarm of fireflies disappears. In the same way, many heretics here, who are like fireflies, display their own virtues in this world which is like the dark fortnight. But when the Buddha, of immeasurable radiance, arises in the world, the heretics become lusterless, like fireflies before the sun.

Thus becoming lusterless, their bodies covered with scabs, boils, and such, and having reached extreme ruin, those heretics went to where the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the great assembly of people were...
310:
They went to those various places and, standing in the alleys, at the junctions, at the crossroads, and in the rest houses, they lamented thus: "Sirs, is only the recluse Gotama a recluse? Are we not recluses? Are only the disciples of the recluse Gotama recluses? Are our disciples not recluses? Is it that only gifts given to the recluse Gotama and his disciples are of great fruit, and not those given to us and our disciples? Is it not that just as the recluse Gotama is a recluse, we too are recluses? Just as the disciples of the recluse Gotama are recluses, are our disciples not also recluses? Just as gifts given to the recluse Gotama and his disciples are of great fruit, are not gifts given to us and our disciples also of great fruit? Just as you give to and honor the recluse Gotama and his disciples, so also give to and honor us and our disciples. Is it not that the recluse Gotama appeared only a few days ago, whereas we have appeared since the very beginning of the world?"

In this way, they cried out in various manners. Then the four assemblies—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—hearing their voices, reported to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the heretics are speaking in such and such a way." Hearing this, the Blessed One said, "Monks, do not have the perception, because of the words of the heretics, that 'there is a recluse outside [this Dispensation].'" Thus, denying the status of a recluse to other heretics and allowing it only within this Dispensation, He spoke this Sutta because of this occurrence: "Monks, only here is there a recluse."

In that Sutta, "idheva" means "only in this Dispensation." This restriction should also be understood in the remaining terms. For the second and subsequent recluses also exist only here, and not elsewhere. "Samaṇo" refers to a Stream-enterer. Therefore, He said: "And what, monks, is the first recluse? Here, monks, a monk, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a Stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for enlightenment. This, monks, is called the first recluse."

"Dutiyo" refers to a Once-returner. Therefore, He said: "And what, monks, is the second recluse? Here, monks, a monk, with the destruction of the three fetters..."
311:
Due to the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, one becomes a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī). Returning to this world only once, he makes an end of suffering. "Monks, this monk is the second ascetic (samaṇa)," He declared.

The third ascetic refers to the Non-returner (Anāgāmī). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "And what, monks, is the third ascetic? Here, monks, with the destruction of the five lower fetters (saṃyojana), a monk is of spontaneous birth [in the Pure Abodes], attaining final Nibbāna there, without ever returning from that world. Monks, this monk is the third ascetic."

The fourth ascetic refers to the Arahant. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "And what, monks, is the fourth ascetic? Here, monks, with the destruction of the taints (āsavas), a monk enters and dwells in the taintless deliverance of mind (cetovimutti) and deliverance by wisdom (paññāvimutti), having realized it for himself in this very life through direct knowledge. Monks, this monk is the fourth ascetic" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.241). Thus, in this context, only the four types of ascetics established in the fruits (phalaṭṭha) are intended.

'Empty' (suñña) means void, hollow, or devoid of essence. 'Other doctrines' (parappavāda) refers to the sixty-two wrong views mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta, namely: four types of Eternalism (Sassatavāda), four types of Partial-eternalism (Ekaccasassatavāda), four types of Finitism and Infinitism (Antānantikavāda), four types of Eel-wriggling (Amarāvikkhepikavāda), two types of Fortuitous Origination (Adhiccasamuppannikavāda), sixteen doctrines of Percipient After-death (Saññīvāda), eight doctrines of Non-percipient After-death (Asaññīvāda), eight doctrines of Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient After-death (Nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda), seven types of Annihilationism (Ucchedavāda), and five doctrines of Nibbāna in the Here and Now (Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda). The doctrines of others outside this Dispensation (Sāsana) are called 'other doctrines.' All those doctrines are empty of these four types of ascetics established in the fruits, because those ascetics do not exist within those views. Not only are they empty of these four, but they are also empty of the twelve types of ascetics when including the four established in the paths (maggaṭṭha) and the four practicing insight (vipassanā) for the sake of the four paths. With this meaning in mind, the Blessed One spoke in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta:

"At twenty-nine years of age, Subhadda,
I went forth in search of what is wholesome.
For over fifty years since I went forth, Subhadda,
I have been a practitioner in the realm of the Righteous Dhamma (Ñāya Dhamma);
Outside of this, there is no ascetic (samaṇa)."

"The second ascetic does not exist, the third ascetic does not exist, the fourth ascetic does not exist. Other doctrines are empty of other ascetics" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.214).
312:
In this context, 'padesavattī' refers to one who has undertaken insight practice (āraddhavipassaka). Therefore, by grouping together the one practicing insight for the sake of the path of stream-entry, the one standing in that path, and the one standing in its fruit, He said, "There is no [first] ascetic [outside]." By grouping together the one practicing insight for the sake of the path of once-returning, the one standing in that path, and the one standing in its fruit, He said, "The second ascetic does not exist [outside]." The same method applies to the remaining two (Non-returning and Arahantship).

Why are these ascetics not found in other [external] doctrines? Because they are not a [suitable] field (khetta). Just as a mustard seed does not remain on the point of a needle, just as fire does not blaze on the surface of water, and just as seeds do not grow on a stone slab; even so, these ascetics do not arise in the doctrines of sectarians (titthiyas) outside the Dispensation. They arise only in this very Dispensation. Why? Because it is a [suitable] field. The unsuitability and suitability of the field for those ascetics should be understood by the absence and presence of the Noble Path. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"In whatever Dhamma-Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, there the [first] ascetic is not found, the second ascetic is not found, the third ascetic is not found, the fourth ascetic is not found. But in whatever Dhamma-Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found, there the [first] ascetic is found, the second ascetic... the fourth ascetic is found. In this Dhamma-Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found; only here, Subhadda, is there the [first] ascetic, here the second ascetic, here the third ascetic, here the fourth ascetic. Other doctrines are empty of other ascetics" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.214).

Thus, because the sectarian doctrine is not a [suitable] field and the Dispensation is a [suitable] field, just as a lion king, the lord of beasts, with deep red paws and a brave mane, does not dwell in a cemetery or on a rubbish heap, but enters the three-thousand-league-wide Himavanta forest and dwells only in a jeweled cave; and just as the Chaddanta elephant king is not born among the nine elephant lineages such as the Gocariya lineage, but is born only in the Chaddanta lineage; and just as the Valāhaka horse king is not born among the lineage of donkeys or inferior horses, but is born only among the Sindh horses on the banks of the Sindhu river; and just as the wish-fulfilling and mind-delighting Mani jewel is not...
313:
Just as a gem does not arise in a rubbish heap or a dust heap and so forth, but arises only within Mount Vepulla; just as the fish-king named Timirapiṅgala does not arise in small square ponds, but arises only in the great ocean which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep; just as the king of Garuḍas (Supaṇṇarājā), who is one hundred and fifty yojanas in size, does not dwell in castor-oil forests and so forth near village gates, but enters the great ocean and dwells only in the Simbalī Lake forest; just as the golden swan king named Dhataraṭṭha does not dwell in pits and so forth near village gates, but dwells only on Mount Cittakūṭa surrounded by ninety thousand swans; just as a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) who rules over all four islands is not born into a low family, but is born only into a noble kshatriya family of unbroken lineage; in the same way, not even a single monk among these monks arises in the assembly of those with other views, but arises only in the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana) surrounded by the Noble Path. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, only here is there a recluse... other doctrines are empty of recluses."

In the phrase "Sammā sīhanādaṃ nadatha," "Sammā" means by way of reason and method. "Sīhanāda" (lion's roar) means an excellent roar, a fearless roar, and an unrivaled roar. Because these four types of recluses exist only in this Dispensation, this proclamation is called an excellent roar (seṭṭhanāda) and a supreme roar (uttamanāda). For one who says, "These recluses exist only in this Dispensation," there is no fear or apprehension from those of other views; thus it is called a fearless roar (abhītanāda). Because not even one of the great teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa can stand up and say, "These recluses also exist in our dispensation," this roar is called an unrivaled roar (appaṭināda). Therefore, it is said, "A lion's roar is an excellent roar, a fearless roar, and an unrivaled roar."

"Ṭhānaṃ khေါ panetaṃ vijjati" means this reason exists. "Yaṃ aññatitthiyā" means for which reason those of other views. Here, one should understand tittha (sect/ford), titthakara (founder of a sect), titthiyā (adherents of a sect), and titthiyasāvakā (disciples of a sect). Tittha refers to the sixty-two types of wrong views. Beings cross over, float, and sink and surface in these views; therefore, they are called tittha (fords). The one who gives rise to those views is called a titthakara. Those who go forth into homelessness after accepting his doctrine are called titthiyā. Those who provide the four requisites to them should be known as titthiyasāvakā. "Paribbājakā" refers to those who have gone forth into homelessness after abandoning the bonds of household life. "Assāso" means a refuge, a foundation, or a support. "Balaṃ" means strength or power. "Yena tumhe" means by which refuge or strength do you speak in this way.
314:
Friends, there are (teachings) taught by that Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. In this statement, the summary meaning is: that Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, having destroyed all defilements, and having realized the unsurpassed Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), knows by knowing the inclinations (āsaya) and underlying tendencies (anusaya) of various beings, and sees by seeing all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma) like an āmalaka fruit placed on the palm of the hand. Furthermore, He knows through such knowledges as the recollection of past lives and sees with the divine eye. He knows through the three knowledges (vijjā) or the six higher powers (abhiññā) and sees with the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu) which is unimpeded in all things. He knows with the wisdom capable of knowing all phenomena and sees with the extremely pure physical eye (maṃsacakkhu) even those forms behind walls that are beyond the range of the eyes of ordinary beings. He knows with the penetrative wisdom (paṭivedhapaññā) which has concentration as its proximate cause and achieves one's own benefit; He sees with the teaching wisdom (desanāpaññā) which has compassion as its proximate cause and achieves the benefit of others. He is called 'Araha' because He has killed the enemies of defilements and because He is worthy of receiving the four requisites and so forth. He is called 'Sammāsambuddha' because He has rightly and by Himself realized the Four Noble Truths. Alternatively, He is the Blessed One who knows the things that cause obstacles and sees the things that lead out of Saṃsāra. He is called 'Araha' because He has killed the enemies of defilements and 'Sammāsambuddha' because He has rightly and by Himself realized all phenomena. Thus, being praised in four ways through the power of the fourfold intrepidity (vesārajjañāṇa), He has taught the four dhammas. We say this because we clearly see these dhammas within ourselves, and not by relying on the support of kings, great ministers, and so forth, or on physical strength.

'Satthari pasādo' refers to the clarity of faith that arises in those who recollect the virtues of the Buddha in such ways as 'Itipi so Bhagavā...'. 'Dhamme pasādo' refers to the clarity of faith that arises in those who recollect the virtues of the Dhamma in such ways as 'Svākkhāto Bhagavatā Dhammo...'. 'Sīlesu paripūrakāritā' means the fulfillment of the virtues loved by the Noble Ones (ariyakanta-sīla). The virtues loved by the Noble Ones are the Five Precepts. Even if a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) has passed into another life and does not know that he is a noble disciple, he does not transgress them. Even if someone were to say, 'Accept this entire kingdom of a Universal Monarch and take the life of a small fly,' there is no reason for him to follow that person's word. Thus, the virtues of the Noble Ones are pleasing, dear, and delightful. Referring to those virtues, it is said, 'Sīlesu paripūrakāritā'. 'Sahadhammikā kho pana' refers to these seven fellow practitioners: monks, nuns, probationary nuns, novice monks, novice nuns, laymen, and laywomen. Among them, a monk is a fellow practitioner with other monks because of having the same training (sikkhā).
315:
Similarly, a bhikkhunī practices the Dhamma together with bhikkhunīs... and so on... a female lay follower (upāsikā) with female lay followers, a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) with stream-enterers, a once-returner (sakadāgāmī)... and so on... with non-returners (anāgāmīs). Therefore, all of them are called 'fellow practitioners' (sahadhammika). Alternatively, in this context, only the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) are intended. For those noble disciples, even in another life, there is no dispute regarding the vision of the Path (maggadassana); thus, they are 'fellow practitioners' because they practice the same Dhamma absolutely. By this term 'sahadhammika', the devotion that arises in those who recollect the virtues of the Saṅgha—in such ways as 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well'—is described. By this much, the four factors of a stream-enterer have been stated.

'Friends, these four things' means: we say this because we see them clearly in ourselves; the Blessed One has declared these four things as our refuge (assāsa) and our strength (bala).

'He who is our teacher'—by this statement, the six great teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa are indicated. Just as nowadays in the Dispensation (sāsana), there is 'household-based affection' (gehasitapema) towards teachers and preceptors, thinking 'our teacher, our preceptor,' they speak of 'devotion to the teacher' with such affection in mind. However, the Elder said: 'A teacher is not for just one or two people; in the world with its devas, there is only one Teacher (the Buddha). Therefore, the sectarians (titthiya), by separating the teacher with the single phrase "our teacher," have contradicted themselves and are defeated by this very statement.' 'Devotion to the Dhamma'—just as nowadays in the Dispensation people are attached, thinking 'our Dīgha Nikāya, our Majjhima Nikāya,' they speak with household-based affection for the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti) they have learned. 'In precepts' (sīlesu) refers to the goat-precept, cow-precept, sheep-precept, dog-precept (animal-like practices), and so on. 'Friends, here in this Dispensation'—in this phrase, 'here' is spoken with reference to devotion. 'What is the superior exertion (adhikappayoga)?' 'That which is such'—what do you mean by saying there is a distinction between you and us? For you also have devotion in four instances, and so do we. In this devotion, are you and we not identical, like two pieces of split gold? Thus they stood, speaking with sweet words.

Then the Blessed One, breaking their sweet words, said: 'Those who speak thus,' and so on. In that passage, 'one goal' (ekā niṭṭhā) means the conclusion of that devotion...
316:
Is that goal (niṭṭhā) one or many? Thus, the Blessed One said, 'You should ask.' This is because there is no doctrine that does not designate a goal at various times. For the Brahmins, the Brahma-world is the goal; for the great ascetics, the Ābhassara realm; for the wanderers (paribbājaka), the Subhakiṇha realm; for the Ājīvakas, the unconscious state (asaññībhava) conceived as 'infinite mind' (anantamānasa). In this Dispensation, however, Arahatship is the goal. All of them claim that Arahatship alone is the goal, yet through the power of their views, they designate the Brahma-world and so on. Therefore, to show that they designate only one goal according to their own beliefs, the Blessed One said, 'Answering rightly' (sammā vyākaramānā), and so on.

Now, while it appeared as if there were two parties—the monks having one goal and the sectarians having one goal—the Blessed One, wishing to show the duty of repeated questioning, said: 'Friend, is that goal for one with lust (sarāga) or for one without lust (vītarāga)?' and so on. In that regard, there is no goal for those stained by lust and so forth. If there were, it would also exist for animals like dogs and jackals. Seeing this fault, the sectarians' answer is shown in the manner: 'Friend, that goal is for one without lust.'

In that passage, 'viddasuno' means for the wise. 'Anuruddha-paṭiviruddha' means one who complies through lust and one who opposes through anger. In the phrase 'papañcārāma papañcarati,' it is called 'ārāma' because one delights in this Dhamma. One is called 'papañcārāma' because one has the Dhamma that expands saṃsāra (papañca) as one's place of delight. One is called 'papañcarati' because one has delight in the papañca-dhamma. 'Papañca' is a designation for craving (taṇhā), views (diṭṭhi), and conceit (māna) that arise in the manner of negligence. Here, however, only craving and views are intended. In the five instances starting with 'sarāga,' although only one defilement (kilesa) appears, its diversity should be understood by its mode. In the place where 'sarāga' is mentioned, it is taken by the power of lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. In 'sataṇha,' it is by the power of craving for existence (bhavataṇhā). In 'saupādāna,' it is by the power of grasping. In 'anuruddha-paṭiviruddha,' it is by the power of the pair (compliance and opposition). In 'papañcārāma,' it is by the power of showing the arising of proliferation. Alternatively, in 'sarāga,' it is taken by the power of the unwholesome root; in 'sataṇha,' it is taken by the power of showing grasping due to craving. The rest is the same as before. However, the Elder said: 'Why distinguish them thus? For this single greed (lobha) is called "lust" (rāga) by the power of staining; it is called "craving" (taṇhā) by the power of creating desire; it is called "clinging" (upādāna) in the sense of grasping; it is called "compliance and opposition" by the power of the pair; and it is called "proliferation" (papañca) in the sense of showing the arising of proliferation.'
317:
Now, wishing to show the view (*diṭṭhi*) which is the root of these defilements (*kilesa*), he said: "Monks, there are these two views," and so forth.

In that text, the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) is the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). The view of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*) is the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). "Clinging to the view of existence" means clinging to the eternalist view through the power of craving and views. "Approached" (*upagata*) means approached through the power of craving and views alone. "Absorbed" (*ajjhosita*) means entered into through the power of craving and views alone. "They are opposed to the view of non-existence" means that all of them, together with the annihilationists, remain constantly engaged in quarrels and disputes, being extremely opposed, saying: "You fools do not know; this world is eternal, this world does not perish." In the second instance, the method is the same.

In the passage beginning with "*samudayañca*," there are two origins of views: the momentary origin (*khaṇika-samudaya*) and the causal origin (*paccaya-samudaya*). The arising of views is called the momentary origin. The eight bases of causes are called the causal origin. They are: the aggregates (*khandha*), ignorance (*avijjā*), contact (*phassa*), perception (*saññā*), thought (*vitakka*), unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*), bad friendship (*pāpamitta*), and the voice of another (*paratoghosa*). "The aggregates are the root and the condition for views, in the sense of being the basis for their arising through clinging. Thus, the aggregates are also the basis of views. Ignorance, contact, perception, thought, unwise attention, bad friendship, and the voice of another are the root and the condition for views, in the sense of being the basis for their arising through clinging. Thus, the voice of another is also the basis of views" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.124). Regarding cessation (*atthaṅgama*), there are also only two: momentary cessation and causal cessation. Momentary cessation refers to exhaustion, vanishing, breaking up, dissolution, impermanence, and disappearance. Causal cessation refers to the Path of Stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*). The Path of Stream-entry is said to be the total eradication of the basis of views.

Gratification (*assāda*) refers to the benefits rooted in the view. With reference to this benefit, it was said: "Whatever view the teacher has, such is the view of the disciples. Because the disciples have such a view, they respect, revere, honor, and worship the teacher, and because of that, they receive the four requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. Monks, this is the gratification of the view obtained in the present life." Danger (*ādīnava*) refers to the peril arising from the grasping of views. That danger should be understood through the power of practices such as the bat-vow, exertion in a squatting posture, sleeping on thorns, the practice of five fires, jumping from a mountain cliff, plucking out hair and beard, and non-breathing meditation (*appāṇaka jhāna*). Escape (*nissaraṇa*) refers to Nibbāna, which is the escape from all views.
318:
"They do not know according to reality" means those who do not know all this according to its true nature. They are not liberated from the entire suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*). By this, he shows that for them, there is no such thing as the final goal (the fruit of Arahantship). "They are liberated from suffering" means they are liberated from the entire suffering of the round. By this, he firmly establishes that the final goal exists only in the Dispensation (*Sāsana*), just as one might decide a legal case between two litigants.

Now, wishing to show the cutting off of views, he said: "Monks, there are these four types of grasping (*upādāna*)," and so forth. The detailed explanation of those types of grasping has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Claiming to teach the full understanding of all graspings" means those who profess, "We speak of the full understanding and transcendence of all graspings." They cannot rightly prescribe the transcendence of all graspings. Some prescribe only the full understanding of the grasping of sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). Some prescribe only the grasping of views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), and some also prescribe the grasping of rules and rituals (*sīlabbatupādāna*). However, there is no one who can prescribe the full understanding of the grasping of the doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*). Wishing to show their distinction, he said: "They prescribe the full understanding of the grasping of sensual pleasures," and so forth. Therein, even all the ninety-six heretical sects prescribe the full understanding of the grasping of sensual pleasures; for they say, "Sensual pleasures should not be indulged in by one who has gone forth," and they do not prescribe that indulging in the objects of sensuality is allowable, but rather prescribe it as unallowable. Those who do indulge in them do so secretly. Therefore, it is said, "They prescribe the full understanding of the grasping of sensual pleasures."

Because they practice by holding onto views such as "There is no fruit of giving," and because they hold that "One is purified by virtue, purified by vows, purified by meditation," and because they do not abandon the perception of self, they cannot prescribe the full understanding of the grasping of views, the grasping of rules and rituals, and the grasping of the doctrine of self. For what reason do they not prescribe it? It is because those venerable ones do not know these three reasons according to their true nature. However, with reference to those who know according to reality that "this should be abandoned" regarding the two causes for prescribing full understanding—namely, views and rules and rituals—the two subsequent sections were spoken. Therein, those who hold that "There is a fruit of giving," and so forth, prescribe the full understanding of the grasping of views. Those who hold that "One is not purified by virtue, not purified by vows, not purified by meditation," prescribe the full understanding of the grasping of rules and rituals. But as for the full understanding of the grasping of the doctrine of self, not even a single person is able to prescribe it. For even those who have obtained the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), regarding the moon and the sun...
319:
The sectarians (titthiyas), who have attained the eight meditative attainments and wander about touching their own limbs, also prescribe the three types of full understanding (pariññā). However, they are unable to abandon the doctrine of self (attavāda). Therefore, they fall repeatedly into the cycle of suffering (vaṭṭa) itself. Indeed, they are like the little rabbit that loathes the earth.

In that analogy, the explanation of the meaning is as follows: It is said that the earth said to the little rabbit, "O little rabbit!" The rabbit asked, "Who is this?" The earth said, "Why do you not know me, while you perform all your postures and void your excrement and urine only upon me?" The rabbit said, "You have seen me well. The place I tread upon is only as much as a place touched by a fingertip. The urine I void is but a small amount. The excrement is only the size of a jujube seed. But the place trodden by animals such as elephants and horses is very large; their urine is the size of a pot, and their excrement is the size of a basket. I have had enough of you!" So saying, it jumped up and landed in another place. Then the earth said to it, "Hey... even though you have gone far, have you not landed only upon me?" That rabbit, again loathing that earth, jumped up and landed elsewhere. In this way, even if it jumps and lands for a thousand years, the rabbit cannot be free from the earth. In the same way, even though the sectarians prescribe the full understanding of all clinging (upādāna), they can only prescribe the transcendence of the three types [of clinging], such as clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). But they are unable to abandon the doctrine of self (attavāda). Being unable to abandon it, they fall repeatedly into the cycle of suffering (vaṭṭa) itself.

Having thus spoken the words that cut off wrong views by way of the doctrine of self which the sectarians cannot transcend, [the Buddha] now, wishing to show the words that cut off [false] devotion, said: "Monks, in such a Dhamma-Vinaya," and so on. In that passage, "Dhamma-Vinaya" means in the Dhamma and in the Vinaya. By both, He shows the teaching that does not lead out [of suffering] (aniyyanika sāsana). "Devotion to the teacher is not rightly directed (sammaggata)" means that in a teaching that does not lead out [of suffering], the teacher, after passing away, may become a lion, a tiger, a leopard, a bear, or a hyena. The disciples of that teacher, however, become deer, pigs, or gazelles. That [teacher], without exercising patience, loving-kindness (mettā), or compassion (anuddayā), thinking, "These were formerly my attendants and donors of the four requisites (paccaya)," pounces upon them and drinks their blood, and eats large chunks of their flesh. Or else, the teacher becomes a cat, and the disciples become chickens or mice. Then, in the same manner as mentioned, he eats them without compassion. Or else, the teacher becomes a hell-warden, and the disciples become hell-beings. That [teacher], without compassion, thinking, "These were formerly my attendants and donors of the four requisites," inflicts various tortures upon them. He makes them travel in flaming chariots, makes them climb mountains of burning coals, and in the Lohakumbhī hell-cauldron...
320:
...throws them [into the cauldron] and subjects them to many painful states. Or else, the disciples, after passing away, become lions and so forth, and the teacher becomes one of the animals like deer. Those disciples, who were formerly donors, without exercising patience, loving-kindness, or compassion towards him, thinking, "We formerly attended upon this person with the four requisites; this was our teacher," bring him to ruin and destruction in the very same manner as mentioned. Thus, in a teaching that does not lead out [of suffering], devotion to the teacher is not rightly directed (sammaggata); even if it lasts for some time, it eventually perishes.

"Devotion to the Dhamma" means that in a teaching that does not lead out [of suffering], devotion to their own Dhamma is merely devotion to the scriptural tradition (pāḷi) consisting of learning, mastering, and reciting; but there is no liberation from the cycle (vaṭṭa-mokkha) in it. Therefore, devotion in this [teaching] only makes the cycle of suffering deeper and deeper; thus, it is said to be not rightly directed because it is contrary to the true nature of a [liberating] teaching.

"Fulfillment of virtues (sīla)" means that in a teaching that does not lead out [of suffering], the fulfillment of virtues by way of "goat-virtue" (aja-sīla) and so forth, because it cannot lead to liberation from the cycle or escape from existence, if it succeeds, it leads to the animal realm; if it fails, it leads to hell. Therefore, that virtue is said to be not rightly directed. "Towards fellow practitioners (sahadhammika)" means that in a teaching that does not lead out [of suffering], among those who are fellow practitioners, some, after passing away, become lions and so forth, while others become deer and so forth. Then, those who have become lions and so forth, without exercising patience and so on towards those who have become deer and so forth, thinking, "These were our fellow practitioners," cause them great suffering in the very same manner as mentioned before. Therefore, in this [teaching], even affection and fondness for fellow practitioners is said to be not rightly directed.

The Blessed One, wishing to show all these reasons together, said: "Monks, for what reason is that? Monks, it is so," and so on. The summary of the meaning there is: Monks, that which I have said, "Devotion to the teacher is said to be not rightly directed," and so on, is exactly so. Why? Because those [instances of] devotion and so forth are in a Dhamma-Vinaya that is poorly proclaimed (durakkhāta)... and not proclaimed by a Fully Enlightened One (asammāsambuddhappavedita). Here, "yathā" is a particle indicating the reason. In that passage, "durakkhāta" means poorly spoken; because it is poorly spoken, it is poorly proclaimed. Furthermore, because it does not lead out for the sake of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala), it is "aniyyanika" (not leading out). Because it does not lead to the subsiding of lust and so forth, it is "anupasamasamvattanika" (not leading to peace). Not by the Fully Enlightened One...
321:
"Sabbaññunā pavedito" means that which is not proclaimed by the Omniscient Buddha (as a means of liberation from the cycle of rebirth) (asammāsambuddhappavedito). Faith in the teachings of those heretics (titthiyas), which do not lead out of the cycle of suffering, do not lead to the stilling of defilements, and are not proclaimed by the Omniscient Buddha, is of no benefit. By this sequence of words, the Blessed One shows that faith in heretics is as profitless as faith in a drunken jackal.

It is told that a black jackal entered a city at night, ate the dregs of liquor (which had been strained through a cloth and discarded), and slept in a Punnāga grove. Waking at sunrise, he thought, "It is impossible to leave at this time; I have many enemies. I must deceive someone." Seeing a Brahmin walking by, he thought, "I will trick this Brahmin," and called out, "O Brahmin!" The Brahmin asked, "Who is calling me?" The jackal said, "It is I, sir; come here for a moment." The Brahmin asked, "Why?" The jackal replied, "Carry me outside the village; I will give you two hundred kahāpaṇas."

The Brahmin agreed and grabbed the jackal by the legs. The jackal said, "You foolish Brahmin, my coins are not just thrown away; coins are hard to come by. Hold me properly." The Brahmin asked, "How should I hold you?" The jackal said, "Tie me in your upper robe, place me on your shoulder, and carry me." The Brahmin did as told. Near the south gate, he asked, "Shall I set you down here?" The jackal asked, "What place is this?" The Brahmin replied, "The main gate." The jackal said, "You foolish Brahmin, do your relatives keep coins at the gate? Carry me further."

Every few steps, the Brahmin asked, "Shall I set you down here?" but the jackal rebuked him. Reaching a safe place, the jackal said, "Set me down here." The Brahmin set him down and held out his robe (to receive the coins). The jackal said, "I said I would give you two hundred coins, but I have many—not just two hundred. While I go to fetch them, stand here looking at the sun." After going a short distance, he turned back and said, "O Brahmin, do not look elsewhere; stand looking only at the sun." Having said this, the jackal entered a Ketaka forest and fled as he pleased. As the Brahmin stood looking at the sun, sweat poured from his forehead and armpits. Then a tree deity said:

"O Brahmin, you have believed the words of a drunken jackal. When there are not even a hundred shells, how could there be two hundred bronze coins?"

Just as faith in the black jackal was useless, so is faith in heretics.
322:
Having shown the profitlessness of devotion in a non-liberating dispensation, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "But, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata..." to show the profitableness of devotion in a liberating (niyyānika) dispensation. In that passage, "He prescribes the full understanding of clinging to sense pleasures" means he prescribes the full understanding of abandoning and transcending clinging to sense pleasures (kāmūpādāna) through the path of Arahantship. However, he prescribes the full understanding of the other three types of clinging through the path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). "Bhikkhus, in such a Dhamma-Vinaya" means, bhikkhus, in such a Dhamma and in such a Vinaya. By both terms, he shows the liberating dispensation. "Devotion to the Teacher" means that whatever devotion one has toward the Blessed One in such a dispensation is said to have reached the right path and leads to liberation from the suffering of existence.

Regarding this devotion, there are these stories: The Blessed One was once staying in the Indasāla Cave on Mount Vediyaka. At that time, an owl would follow the Blessed One halfway when he entered the village for alms and would go out to meet him halfway when he left the village. One day, in the evening, the owl came down from the mountain to the Perfectly Enlightened One, who was seated surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. After paying homage, the owl lowered its wings, joined its claws in salutation, bowed its head, and stood worshipping the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala). The Blessed One looked at the owl and smiled. The Elder Ānanda asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for the manifestation of this smile?" The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, look at this owl. Having gained faith in me and in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, after wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Somanassa," and he spoke these verses:

"O owl of Mount Vediyaka, with round eyes, who has lived there for a long time,
You are happy, O Kosiya, for you behold the Noble Buddha who has arisen in due time.
Having gained faith in me and in the unsurpassed Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
For a hundred thousand aeons, this owl shall not go to a state of misery.
After passing away from the deva world, urged by his root of merit,
He will become the one known as Somanassa, a Paccekabuddha of infinite wisdom."

In this regard, there are also other stories such as the story of Sumana the florist in the city of Rājagaha, the story of the great drummer, the story of the peacock hunter, the story of the lute player, and the story of the conch blower.
323:
The stories should be explained in detail. In this way, faith in the Teacher within the liberating Dispensation is the arrival at the right path.

Regarding 'faith in the Dhamma': faith in the Dhamma within the liberating Dispensation is the arrival at the right path. If even animals who listen by merely taking the sound as a sign can be granted prosperity, what more need be said for those who understand the ultimate meaning? This meaning should be understood through the stories of Maṇḍūka, the son of the gods, and others.

Regarding 'fulfillment of the virtues': the fulfillment of the virtues within the liberating Dispensation is also the arrival at the right path, bringing about the bliss of heaven and liberation. In this context, the stories of Chattamāṇavaka, the Sāmaṇera, and others should be illustrated.

Regarding 'towards fellow practitioners': affection and fondness for fellow practitioners within the liberating Dispensation is also the arrival at the right path, bringing about great prosperity. This meaning should be illustrated by the Vimānavatthu and Petavatthu. For it was said:

'I gave milk-rice to a monk wandering for alms... (and so on) ...
Molasses... sugarcane pieces... wood-apple... watermelon...
Cucumber... creeper-fruit... phārusaka fruit... a hand-made flag...
A handful of vegetables... a handful of flowers... radish... a handful of neem leaves...
Sour gruel... bowl-washing water... a waistband...
A shoulder strap... a meditation band... a fan... a palmyra fan...
A peacock-feather fan... an umbrella... sandals... cake... sweetmeats...
I gave fried snacks to a monk wandering for alms...
Look at my mansion, I am a goddess who can assume any form at will.'

The phrase 'Taṃ kissa hetu' (What is the reason for that?) and so on should be understood by connecting them according to the method already mentioned.
324:
Now, to show the cause of those types of clinging which the sectarians cannot correctly define but which the Tathāgata defines, he said: 'Monks, these (four types of clinging),' and so on. Therein, among the terms such as 'kiṃnidānā' (what is the cause?), all terms like 'nidāna' are synonyms for 'cause' (kāraṇa). A cause is called 'nidāna' because it hands over the result, as if saying, 'Friends, take this result.' It is called 'samudaya,' 'jāti,' and 'pabhava' because the result arises from it, originates from it, and springs from it. The meaning of the terms here is: 'kiṃnidānā' means 'what is the cause of these?'; 'kiṃsamudayā' means 'what is the origin of these?'; 'kiṃjātikā' means 'what is the birth of these?'; 'kiṃpabhavā' means 'what is the source of these?'. Since craving (taṇhā) is the cause, origin, birth, and source of those types of clinging in the sense already mentioned, he said: 'They have craving as their cause,' and so on. The meaning of all terms should be understood in this way. Because the Blessed One knows not only the cause of clinging but also the cause of craving which is the cause of clinging, and the cause of feeling (vedanā) etc., which are the causes of craving, he said: 'Monks, this craving also,' and so on.

'Yato ca kho' means 'at which time.' 'Avijjā pahīnā hoti' means that ignorance, the root of the round of rebirths, is abandoned by the cessation of non-arising. 'Vijjā uppannā' means the knowledge of the path of Arahantship has arisen. 'Through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge' means because that monk has abandoned ignorance and because knowledge has arisen. 'He no longer clings to the clinging to sensual pleasures' means he no longer takes or adheres to the clinging to sensual pleasures, nor to the remaining types of clinging. 'Not clinging, he is not agitated' means that by not taking any clinging in this way, he is not agitated by the agitation of craving. 'Being unagitated' means not producing craving. 'He personally attains Nibbāna' means he attains Nibbāna by himself through the extinction of defilements. Having thus shown the destruction of the taints (āsava) of that monk, he now said: 'Birth is exhausted,' and so on, to show the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa) of the monk who has destroyed the taints. The meaning of that is just as already stated.

## The Commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
325:
## 2. Mahāsīhanāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā
## Vesālī Nagara Vaṇṇanā
This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta. In that Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, "Vesāliyaṃ" means in the city thus named Vesālī. It is heard that the city came to be called "Vesālī" because it became progressively extensive and wide. Regarding that Vesālī, the sequential account is as follows: A child was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Having realized she was pregnant, the queen informed the king. The king provided the necessary pregnancy care. Being well-protected, when the pregnancy reached maturity, she entered the maternity chamber.

It is customary for meritorious women to be delivered of their pregnancy at dawn; as the queen was one of those meritorious ones, she gave birth at dawn to a lump of flesh resembling a bandhujīvaka flower that had been soaked in lac.

Then, she thought, "Other queens give birth to sons who resemble golden statues, but I, the Chief Queen, have given birth to a lump of flesh. Disgrace will surely come upon me in the presence of the king." Fearing such disgrace, she placed the lump of flesh in a vessel, covered it, sealed it with the royal seal, and had it cast into the current of the Ganges River. As soon as it was discarded by humans, the deities arranged for its protection. On that vessel, they tied a gold plate upon which was written in vermilion: "The offspring of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī." Thereafter, the vessel floated along the current of the Ganges, unmolested by dangers such as waves.

At that time, a certain ascetic was living on the banks of the Ganges, supported by a family of cowherds.
