When he descended to the Ganges early in the morning, he saw the vessel floating towards him and, perceiving it to be refuse, took it. Then, seeing the gold plate with the inscription and the royal seal, he opened it and saw the lump of flesh. Upon seeing it, the thought occurred to him: "This might be an embryo, for this lump of flesh has no foul or putrid smell." He took it to his hermitage and placed it in a clean spot. After the lapse of half a month (fifteen days), it became two lumps of flesh. The ascetic saw this and kept them even more carefully. Then, after another half a month (fifteen days), five protrusions appeared on each lump of flesh for the formation of hands, feet, and the head. Then, after another half a month (fifteen days), one lump of flesh became a boy resembling a golden statue, and the other became a girl.

Parental affection for the children arose in the ascetic, and milk began to flow from his thumb. From then on, he obtained milk-rice; the ascetic would eat the rice and give the milk to the children...
326:
(The ascetic) would pour the milk into the mouths of the children. Whatever food entered the stomachs of those children was clearly visible from the outside, as if it had entered a crystal vessel; thus, they appeared to have no skin. Other teachers, however, say that the skin of those children was so thin that it appeared as if it were joined together. Thus, they became known as 'Licchavī' either because of their skinless appearance or because of their joined skin.

While raising the children, the ascetic would enter the village for alms only when the sun was high and return when the day was far spent. Knowing his arduous task, the cowherds said, "Venerable sir, raising children is an obstacle for those who have gone forth. Please give the children to us; we will raise them. You, sir, should only practice your own ascetic duties." The ascetic agreed, saying, "Very well." On the following day, the cowherds leveled the road, scattered flowers, raised banners and flags, and came to the hermitage playing musical instruments. The ascetic said, "These children are of great merit; raise them with diligence. When they have grown up, marry them to one another. Please the king with the five products of the cow, obtain a portion of land, and build a city. Consecrate the prince there." Having said this, he handed over the children. The cowherds agreed, saying, "Very well," and took the children away to raise them.

When the children grew up and were playing, they would strike and kick other cowherd children with their hands and feet at the places where they quarreled. Those children would cry, and when asked by their parents, "Why are you crying?", they would say, "These children, who have no parents and were raised by the ascetic, hit us excessively." Then their parents said, "These children harm and cause suffering to other children; they should not be associated with, they should be shunned (vajjitabbā)." Based on this saying that they should be shunned, that region, which was one hundred yojanas in extent, came to be called the 'Vajjī' country.

Then the cowherds pleased the king and obtained that land. They founded a city there and, having consecrated the prince who was sixteen years of age, made him king. They married him to the princess and made a pact: "No woman from outside shall be brought in, and no woman from here shall be given to anyone else." From their first union, twins were born—a son and a daughter. In this manner, twins were born sixteen times. As those children grew up in due course, the parks, gardens, dwellings, and retinues became insufficient to accommodate them. Therefore, the city was expanded three times, each time by a distance of one gāvuta...
328:
"...directs the mind, inclines the mind towards knowledge and vision" (DN 1.235)—here, it refers to insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). "You are incapable of the supreme enlightenment of knowledge and vision" (AN 4.196)—here, it refers to the Path (magga). "This other pleasant dwelling... attained as a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, is a superhuman state" (MN 1.328)—here, it refers to Fruition (phala). "Knowledge and vision arose in me: my liberation of mind is unshakable; this is the last birth; now there is no more renewed existence" (Mahāvagga 16)—here, it refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). "Knowledge and vision arose in me: Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago" (MN 2.340)—here, it refers to omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). In this context, however, the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga) is intended. It is that path knowledge that Sunakkhatta denies in the Blessed One.

"Dhamma hammered out by reasoning"—with these words, he denies the Blessed One's status as a Teacher. Sunakkhatta had this thought: "The ascetic Gotama has never approached teachers to learn any subtle extraordinary Dhamma; he merely preaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, having thought, 'It will be like this, it will be like this.'"

"Dhamma followed by inquiry"—with these words, he admits the Blessed One's mundane wisdom. He thought: "The ascetic Gotama is wise; he preaches a Dhamma followed by inquiry, having turned this way and that the inquiry called wisdom, which is like a thunderbolt, thinking, 'It will be like this, it will be like this.'"

"Dhamma that is self-evident"—with these words, he denies the Blessed One's direct realization of the Dhammas. Sunakkhatta had this thought: "The ascetic Gotama does not possess any subtle extraordinary Dhamma such as insight, the path, fruition, or reviewing knowledge. However, he has gained a following; the four classes of people surround him just as they surround a universal monarch. His lips are beautiful, his tongue is soft, his voice is sweet, and his speech is faultless. Therefore, whatever occurs to him, he takes that and speaks as if it were self-evident, thereby pleasing the great multitude."

"For the sake of which benefit the Dhamma is taught" means: the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) to abandon lust (rāga); the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) to abandon hatred (dosa); the five dhammas to abandon delusion (moha); and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) to cut off thoughts (vitakka).

"That Dhamma leads one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering" means: for one who practices according to what has been taught, that Dhamma leads to the destruction of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha) through the right method and reason; it accomplishes that benefit.
329:
He points it out. However, Sunakkhatta did not say these words of his own accord. In truth, although he wished to say that the Dhamma of the Buddhas does not lead out of suffering (aniyyānika), he was unable to do so. Why? Because he was afraid of being rebuked. In the city of Vesālī, there were many lay followers who were Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners. Those lay followers would have rebuked him as mentioned before, saying: "Sunakkhatta, do you say that the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One does not lead out of suffering? If this Dhamma does not lead out of suffering, why have so many Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners arisen in this city?" Fearing such a rebuke, Sunakkhatta was unable to say it does not lead out of suffering; instead, like an arrow shot by Ajjuna, he said, "His Dhamma is not in vain, it leads out [of suffering], but there is nothing within it [of superhuman states]."

"Assosi kho" (He heard) means that [Venerable Sāriputta] heard those words being spoken by him in various assemblies of brahmins, wealthy merchants, and others in Vesālī, but he did not stop him. Why did he not stop him? Because of compassion. For it occurred to him: "This Sunakkhatta is angry and is sputtering with the heat of his wrath like a burning bamboo forest or a furnace into which salt has been thrown. If I were to stop or refute him, he would bear a grudge against me as well. If that happens, his bearing of a grudge against both the Tathāgata and me—against these two persons—will be an extremely heavy burden for him." Thus, out of compassion, he did not stop him. Alternatively, he thought: "Speaking words of dispraise against the Buddhas is like finding fault with the full moon. Who will accept his words? When his own saliva is exhausted and his mouth is dry, he will stop on his own." For this reason, too, he did not stop him. "Piṇḍapātapāṭikkanto" means having returned from the search for alms-food.

"Kodhana" means one who is fierce and harsh. "Moghapurisa" means a vain or empty man. When a person lacks the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits in that particular existence, the Buddhas call him a "moghapurisa." Even if the supporting condition exists, if at that moment the Path or Fruit has not yet been attained, they still call him a "moghapurisa." As for this Sunakkhatta, since the supporting condition for the Paths and Fruits in that existence had been completely severed, he was called a "moghapurisa." "Kodhā ca panassa esā vācā bhāsitā" means that he spoke these words out of anger.
330:
Why was this Sunakkhatta angry with the Blessed One? In the past, this Sunakkhatta approached the Blessed One and asked about the preliminary practice (parikamma) for the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu). Then the Blessed One taught it to him. Having developed the Divine Eye and expanded the light, Sunakkhatta looked upon the celestial realms and saw the devas and devīs enjoying celestial splendor in the Nandana Grove, Cittalatā Grove, Phārusaka Grove, and Missaka Grove. Thinking, "How sweet must be the voices of these devas who abide in such perfection of existence?", he desired to hear their voices. He approached the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala) and asked about the preliminary practice for the Divine Ear element (dibba-sota-dhātu). However, the Blessed One, knowing that Sunakkhatta lacked the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Divine Ear element, did not teach him the preliminary practice. Indeed, the Buddhas do not teach the preliminary practice to one who is devoid of the supporting condition.

Sunakkhatta, bearing a grudge against the Blessed One, thought: "First, I asked the ascetic Gotama for the preliminary practice for the Divine Eye; he taught it to me, thinking, 'Let it be successful for him or not.' But I, through my own personal effort, achieved that attainment. Then I asked for the preliminary practice for the Divine Ear element, and he did not teach it to me. Surely he thinks: 'If this one who has gone forth from the royal clan achieves the knowledge of the Divine Eye, the knowledge of the Divine Ear element, the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, he will become my equal.' Out of envy and stinginess (issā-macchariya), he does not teach me." Bearing an even greater grudge, he discarded his saffron robes and returned to the lay life, yet he did not remain quiet but wandered about slandering the Possessor of Ten Powers with false and empty words. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Sunakkhatta spoke these words out of anger."

"Sāriputta, this is indeed praise" means: Sāriputta, while the Tathāgata was fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, he strove for this very purpose, thinking, "May my teaching of the Dhamma lead out of suffering (niyyānika)." Therefore, if anyone speaks thus, he is only speaking the praise of the Tathāgata. "Sāriputta, this is indeed praise" shows that this is a quality of the Tathāgata, not a fault.

What is shown by the words beginning with "Sāriputta, it is also possible that..."? It shows that the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) which Sunakkhatta denied actually exist within Him. The Blessed One said: "Sāriputta, this vain man Sunakkhatta says that there is no superhuman state in the Tathāgata. Yet in Me, there is the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), there is the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (iddhividha-ñāṇa), there is the knowledge of the Divine Ear element (dibba-sota-dhātu-ñāṇa), there is the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa)..."
331:
There is the knowledge of the ten powers; there is the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence; there is the knowledge of being unshakable in the eight assemblies; there is the knowledge of distinguishing the four modes of birth; there is the knowledge of distinguishing the five destinations. All these are indeed superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). To show that this vain man (mogha-purisa) will not have even a trace of the knowledge of the lineage of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya-ñāṇa) capable of understanding even one of these superhuman states, the Buddha began this teaching with the words "Even this, Sāriputta..." and so forth.

In that Pali text, it is called "anvaya" because it follows the established sign in a certain manner. It means one knows, or one understands accordingly. The following of the Dhamma is called "dhammanvaya." It is a designation for the wisdom that knows various truths such as the knowledge of omniscience. By saying "Iti pi so Bhagavā" and so forth, the Buddha shows that this vain man will not have even the knowledge of the lineage of the Dhamma to know that such a superhuman state, known as my knowledge of omniscience, truly exists. In the same way, the application should be understood for the knowledge of psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) and others.

## Explanation of the Ten Powers and Others

In this context, although the three true knowledges (vijjā) should be mentioned immediately after the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), if those three knowledges were mentioned, the ten powers of the Tathāgata would not be fully completed above. Therefore, without mentioning those knowledges, desiring to show the ten powers of the Tathāgata in full, the Buddha said, "Sāriputta, these ten are the ten powers of the Tathāgata," and so forth. In that Pali text, "Tathāgata-balas" are the powers belonging only to the Tathāgata, not shared with others. Or, it means the powers that have come just as the powers of previous Buddhas came through the perfection of their accumulation of merit. That power of the Tathāgata is of two kinds: physical power (kāyabala) and knowledge power (ñāṇabala). Among them, physical power should be understood according to the lineage of elephants. This was said by the ancient teachers thus:

"The Kālāwaka lineage, the Gaṅgeyya lineage,
the Paṇḍara lineage, the Tamba lineage, the Piṅgala lineage,
the Gandha lineage, the Maṅgala lineage, the Hemavata lineage,
the Uposatha lineage, and the Chaddanta lineage are the ten."

These are the ten lineages of elephants. Among these lineages, Kālāwaka should be understood as the ordinary elephant lineage. The physical strength of ten men is equal to the strength of one Kālāwaka elephant. The strength of ten Kālāwaka elephants is equal to the strength of one Gaṅgeyya elephant. The strength of ten Gaṅgeyya elephants is equal to the strength of one Paṇḍara elephant. The strength of ten Paṇḍara elephants is equal to the strength of one Tamba elephant. The strength of ten Tamba elephants is equal to the strength of one Piṅgala elephant. The strength of ten Piṅgala elephants is equal to the strength of one Gandha elephant. The strength of ten Gandha elephants is equal to the strength of one Maṅgala elephant. The strength of ten Maṅgala elephants is equal to the strength of one Hemavata elephant. The strength of ten Hemavata elephants is equal to the strength of one Uposatha elephant.
332:
The strength of ten Uposatha elephants is equal to the strength of one Chaddanta elephant. The strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is equal to the strength of one Tathāgata. This strength is also called the "Nārāyaṇa-saṅghāta-bala" (the strength of the Nārāyaṇa combination). That strength is equivalent to the strength of a thousand crore ordinary elephants, or by the count of men, the strength of a thousand crore men. This is the physical power (kāyabala) of the Tathāgata.

As for the knowledge power (ñāṇabala), it has already been mentioned in the Pali. They are the ten powers of knowledge (dasabala-ñāṇa), the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja-ñāṇa), the knowledge of being unshakable in the eight assemblies, the knowledge of distinguishing the four modes of birth, and the knowledge of distinguishing the five destinations. The seventy-three knowledges and seventy-seven knowledges mentioned in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, as well as many other thousands of knowledges, are called knowledge power. Here too, knowledge power is intended. Knowledge is called "bala" (power) because of its unshakable nature and its nature of providing support.

"Yehi balehi samannāgato" means being well-endowed with the ten powers of knowledge. "Āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ" means the supreme place, the highest position. Or, "Āsabha" refers to the previous Buddhas, and it means their place. Alternatively, a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows is called "usabha," and a bull that is the leader of a thousand cows is called "vasabha." Or, the leader of a hundred cow-pens is an "usabha," and the leader of a thousand cow-pens is a "vasabha." A bull that is superior to all cattle, capable of enduring all dangers, pure and inspiring, capable of bearing great burdens, and unshakable even by the sound of hundreds of thunderclaps is called "nisabha"; here, that bull is intended by the term "usabha." This is indeed a synonymous term for that bull. The place of that usabha is called "āsabha." "Ṭhāna" (place/standing) means standing firm by pressing the earth with four feet. This is called "āsabha" because it is like the āsabha (the lordly bull). Just as the bull called nisabha, being endowed with the strength of an usabha, stands firm by pressing the earth with four feet, so too the Tathāgata, being endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, stands firm with the four feet of self-confidence (vesārajja), pressing the earth of the eight assemblies, unshakable by any enemy or adversary in the world with its devas. While standing thus, he claims that supreme place (āsabha-ṭhāna), reaches it, and without rejecting it, takes it upon himself. Therefore, it is said, "He claims the supreme place (āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti)."

"Parisāsu" means in the eight assemblies. "Sīhanādaṃ nadati" means he roars the supreme roar, the fearless roar, or he roars a roar similar to the roar of the lion-king. This is the meaning.
333:
This meaning is shown by the Sīhanāda Sutta. Alternatively, just as a lion is called 'Sīha' because it can endure (sahanato) [danger] and destroy (hananato) [enemies], so too the Buddha is called 'Sīha' because He can endure worldly conditions (loka-dhamma) and destroy the doctrines of others. The roar of such a lion-like Buddha is called 'Sīhanāda' (Lion's Roar).

In this context, just as a lion, endowed with the strength of a lion, being courageous in all places and free from hair-standing fear, roars the lion's roar; so too the lion-like Buddha, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, being courageous among the eight assemblies and free from hair-standing fear, roars the Sīhanāda, which is endowed with the beauty of various teachings in such ways as 'This is form,' and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies.'

In the phrase 'Brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti' (He sets in motion the Divine Wheel), 'Brahma' means noble, especially noble, or excellent. The word 'Cakka' (wheel) is seen in the sense of:
Prosperity (sampatti), physical marks (lakkhaṇa), parts of a chariot (rathanga), postures (iriyāpatha), giving (dāna), the jewel-wheel (ratana-cakka), the Dhamma-wheel (dhamma-cakka), the chest-wheel (ura-cakka), and so on. In this context, the Dhamma-wheel is intended, and that Dhamma-wheel should be understood in two ways.

In such passages as 'Monks, there are these four wheels, endowed with which devas and humans...', the word 'cakka' is evident in the sense of prosperity (sampatti). In the passage 'Wheels were born on the soles of the feet,' it is evident in the sense of physical marks (lakkhaṇa). In the passage 'As the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the load,' it is evident in the sense of a chariot part (rathanga). In the passage 'Having four wheels and nine doors,' it is evident in the sense of postures (iriyāpatha). In the passage 'Give, enjoy, do not be negligent, turn the wheel for all living beings,' it is evident in the sense of giving (dāna). In the passage 'The divine jewel-wheel appeared,' it is evident in the sense of the jewel-wheel. In the passage 'The wheel set in motion by me,' it is evident in the sense of the Dhamma-wheel. In the passage 'The wheel revolves on the head of the person overcome by desire,' it is evident in the sense of the chest-wheel (ura-cakka). In the passage 'Even with a wheel having a razor-edge,' it is evident in the sense of a weapon-wheel. In the passage 'Thunderbolt-wheel,' it is evident in the sense of a thunderbolt-circle. In this context, however, the word 'cakka' is intended as the Dhamma-wheel.

That Dhamma-wheel is of two kinds: Knowledge of Penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and Knowledge of Teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). Among them, the knowledge produced by wisdom, which brings one's own noble power, is the Knowledge of Penetration. The knowledge produced by compassion, which brings the noble power of the disciples, is the Knowledge of Teaching. Among them, the Knowledge of Penetration is of two kinds: 'arising' (uppajjamāna) and 'arisen' (uppanna). That knowledge is 'arising' from the Great Renunciation until the Path of Arahantship, and is called 'arisen' at the moment of Fruition (phala). Or, from the Tusita heaven until...
334:
...the moment the Path of Arahantship arises at the seat of the Great Enlightenment, it is called 'arising' (uppajjamāna), and at the moment of Fruition, it is called 'arisen' (uppanna). Or, from the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Path of Arahantship arises, it is called 'arising,' and at the moment of Fruition, it is called 'arisen.' The Knowledge of Teaching is also of two kinds: 'being set in motion' (pavattāmāna) and 'set in motion' (pavatta). That Knowledge of Teaching is 'being set in motion' until the moment the Path of Stream-entry arises for Aññā Koṇḍañña, and is called 'set in motion' at the moment of Fruition. Among these two, the Knowledge of Penetration is supramundane (lokuttara), while the Knowledge of Teaching is mundane (lokiya). Indeed, both of these are unique and not shared with others; they are the Buddha's own personal (breast-born) knowledge.

Now, to show in detail those powers endowed with which the Tathāgata claims the supreme (āsabha) place, which were initially stated as 'Sāriputta, these ten are the Tathāgata's powers of a Tathāgata,' the question is asked: 'Which ten?' and it is said: 'Sāriputta, here the Tathāgata understands cause as cause,' and so on. In that passage, 'ṭhānañca ṭhānato' means (understanding) cause as cause. It is called 'ṭhāna' (cause/ground) because the effect resides there, and because it arises and persists depending on that cause. The Blessed One, knowing 'Such and such things are the causes and conditions for the arising of such and such things; that is a cause (ṭhāna). Such and such things are not the causes and conditions for the arising of such and such things; that is a non-cause (aṭṭhāna),' understands as it really is the cause as cause and the non-cause as non-cause. In the Abhidhamma, this is already explained in detail in such ways as: 'Among them, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of cause as cause and non-cause as non-cause as it really is?' The word 'yampi' means 'by which knowledge' (one understands). 'Idampi sāriputta tathāgatassa' means this knowledge of cause and non-cause is also called a Tathāgata's power of a Tathāgata. Thus, the connection in all phrases should be understood.

'Kamma-samādānānaṃ' means (knowing the results) of wholesome and unwholesome actions performed after undertaking them; or the action itself is called 'kamma-samādāna.' 'Ṭhānaso hetuso' means by way of condition (paccaya) and by way of cause (hetu). In that context, destination (gati), physical excellence (upadhi), time (kāla), and effort (payoga) are the grounds (ṭhāna) for the result (vipāka). Kamma is the cause (hetu). The detailed explanation of this knowledge has already appeared in the Abhidhamma in such ways as: 'Some evil undertakings of action, being obstructed by the excellence of destination (gati-sampatti), do not ripen,' and so on.

'Sabbatthagāminīṃ' means leading to all destinations (gati) and leading to what is not a destination (Nibbāna). 'Paṭipadaṃ' means the path (magga). 'Understands as it really is' means even when many people are killing a single living being...
335:
He understands the unerring nature of the practices known as wholesome and unwholesome volitions even in a single object, in this way: 'This person's volition will lead to hell; this person's volition will lead to the animal realm.' The detailed explanation of this knowledge has already appeared in the Abhidhamma in such a way as: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the practice leading to all destinations as it really is? Here, the Tathāgata understands: This is the path, this is the practice leading to hell,' and so forth.

'Anekadhātu' (many elements) refers to the many elements such as the eye-element and so on, or the sense-sphere element and so on. 'Nānādhātu' (various elements) refers to the various elements by way of the different characteristics of those very elements. 'Loka' (world) refers to the world of aggregates, bases, and elements. 'Understands as it really is' means penetrating the unerring nature of those various elements. This knowledge is also detailed in the Abhidhamma: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the world with its many and various elements as it really is? Here, the Tathāgata understands the variety of aggregates,' and so forth.

'Nānādhimuttikata' refers to the state of having various inclinations, such as low inclinations and so on. This knowledge is also detailed in the Abhidhamma: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the various inclinations of beings as it really is? Here, the Tathāgata understands: There are beings with low inclinations,' and so forth.

'Parasattānaṃ' refers to noble beings. 'Parapuggalānaṃ' refers to other inferior beings. Alternatively, both these terms have the same meaning, but are taught in two ways according to the types of beings to be guided (veneyya). 'Indriyaparopariyatta' refers to the superiority or inferiority of the faculties such as faith and so on, as well as their growth and decline. The detailed explanation of this knowledge has already appeared in the Abhidhamma: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the proficiency in the faculties of other beings and other persons as it really is? Here, the Tathāgata understands the inclinations (āsaya) of beings, he understands their underlying tendencies (anusaya),' and so forth.

'Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ' refers to the four jhānas starting with the first jhāna; the eight deliverances starting with 'Possessing form, one sees forms'; the three concentrations starting with 'with initial and sustained application'; and the nine successive attainments starting with the attainment of the first jhāna. 'Saṃkilesa' (defilement) refers to the states partaking of decline. 'Vodāna' (purification) refers to the states partaking of distinction. 'Vuṭṭhāna' (emergence) means that purification is also emergence.
336:
'Emergence from this or that concentration' (as stated in the Vibhaṅga) refers to the mastered jhānas, the bhavaṅga, and the fruition attainments, which are also called emergence (vuṭṭhāna). A lower mastered jhāna is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for a higher one. Therefore, it is said, 'Purification (vodāna) is also emergence (vuṭṭhāna).' Through the bhavaṅga, there is emergence from all jhānas. Through fruition attainment, there is emergence from the attainment of cessation. With reference to such emergence, it is said, 'Emergence from this or that concentration is also called emergence.'

This knowledge is also detailed in the Abhidhamma (Vibhaṅga): 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence from jhānas, deliverances, concentrations, and attainments as it really is? There are four types of meditators; a certain meditator, though successful, perceives it as a failure,' and so forth. The detailed explanation and decision regarding the seven knowledges are stated in the Vibhaṅga commentary named Sammohavinodanī. The account of the knowledge of recollection of past lives and the divine eye knowledge is detailed in the Visuddhimagga. The account of the knowledge of the destruction of taints is detailed in the Bhayabherava Sutta (commentary).

'These, Sāriputta' confirms the powers previously mentioned: 'Sāriputta, these are the ten powers of a Tathāgata.' In this regard, there is a view of others: 'There is no separate knowledge called the Ten Powers; it is merely a division of Omniscience.' This should not be viewed in that way. The Ten Powers knowledge is distinct, and Omniscience is also distinct. The Ten Powers knowledge knows only its respective function. Omniscience knows that function of the Ten Powers as well as everything else remaining.

Among the Ten Powers, the first knowledge knows only what is a cause and what is not a cause. The second knows only the variety of kamma and its results. The third knows only the distinction of kamma. The fourth knows only the cause of the variety of elements. The fifth knows only the inclinations and dispositions of beings. The sixth knows only the sharpness or dullness of the faculties. The seventh knows only the defilement and so on of the jhānas and so forth. The eighth knows only the succession of aggregates lived in the past. The ninth knows only the passing away and rebirth of beings. The tenth knows only the distinction of the Four Noble Truths.

Omniscience, however, knows what is to be known by these Ten Powers as well as what is beyond them. But it cannot perform all the functions of those Ten Powers. That Omniscience cannot become a jhāna to attain absorption, it cannot become a psychic power to perform transformations, and it cannot become a path to exhaust the defilements. Furthermore, a proponent of another view should be asked: 'Is this Ten Powers knowledge accompanied by initial and sustained application, with sustained application only, or without initial and sustained application? Is it of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere? Is it mundane or supramundane?' When asked, a knowledgeable person will say that the seven knowledges in sequence are accompanied by initial and sustained application. The knowledges after that...
337:
It will be said that the two subsequent knowledges are without applied and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra). It will be said that the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) is sometimes with applied and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra), sometimes with sustained thought only (avitakka-vicāramatta), and sometimes without applied and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra). Similarly, it will be said that, in sequence, seven knowledges belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the two knowledges following them belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and the final one is supramundane (lokuttara). However, it will be said that the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) is only with applied and sustained thought, only of the sense sphere, and only mundane (lokiya).

Having thus provided the word-by-word commentary on these Ten Powers (dasabalañāṇa) in sequence, now: first of all, the Blessed One, through the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa), sees the absence of the obstacle of defilement (kilesāvaraṇa), which is the cause for the attainment or non-attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of taints by beings to be led (veneyya). He sees this by seeing the cause of mundane right view and by seeing the absence of the cause of fixed wrong view. After seeing thus, He sees the absence of the obstacle of result (vipākāvaraṇa) in those beings through the knowledge of the results of kamma (kammavipakāñāṇa), by seeing their triple-rooted rebirth (tihetu-paṭisandhi). Through the knowledge of the way leading to all destinations (sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadāñāṇa), He sees the absence of the obstacle of kamma (kammāvaraṇa) by seeing the absence of kamma with immediate result (anantariya-kamma). For those beings who are thus without obstacles, He sees their specific conduct through the knowledge of many and various elements (anekadhātunānāဓာတုဉာဏ်) by seeing the diversity of elements, in order to give a suitable Dhamma teaching. Furthermore, through the knowledge of the various dispositions of beings (nānādhimuttikatañāṇa), He sees their inclinations, in order to teach the Dhamma according to their inclinations even if they have not yet made an effort. To teach the Dhamma to beings with such seen inclinations according to their capacity and strength, He sees the maturity or immaturity of their faculties through the knowledge of the degree of faculties of others (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa), by seeing the sharpness or dullness of faith and so on. If those beings whose maturity of faculties is thus known are far away, He quickly approaches them by means of special psychic power, being proficient in the first jhāna and so on. Having approached them, He sees their past habits through the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), and their present specific state of mind through the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇa) obtained by the power of the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇa); then, by the power of the knowledge of the destruction of taints, being free from delusion regarding the practice leading to the destruction of taints, He teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of taints. Therefore, it should be understood that these Ten Powers are spoken of in this sequence.

Regarding the words "Sāriputta, without abandoning that speech" and so on, one who says, "I will not speak such words again," is said to abandon that speech. One who thinks, "I will not let such a thought arise again," is said to abandon that thought. One who abandons by saying, "I will not hold such a view again," is said to relinquish that view. One who does not do so neither abandons nor relinquishes. It should be understood that such a person is just as if he were carried and placed in hell by the guardians of hell; he is indeed placed in hell.
338:
Now, wishing to show a simile that accomplishes the meaning of that phrase (such as "yathābhataṃ nikkhitto"), He spoke the words beginning with "seyyathāpi" (just as). In that passage, among the words beginning with "sīlasampanno" (endowed with virtue), mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom should be understood. It is also appropriate to explain them solely in terms of the supramundane. Indeed, this person is endowed with virtue through right speech, right action, and right livelihood; endowed with concentration through right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; and endowed with wisdom through right view and right intention. Sāriputta, just as that bhikkhu endowed with such qualities as virtue satisfies the fruit of Arahantship in this very life, in this very self-identity, or attains the fruit of Arahantship, I say this matter is exactly like that. This means that just as the fruit (phala) arises immediately after the path (magga) without fail, so too, for this person, rebirth in hell occurs immediately after death (cuti) without fail. In the entire word of the Buddha, the three Piṭakas, there is no simile spoken that is firmer than this simile.

In the word "vesārajjāni" (intrepidities), the quality that is the opposite of timidity (sārajja) is called intrepidity (vesārajja). This is the name for the knowledge accompanied by joy (somanassa) that arises in the Blessed One when He reviews His absence of timidity in four areas. "To you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One" (sammāsambuddha) means to You who acknowledge, "I am a Perfectly Enlightened One; all dhammas have been fully realized by Me." "Unrealized" (anabhisambuddhā) means "these certain dhammas have not been fully realized by You." "In that regard" (tatra vata) means "certainly in those dhammas shown as unrealized." "With reason" (sahadhammena) means with speech accompanied by cause and reason. Prattling like Sunakkhatta is not to be taken as a standard. In the phrase "this is a sign" (nimittametaṃ), both the person and the dhamma are intended as the "sign" (nimitta). The meaning here is: "I do not see that person who will challenge Me, nor do I see that dhamma by pointing out which one would challenge Me, saying, 'This certain dhamma has not been fully realized by You.'" "Attained security" (khemappatta) means reached safety; the remaining two terms are merely synonyms for this. All of this is spoken with reference to the knowledge of intrepidity (vesārajjañāṇa). For when the Possessor of the Ten Powers reviews, "I say 'I am a Buddha' while being a Buddha by nature, as I do not see any person who would challenge Me or any unrealized dhamma that would be a cause for challenge, saying 'this certain dhamma is not realized by You'," a very powerful joy arises. The knowledge associated with that joy is called intrepidity (vesārajja). With reference to that knowledge, He said "attained security" and so on. Thus, the meaning should be understood in all respects.

In the phrase "obstructive things" (antarāyikā dhammā), they are called obstructive because they create an obstacle. In terms of meaning, they are the seven classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha) committed intentionally. Indeed, an offense committed intentionally, even if it is as minor as a dukkaṭa or dubbhāsita, creates an obstacle to the paths and fruits. But here...
339:
Sexual intercourse is intended. For anyone who engages in sexual intercourse, it is undoubtedly an obstacle to the Paths and Fruits. "For the sake of which among them" means for the sake of the destruction of defilements, such as the destruction of lust. "The Dhamma has been taught" means the Dhamma such as the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā) has been taught. "In that, indeed, me" refers to me [the Buddha] in that non-emancipating doctrine conceived by others. The remaining words should be understood in the manner already stated.

## Commentary on the Eight Assemblies

Why was this teaching, "Sāriputta, there are these eight assemblies," undertaken? It was undertaken to show the power of the Knowledge of Intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa). To explain further: just as the skill of a Dhamma speaker is known by his ability to enter a prominent assembly and please the minds of the wise with a discourse capable of satisfying them, so too, by reaching these eight assemblies, the intrepid nature of the Knowledge of Intrepidity can be known. Thus, wishing to show the power of the Knowledge of Intrepidity, he said, "Sāriputta, there are these eight assemblies," and so on.

In that text, "the assembly of nobles" (khattiya-parisā) refers to the place where nobles have gathered and are seated; this method applies everywhere. The "assembly of Māras" (māra-parisā) should be understood as the place where the followers of Māra have gathered and are seated, not the Māras themselves. All these assemblies are taken in the sense of showing a formidable place. Humans are unable to say even ordinary words like "The king is sitting here," and sweat pours from their armpits. Thus, the assembly of nobles is formidable. Brahmins are skilled in the three Vedas; householders are skilled in various vocations and in the study of letters; and recluses (samaṇas) are skilled in their own doctrines and the doctrines of others. To deliver a Dhamma discourse in their midst is indeed a great burden. Non-humans (amanussas) are also formidable. At the mere mention of "non-human," the whole bodies of humans tremble; upon seeing their forms or hearing their sounds, beings lose consciousness. Thus, the assembly of non-humans is formidable. Delivering a Dhamma discourse in those assemblies is also a very great burden. Thus, it should be understood that they are taken in the sense of showing a formidable place.

"He enters" (ajjhogāhati) means he goes into. "Many hundreds of noble assemblies" refers to assemblies such as the meeting with King Bimbisāra, the meeting with relatives, and the meeting with the Licchavīs. It is also found in other world-systems (cakkavāḷas). If it is asked, "Does the Blessed One go to other world-systems as well?" the answer is, "Yes, he goes." In what form? Just as they are, so is he. Therefore, he [the Buddha] said—
340:
“Ānanda, I recall having approached many hundreds of assemblies of nobles. There, whatever their appearance was, such was my appearance. Whatever their voice was, such was my voice. I instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged them with a Dhamma talk. While I was speaking, they did not know me, wondering, ‘Who is this that speaks? Is it a deva or a human?’ Having instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged them with a Dhamma talk, I vanished. When I had vanished, they did not know me, wondering, ‘Who is this that has vanished? Is it a deva or a human?’” (DN 2.172).

Nobles are adorned with armlets, bracelets, garlands, perfumes, and so on, wearing clothes of various colors, wearing jeweled earrings, and bearing topknots. Does the Blessed One also adorn himself in this way? Those nobles may be fair-skinned, dark-skinned, or of a golden complexion. Does the Teacher also have such a nature? The Teacher goes only in his capacity as a renunciant, but he appears to them as having a form like theirs. He shows himself seated on the royal throne. Then, the thought occurs to those nobles, “Today our king is exceedingly radiant.” Those nobles may have broken voices, harsh voices, or voices like a crow's. The Teacher, however, speaks the Dhamma only with a Brahma-voice. The statement “My voice was like theirs” is said with reference to the specific language of that particular world-system. When people hear that voice, they think, “Today the king speaks with a sweet voice.” When the Blessed One has finished the discourse and departed, and they see the king return, the investigation arises, “Who was that?”

This is what is meant: “Who was this that just now, in this place, spoke in the Māgadha language or the Sīhaḷa language with a sweet voice and then vanished? Was it a deva or a human?” Why does he teach the Dhamma to those who do not know in this way? It is for the sake of establishing a habitual tendency (vāsanā). For Dhamma heard in this way becomes a supporting condition (paccaya) in the future. Thus, he teaches with the future in mind.

“Had sat together before” (sannisinna-pubbaṃ) means having previously sat together in a gathering. “Had talked together before” (sallapita-pubbaṃ) means having previously engaged in conversation. “Discussion” (sākacchā) means having previously engaged in Dhamma discussion. In phrases such as “many hundreds of assemblies of Brahmins,” the occurrence should be understood through events such as the meeting with Soṇadaṇḍa and through other world-systems.
342:
"...Brahma, I know the destination of [your] mind (ajjhāsayagati) and I know [your] splendor (juti).' In this passage, it is called 'destination of disposition' (ajjhāsayagati). 'Disappearance (vibhava) is the destination of phenomena; Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant.' In this passage, it is called 'destination of disappearance' (vibhavagati). 'There are only two destinations, no others.' In this passage, it is called 'destination of attainment' (nipphattigati). Among those, here 'rebirth destination' (gatigati) is intended.

In the words such as 'niraya' (hell), it is called 'niraya' because it is devoid of happiness (nirati) or because it is devoid of enjoyment (nirassāda). They are called 'animals' (tiracchāna) because they go horizontally (tiriyaṃ). Their species is the 'animal realm' (tiracchānayoni). It is called the 'realm of the departed' (pettivisaya) because it is the domain of those who have reached the state after death (pecca). They are called 'humans' (manussa) because of the prominence of the mind. They are called 'deities' (deva) because they sport with the five cords of sensual pleasure and their own powers. In the passages such as 'Sāriputta, I know hell,' 'hell' refers to the aggregates along with the location. The same method applies to the animal species and so on. By both terms 'magga' (path) and 'paṭipadā' (way), only the kamma that leads to the stated destination is shown. 'Yathā ca paṭipanno' (and how one has practiced) points to both the path and the practice together. In the words such as 'apāya,' it is called 'apāya' because it is devoid of 'aya,' which means growth or happiness. It is called 'duggati' (woeful destination) because it is the destination and refuge of suffering. It is called 'vinipāta' (perdition) because evildoers fall into it. 'I also know Nibbāna' is said to show that he knows not only the destinations of rebirth, but also Nibbāna, which is the escape from those destinations. Here, by both 'magga' and 'paṭipadā,' only the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is intended.

## Explanation of the Manner of Knowledge's Occurrence
Now, wishing to show the manner in which his knowledge occurs in the seven and eight places mentioned, he said, 'Sāriputta, here I...' and so on.

In that context, 'ekantadukkha' means constant suffering or uninterrupted suffering. 'Tibba' means intense. 'Kaṭuka' means harsh. 'Seyyathāpi' and so on are said for the purpose of showing a simile. There, 'kāsu' refers to a pit and also to a heap.

'Why, charioteer, are you digging a pit (kāsu) in such a hurry? Tell me, friend, when I ask you, what will you do with the pit?' In this verse, a pit is called 'kāsu'.
343:
“Other people, with their bodies burnt all around, fall into the pit of glowing coals, weeping” (as stated in the Jātaka). 

In this (Jātaka), the word 'kāsu' refers to a heap. However, in this (Mahāsīhanāda Sutta), a pit is intended. Therefore, it is said, “exceeding a man’s height.” In that term 'sādhika-porisa', it is called 'sādhika-porisa' because the measurement in that pit exceeds a man’s height; it means it is more than five cubits. The phrase “without flames or smoke” is spoken to show the intensity of the heat. This is because when there are flames or smoke, wind arises, and due to that wind, the heat is not as intense. 'Ghamma-pareto' means one who is followed by heat (oppressed by heat). 'Tasito' means one in whom craving (thirst) has arisen. 'Pipāsito' means one who desires to drink water. 'Ekāyanena maggena' means by a path that is a single way, a road from which one cannot deviate because of the continuous thickets of thorn trees on both sides. 'Paṇidhāya'—there is no such thing as an 'aspiration' for a pit of glowing coals; however, because the posture is set directed toward the pit of glowing coals, it is spoken thus.

In the phrase 'evameva kho', this is the comparison of the simile. Hell (Niraya) should be understood as the pit of glowing coals. The karma leading to hell should be understood as the path going to the pit of glowing coals. The person possessed of that karma should be understood as the person who has entered the path. The Blessed One, endowed with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), should be understood as the man with sight. Just as that man, seeing the person who has entered the path, knows, “This person, going by this path, will fall into the pit of glowing coals,” in the same way, the Blessed One, seeing someone performing any karma such as killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), knows, “This person, having done this karma, will be reborn in hell.” Just as that man later sees him fallen into the pit of glowing coals, in the same way, the Blessed One later, wondering “Where was that person reborn after doing that karma?”, increases the light and, looking with the divine eye, sees him reborn in hell, experiencing great suffering such as the fivefold binding (pañca-vidha-bandhana). In that case, although the appearance of the person while performing the karma is one way, and the appearance when reborn in hell is another, yet to the Blessed One who is looking with the thought, “Where was that being reborn after doing that karma?”, even if that being is standing in the midst of many thousands of beings, the realization “This is that very person” appears clearly. This is called “the power of the divine eye.”

In the second simile (the cesspool simile), because there is no intense heat in a cesspool as there is in a pit of glowing coals, He did not say “it is exclusively painful,” but said “it is painful,” and so on. In this case also, the comparison of the simile should be understood in the same manner as the previous method. This person also, the Blessed One...
344:
...sees him reborn in any state among animal births such as the elephant kind, experiencing great suffering through beating, binding, dragging, and being pulled from place to place.

In the third simile, 'tanu-patta-palāsa' does not mean having leaves as thin as a layer of clouds, but this is said in reference to that tree having sparse leaves. 'Kabara-chāyo' means having sparse shade. 'Dukkha-bahulā' is said because in the realm of hungry ghosts (petti-visaya), suffering is predominant, and happiness is very slight and only to be experienced occasionally. In this simile also, the comparison between the simile and the subject should be understood in the same manner as the previous method.

In the fourth simile, 'bahala-patta-palāsa' means covered with leaves without any gaps. 'Santa-chāyo' means having dense shade like a stone umbrella. 'Sukha-bahulā vedanā' means that in the human world, among families such as the noble class (khattiya), one experiences feelings that are mostly pleasant; it shows that He sees him experiencing those feelings while either lying down or sitting. Here also, the comparison of the simile should be understood in the same manner as the previous method.

In the fifth simile, 'pāsādo' means a long mansion. 'Ullittāvalitta' means a building that is plastered with mortar paintings on the inside and smoothly plastered with mortar on the outside. 'Phusitaggaḷa' means having door leaves that are well-fitted together with the doorposts. 'Gonakatthatā' means spread with a black wool carpet having fleece longer than four inches. 'Paṭikatthatā' means spread with a white covering made of wool. 'Paṭalikatthatā' means spread with a wool covering thick with floral designs. 'Kadalimiga-pavara-paccattharaṇā' means spread with an excellent rug made from the hide of the kadali-deer. It is said that they make that rug by placing the kadali-deer hide over a white cloth and sewing them together. 'Sauttaracchadā' means being together with a red canopy fastened above. 'Ubhato-lohita-kūpadhānā' means having red pillows placed at both ends of the couch, namely a head-pillow and a foot-pillow. Here also, the comparison of the simile should be understood in the same manner as the previous method.

Furthermore, the application in this context is: Just as that man knows a person who has entered the path, “This person, going by this path, will ascend the mansion, enter the gabled chamber, and either sit or lie down on the couch,” in the same way, the Blessed One, upon merely seeing a person performing any wholesome karma among the bases of meritorious action (puñña-kiriya-vatthu) such as giving (dāna), knows, “This person, having done this merit, will be reborn in the celestial world.” Just as that man...
345:
Later, just as that man, having ascended that palace and entered the upper chamber, would see [himself] sitting or lying on a couch, experiencing absolute and continuous happy feeling; so too, the Blessed One, at a later time, wondering "Where was this person reborn after performing that good deed?", increases the light [of the kasina] and, looking with the divine eye, sees him reborn in the heavenly realm, enjoying divine splendor surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs in the Nandana Grove and so on.

## Commentary on the Section on the Destruction of Taints

In the section on the destruction of taints, it is not said "with the divine eye" but "I see him." Why? Because there is no restriction. This person can be seen with the divine eye, known with the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), and certainly known with the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). The phrase "absolute happy feeling" (ekantasukha vedanā) is the same as heavenly happiness in terms of wording, but different in meaning. Heavenly happiness is not absolute happiness because the fever of passion (rāga) still exists. Only the happiness of Nibbāna is absolute happiness in every way because all fevers have been stilled. Even in the simile, it says "as if there is absolute happiness in the palace," but that is not yet absolute happiness because the fatigue of the journey has not subsided, and there may be hunger and thirst. Only the happiness of a person who descends into a pond in the forest, washes away dust and dirt, stills the fatigue of the journey, eats lotus roots and stalks, drinks sweet water, thus removing hunger and thirst, changes into fresh clothes, wearing fine cloth, using a bag of rice as a pillow, squeezing out the water-cloth and placing it on the chest, and lies down being fanned by a gentle breeze—that is absolute happiness in every way.

Comparing this simile: The pond should be seen as the Noble Path. The path to the pond is like the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapatipadā). The person on the path is like the practitioner endowed with the practice. The man with sight is like the Blessed One with the divine eye. The forest is like Nibbāna. Just as that man, upon seeing the person on the path, knows: "This person, going by this path, will bathe in the pond and sit or lie down at the foot of a tree in the delightful forest"; so too, the Blessed One, seeing a person who is still fulfilling the practice, still delimiting mind and matter, still discerning causes, and still practicing insight (vipassanā) on the three characteristics, knows: "This person, having fulfilled this practice and exhausted all taints, [will attain] the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) called the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom..."
346:
...and will dwell having attained it." Just as that man later sees [the other] bathing in that square pond, entering the forest, and sitting or lying down, experiencing absolute happy feeling; so too, the Blessed One later sees that person, having fulfilled the practice, developed the path, and realized the fruit, reaching the noble state of the bed of cessation (nirodha), and entering the attainment of fruition with Nibbāna as the object, experiencing absolute happy feeling.

## Explanation of Purity through Austerities and so on

"Sāriputta, I recall having practiced the fourfold [austerity]"; why was this discourse started? It was started by way of a specific connection. It is said that this Sunakkhatta held the view that purity comes through the practice of austerities. Then, the Blessed One started this discourse to show him: "I, while remaining in one existence, performed difficult austerities endowed with four factors; there is no one like me who is a doer of difficult things. If there were purity through difficult austerities, I alone would be the pure one." Furthermore, this Sunakkhatta was pleased with difficult austerities, and his state of being pleased is to be understood according to the method in the Pāthika Sutta: "Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi prince saw Korakkhattiya, the naked ascetic, who went on all fours, crouched on the ground, and ate food with his mouth like a dog. Seeing him, he thought: 'Friends, this ascetic is indeed of good nature; going on all fours, he eats with his mouth alone the food thrown on the ground; he eats with his mouth alone,'" and so on.

Then the Blessed One, thinking: "This man is pleased with difficult austerities; I too, while remaining in this existence, performed difficult austerities endowed with four factors; though he is pleased with difficult austerities, he should be pleased with me, yet he has no such devotion toward me," started this discourse to show this.

In that context, "Brahmacariya" refers to giving (dāna), service (veyyāvacca), the precepts (sikkhāpada), the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), teaching the Dhamma, abstinence from sexual intercourse, contentment with one's own wife, observing the Uposatha, the Noble Path, the entire Dispensation (sāsana), intention (ajjhāsaya), and energy (vīriya).
347:
“O Nāga King, what is your practice (vow)? What is your holy life (brahmacariya)? By the result of what well-performed merit do you possess such psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy? Is this your great celestial mansion?

O Wise One, in the human world, both my wife and I were faithful donors. At that time, my house was like a well or a pond, and we satisfied recluses and brahmins.

That deed is my practice (vow); that deed itself is the holy life (brahmacariya). By the result of that well-performed merit, I possess psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy. O Wise One, this is indeed my great celestial mansion.” (He answered).

In this Punnakajātaka, giving (dāna) is called brahmacariya.

“Why does your palm grant whatever is desired? Why does honey flow from your palm? By what holy life does the fruit of merit manifest in your palm?

By such (service) the palm grants whatever is desired; by such a deed honey flows from the palm; by that holy life (service), the fruit of merit manifests in my palm.” (He said).

In this Aṅkurapetavatthu, service (veyyāvacca) is called brahmacariya. In the Tittirijātaka, in the words, “Monks, thus was that holy life called Tittiriya in the past,” the five precepts (pañcasīla) are called brahmacariya. In the Mahāgovindasutta, in the words, “Pañcasikha, that holy life of mine does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, but only to rebirth in the Brahma world,” the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) are called brahmacariya. In the verse, “Established in a single holy life, a thousand people transcended death,” the teaching of the Dhamma (dhammadesanā) is called brahmacariya. In the Sallekhasutta, in the words, “Others will be unchaste, but here we shall be chaste (brahmacārī),” abstaining from sexual intercourse (methunavirati) is called brahmacariya.
348:
“We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us. Apart from those wives, we practice the holy life with other women; therefore, our young ones do not die.” (J. 1.10.97). In the Mahādhammapālajātaka, contentment with one's own wife (sadārasantosa) is called brahmacariya.

“Through low brahmacariya, one is born in a royal family; through middling brahmacariya, one attains divinity; through supreme brahmacariya, one is purified from defilements.” (J. 1.8.75). Thus, in the Nimijātaka, the eightfold uposatha observed by way of self-restraint (attadamana) is called brahmacariya.

“Pañcasikha, this holy life of mine leads to absolute disenchantment, to dispassion... this is the Noble Eightfold Path.” (DN 2.329). In the Mahāgovindasutta, the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is called brahmacariya.

“This holy life is successful, prosperous, widespread, known by many, and extensive, well-proclaimed among devas and humans.” (DN 3.174). In the Pāsādikasutta, the Dispensation (sāsana) comprising the three trainings (sikkhattaya) is called brahmacariya.

“Gāmaṇi, for those who act without haste, the expectation of fruit is fulfilled. Know thus: I am one whose holy life is mature.” (J. 1.1.8). Here, intention (ajjhāsaya) is called brahmacariya. However, here energy (vīriya) is intended as brahmacariya. This very sutta is evidence for energy as brahmacariya. That brahmacariya is said to be endowed with four factors because four difficult tasks were performed in a single existence.

In the phrase “I was an ascetic (tapassī),” the word ‘sudaṃ’ is a mere particle; it means “I was one who relied on practice.” ‘Paramatapassī’ means a supreme ascetic, the best among those who rely on practice. “I was coarse (lūkha)” means I was one who lived austerely. ‘Jegucchī’ means one who loathes evil. “I was secluded (pavivitta)” means I was one who lived in solitude. “Sāriputta, in that practice, this was my deed” means “In that fourfold holy life, my state of being an ascetic was thus; in the state of relying on practice, my state of being an ascetic, such as not wearing clothes, occurred.”
349:
Among those practices, *acelaka* refers to one who is unclothed, a naked ascetic. *Muttācāra* refers to one whose conduct is loose, being devoid of the conduct of worldly sons of good family; such a person performs acts like defecating, urinating, and eating while standing, detached from the social norms of noble laymen. *Hatthāpalekhana* refers to licking one's hand with the tongue while food is still in the hand, or it indicates wiping with the hand after defecating, perceiving the hand itself as a piece of wood. It is said they designate a piece of wood as a living being; therefore, desiring to fulfill their practice, they acted in this way. Because he does not come even when told, 'Come, venerable sir,' to receive alms, he is called *na-ehibhaddantika*. Because he does not stop even when told, 'Stop, venerable sir,' he is called *na-tiṭṭhabhaddantika*. The heretics do not perform both of these actions, thinking, 'If I do this, it would amount to following his words.' He shows, 'I too have acted in that way.' *Abhihaṭa* means alms-food brought in advance. *Uddissakata* means alms-food about which it is announced, 'This was prepared specifically for you, venerable sir.' *Nimantana* means not accepting or taking alms-food invited by saying, 'Please come to such-and-such a family, street, or village.'

He does not accept alms-food given by taking it out of a pot (*kumbhi*). He does not accept alms-food given from a small jar or basket (*kaḷopi*). Why? Because he fears that the pot or basket might be struck with a ladle on his account. He does not accept alms-food given across a threshold (*eḷaka*). Why? Because he thinks, 'This person is obtaining an obstruction because of me.' The same method applies to sticks and pestles. He does not accept alms-food given by one of two people eating who gets up to give. Why? Because it would interfere with the mouthful of the one eating. Regarding the terms 'not from a pregnant woman' and so on, he does not accept it because the child in the womb of the pregnant woman might be distressed, or it would interfere with the milk of the child of a nursing mother, or it would interfere with the pleasure (*rati*) of a woman who is with a man. *Saṅkittī* refers to meals prepared collectively. It is said that during times of famine, the disciples of the naked ascetics collect rice and so on from various places for the sake of the naked ascetics and cook a meal. The preeminent naked ascetic does not accept even that meal.

In a place where a dog is waiting, thinking, 'I will get a morsel of food,' he does not accept food brought without giving it to that dog. Why? Because it would interfere with the dog's morsel. *Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī* refers to flies that fly in swarms. If people, seeing a naked ascetic, enter the kitchen thinking, 'We will give alms to this person,' and as they enter, the flies hiding in the jars and so on fly up and move about in swarms.
350:
He does not accept alms-food brought from there. Why? Because he considers, 'An interference with the feeding ground of the flies has occurred because of me.' I too have acted in that way. *Na thusodakaṃ* refers to *loṇasovīraka* medicine made from all kinds of grain ingredients. In this context, only the drinking of intoxicants is blameworthy, but this naked ascetic perceives all of it as blameworthy.

*Ekāgārika* is one who returns after receiving alms from only one house. *Ekālopika* is one who subsists on only one mouthful. The same method applies to terms like *dvāgārika* (two houses) and so on. *Ekissāpi dattiyā* means eating from a single small bowl. A *datti* is a small bowl in which the first portion of alms-food is placed. *Ekāhika* means eating every other day. *Addhamāsika* means eating once every half-month. *Pariyāyabhattabhojana* means eating meals by rotation. This refers to eating meals brought according to a rotation of days, such as a one-day rotation, two-day rotation, seven-day rotation, or half-month rotation.

*Sākabhakkha* is one who eats green vegetables. *Sāmākabhakkha* is one who eats millet. Among the terms like *nīvāra*, *nīvāra* refers to a type of rice that grows spontaneously in the forest. *Daddula* refers to the scraps of hide discarded by leather-workers after scraping the hide. *Haṭa* refers to water-moss, or the resin of trees like the *kaṇikāra*. *Kaṇa* refers to rice-bran. *Ācāma* refers to the burnt rice (crust) sticking to the rice pot; he takes and eats it from the place where it is discarded. Some also call it 'rice-scum.' Terms like *piññāka* (sesame press-cake) are well-known. *Pavattaphalabhojī* is one who eats fallen fruit.

*Sāṇāni* are garments made of hemp. *Masāṇāni* are garments made of mixed fibers. *Chavadussāni* are cloths discarded from a corpse, or garments made by weaving *eraka* grass and so on. *Paṃsukူလာနိ* are rags discarded on the ground. *Tirītāni* are garments made of tree bark. *Ajina* is the skin of the *ajina* antelope. *Ajinakkhipa* is that same skin split down the middle. It is also called *sakhuraka*. *Kusacīra* is a garment made by weaving *kusa* grass. The same method applies to *vākacīra* (bark-fiber) and *phalakacīra* (wooden-slat) garments. *Kesakambala* is a blanket made of human hair. Regarding this, it was said: 'Monks, of all woven garments, a hair-blanket is said to be the worst. Monks, a hair-blanket is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly in color, bad in smell, and unpleasant to the touch.' *Vālakambala* is a blanket made of horsehair and so on. *Ulūkapakkhaka* is a garment made by weaving owl feathers. *Ubbaṭṭhaka* is one who always remains standing. *Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutta* is one who is devoted to the exertion of squatting; even when moving, he does so while squatting...
351: He goes jumping and jumping. 'Kaṇṭakāpassayika' (lying on a bed of thorns) means he drives either iron thorns or natural thorns into the ground, spreads a hide over them, and demonstrates, 'I shall perform standing, walking, and so forth there.' 'Seyyaṃ' (bed) means he intends, 'Even when sleeping, I shall take my rest only upon those thorns.' 'Sāyatatiyaka' (having evening as the third) is so called because the evening is the third [time]. It shows that he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water, thinking, 'I shall wash away evil three times a day—morning, noon, and evening.' 'Nekavassagaṇika' means produced through many groups of years. 'Rajojalla' means dirt and filth; he says this referring to the time he undertook the practice of bearing dirt and filth. 'Jegucchismiṃ' means in the state of loathing evil. 'Yāva udakabindumhipi' (even down to a drop of water) means, 'My compassion was established even toward a drop of water; what need is there to mention other things like pebbles, potsherds, rods, or sand?' Those of wrong view designate a drop of water and those pebbles, potsherds, etc., as small living beings. Therefore, he said, 'My compassion was established even toward a drop of water.' I do not kill or destroy even a drop of water. For what reason? 'Lest I cause the destruction of small beings that have come into uneven places.' This means, 'Lest I cause the slaughter or destruction of small beings known as water drops that have reached uneven places such as hollows, high ground, tips of grass, or tree branches.' He shows this meaning by saying, 'I step forward only with mindfulness.' Among the naked ascetics (Acelakas), it is said there is no such thing as being 'virtuous' from the moment they step on the ground. Even when going for alms, they go as those without virtue; when eating in the houses of supporters, they eat as those without virtue; and when returning, they return as those without virtue. However, when they sweep a plank with peacock feathers, undertake a vow of virtue, and sit down, only then are they called 'virtuous.' 'Vanakammika' refers to one who wanders in the forest for the sake of roots, tubers, and various fruits. 'Vanena vanaṃ' means from forest to forest; this method applies everywhere. 'Sampatāmi' means I go. 'Āraññaka' means one born and raised in the forest; he says this referring to the time he was an Ājīvaka. It is said that the Bodhisatta entered that renunciation [of other sects] to win over those of other sects, but even though he knew it was useless, he did not leave the monkhood. This is because when Bodhisattas reach any state, they are of a nature not to turn back from it. After renouncing, he entered the forest, thinking, 'Let no one see me.' Therefore, he said, 'May they not see me, and may I not see them.' 'Goṭṭhā' means cowsheds. 'Paṭṭhitagāvo' means cows that have gone out. In that context, 'Catukkuṇḍika' (on all fours) refers to the state of being separated from the cowherds' cows while remaining in the forest...
352:
...seeing [the calves], he places two hands and two knees on the ground, thus approaching on all fours. 'I ate those [calf dung]' means the dung of old cows is fibrous and lacks essence; therefore, avoiding those, he ate to his fill the nutrient-rich dung of young calves that grow only by drinking milk, and then re-entered the forest grove. Referring to that, he said, 'I ate those.' 'As long as my [excrement]' means for as long as my own urine and excrement were not exhausted. The meaning is, 'As long as the use of the [bodily] gates (defecation) continued for me, I ate only that [excrement].' As time went on, when his flesh and blood were exhausted and the function of the gates was cut off, he ate the dung of calves. 'In the great loathsome food' means in the great repulsive food, meaning food that has abandoned its natural state.

"There, Sāriputta, in the fearfulness of that fearful forest grove it was so"—in this passage, the word 'Tatra' refers back to the previous statement. 'Sudaṃ' is a particle used merely to complete the verse. 'Sāriputta' is an address. Here is the connection of the meaning: 'Tatra' refers to what was called 'a certain fearful forest grove'; in that fearful forest grove mentioned, in its fearfulness, the act of fearing occurs. What happens? This happens: 'Whoever is not free from lust... (enters), his hair stands on end.'

Alternatively, 'Tatra' is a locative case with a possessive meaning (sāmī-attha). 'Su' is a particle as in "Kiṃ su nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā," etc. 'Idaṃ' is a word showing the intended meaning as if before one's eyes. 'Sudaṃ' is 'Su' + 'Idaṃ'; it should be understood that the letter 'i' is dropped due to sandhi. It is like in "cakkhundriyaṃ, itthindriyaṃ, anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ, kiṃ sūdhavittaṃ," etc. Here is the connection of the meaning: 'Sāriputta, in the fearfulness of that fearful forest grove, this [fearing] occurred.' 'Bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ' means in the state of being fearful. It should be seen that one letter 'ta' is dropped. Or the original reading is 'Bhiṃsanakattasmiṃ.' Or where it should be said 'Bhiṃsanakatāya,' a change of gender has been made. This locative case is in the sense of cause (nimittattha). Therefore, the connection should be understood thus: 'In the state of being fearful, this [fearing] occurs; because of the state of being fearful, by reason of the state of being fearful, due to the state of being fearful, this [fearing] occurs.' Whoever is not free from lust enters that forest grove. Generally, his hair...
353:
The hairs [of the body] stood up in great numbers. They stood facing upwards, being like needles and like thorns. A few hairs did not stand up. Or it means that for many beings, the hair stands on end, but for a few extremely brave men, the hair does not stand on end.

*Antaraṭṭhaka* refers to the eight nights between the two months: the last four days of the month of Māgha and the first four days of the month of Phagguna. 'In the open' means that the Bodhisatta stayed in the open during the nights when snow fell. At that time, drops of frost stayed in the pores of the Bodhisatta like strings of pearls. The body was as if covered with a white silk cloth. 'In the forest during the day' means that although one might find relief during the day when the frost drops disappear due to the heat of the sun, this Bodhisatta entered the forest as soon as the sun rose. Even in that forest, the frost melting from the sun's heat fell upon his body. 'Staying in the open during the day and in the forest at night' means that during the summer, he stayed in the open during the day. Because of that, streams of sweat flowed from his armpits. Although one might find relief at night, this Bodhisatta entered the forest as soon as the sun set. Then, his body was scorched within the forest, which still held the heat of the day, as if he had been thrown into a pit of glowing coals. *Anacchariyā* means not wonderful (*anu-acchariya*). *Paṭibhāsī* means it appeared or became clear.

*Sotatto* means scorched by the heat of the sun during the day and by the heat of the forest at night. *Sosinno* means thoroughly soaked by frost at night and by frost-water during the day. *Bhiṃsanake* means in a forest that causes terror. *Naggo* means being without clothes. It is intended to show that if there were clothes, ornaments, or a cloak, one might not suffer excessively from the cold or heat, but he did not even have that. He was also one who did not warm himself by a fire. *Esanāpasuto* means one who strives to seek purity. *Munī* means at that time he spoke of himself, regarding himself as a sage (*muni*).

*Chavaṭṭhikāni* means skeletons or bones that are about half-burnt. *Upadhāya* means to show that he made his bed there, arranging them so that head-rests and foot-rests were apparent, and slept upon those skeletons. *Gāmaṇḍalā* means cowherd boys. It is said that those boys went to the Bodhisatta and said, 'O Sumedha, why are you sitting in this place? Tell us.' The Bodhisatta sat with his face cast down and said nothing. Then those boys, saying 'We will not let you go until you speak,' surrounded him, spat on him, and let saliva fall on his body.
354:
Even when they did this, the Bodhisatta did not speak. Then those boys, saying 'Will you not speak?', urinated upon him, releasing their urine over the Bodhisatta. Even then, the Bodhisatta did not speak. Then, saying 'Speak! Speak!', they scattered dust over him. Even then, the Bodhisatta did not speak. Then, saying 'Will you not speak?', they took small sticks and bamboo splints and thrust them into his ear-holes. The Bodhisatta, enduring the intense and bitter painful feelings, remained as still as a corpse, thinking, 'I will not do anything to anyone.' Therefore, he said, 'Sāriputta, I do not remember (there was not) any evil thought arising toward them.' It means that I did not allow even an evil thought to arise toward them. '*Upekkhā-vihārasmiṃ hoti*' means dwelling in equanimity. '*Vihāra*' itself is meant by '*vihārasmiṃ*'. Therefore, here in '*idaṃsu me*', the meaning should be understood as '*ayaṃsu me*'. In this way, other such terms should also be understood. By this, he shows the dwelling in equanimity (*upekkhā-vihāra*) that he fulfilled ninety-one aeons ago from now. Referring to that, he said:

'Though I reach happiness, I do not rejoice; in suffering, I am not dejected. I am balanced in all things; this is my Perfection of Equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*).'

## Explanation of Purity through Food

Purity through food means there are those who hold the view that one can be purified by a small amount of food, such as jujube fruits (*kola*), etc. '*Evamāhaṃsu*' means they spoke in this way. '*Kolehi*' means with jujube fruits. '*Kolodakaṃ*' means a drink made by crushing jujube fruits. '*Kolavikatiṃ*' means various kinds of jujube products, such as jujube cakes, jujube jam, etc. '*Etaparamo*' means one for whom this much is the maximum. It means that ninety-one aeons ago, the jujube fruit was not as large as a wood-apple or a palmyra fruit, but was only the size of a jujube fruit of the present time.

'*Adhimattakasimānaṃ*' means the state of being extremely emaciated. '*Āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā*' shows that his limbs and parts of the body became like the joints of the *āsītika* creeper or the *kāḷa* creeper, which wither at the joints and bulge in the middle. '*Oṭṭhapadaṃ*' means that just as a camel's footprint is deep in the middle, because the Bodhisatta's flesh and blood had withered and his rectum had sunk inwards, his buttocks were deep in the middle.
355:
It was raised in the middle like a mark stepped on by the notch of an arrow. 'Vaṭṭanāvaḷī' means that just as a string of beads threaded with a cord is sunken between the beads and raised where the beads are, similarly, the backbone was uneven, being high and low. 'Jarathālāya gopānasiyo' means the rafters of a dilapidated hall; they have come loose from the ridgepole and rest on the roof-ring, or having come loose from the roof-ring, they rest on the ground. In this way, one rafter is above and another is below, being in a state of disarray. However, for the Bodhisatta, the ribs were not like that. For when the Bodhisatta's blood had dried up and his flesh had wasted away, the skin between the ribs sank downwards. It is in reference to this that these words were spoken.

'Okkāyikā' refers to the eyes that have sunken downwards. Indeed, when the Bodhisatta's blood had dried up and his flesh had wasted away, the eye-sockets remained touching the brain. Because of that, such pupils appeared in the Bodhisatta's eyes. 'Āmakacchinna' refers to a bitter gourd that has been plucked when it is very tender. Just as that gourd withers when exposed to the wind and the heat of the sun, it was like that. 'Yāvassu me Sāriputta' means 'Sāriputta, the skin of my belly clung to my backbone.' Or else, the connection of meaning here should be understood as: 'Sāriputta, while I was practicing the austerities which were extremely difficult, the skin of my belly clung to my backbone.' When it is said, 'I would grasp only the backbone,' it means grasping it together with the skin of the belly. When it is said, 'I would grasp only the skin of the belly,' it means grasping it together with the backbone. 'I fell forward' means that when he sat down to defecate or urinate, the urine did not come out at all, and only one or two pieces of excrement came out. This caused intense pain. Sweat poured from his body, and he fell forward on the ground right there. Therefore, it was said, 'I fell forward.' 'That very body' refers to the body of ninety-one aeons ago. However, in the Mahāsaccaka Sutta, 'this very body' was said in reference to the body of the final existence.
