'With rotting roots' means that as long as there is flesh or blood, the hairs remain firm. But in their absence, like hairs on a piece of hide, they come off in the hand just by stroking them with the hand. In reference to this, it was said, 'The hairs, rotting at the roots, fell from the body.'

'The extraordinary noble knowledge and vision capable of making one a Noble One' refers to the supramundane Path (lokuttara-magga). 'Because of not attaining this noble wisdom' means because of not attaining insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). 'Which is this noble wisdom' refers to the Path-wisdom that is attained. The meaning of this statement is: just as Path-wisdom is attained now because of attaining insight-wisdom, so too...
356:
The meaning is that because of not attaining insight-wisdom ninety-one aeons ago, I did not attain supramundane Path-wisdom. However, the Elders who were Reciters of the Middle Length Discourses (Majjhima-bhāṇaka) said that both the wisdom referred to as 'by this wisdom alone' and the wisdom referred to as 'which is this noble wisdom' are indeed Path-wisdom. Then the monks asked, 'Venerable sirs, if that is so, does this mean that because the Path was not yet attained, I did not attain the Path?' They replied, 'Friends, although we cannot clearly explain the reason, both are indeed Path-wisdom.' In this matter, this explanation alone is appropriate. Otherwise, the designation 'which is this' would be unsuitable.

## Explanation of Purification through Saṃsāra and so forth
'Saṃsārena suddhi' means they say that one is purified by wandering for a long time in saṃsāra. 'Upapattiyā suddhi' means they say that one is purified by being reborn many times. 'Āvāsena suddhi' means they say that one is purified by dwelling in many places. In all three cases, it refers only to the aggregates (khandhas): 'saṃsāra' by way of wandering, 'upapatti' by way of being reborn, and 'āvāsa' by way of dwelling. 'Yaññena' means they say that one is purified by performing many sacrifices. 'Muddhāvasittena' means by the status of a king whose head has been anointed through the three types of royal consecration. 'Aggipāricariyāya' means they say that one is purified by much fire-worship.

'Daharo' means a young person. 'Yuvā' means one endowed with youth. 'Susukāḷakeso' means one with very black hair. By the phrase 'endowed with auspicious youth,' it is shown that the youth of a young man endowed with such youth is auspicious and beautiful. 'Paṭhamena vayasā' means being endowed with the first stage of life, which is thirty-three years. 'Paññāveyyattiyena' means by way of maturity and proficiency in wisdom. 'Jiṇṇo' means one decayed by old age. 'Vuddho' means one whose limbs and organs have fully grown. 'Mahallako' means one who is senior by birth. 'Addhagato' means one who has traveled a long journey, one who has passed through a long time. 'Vayo anuppatto' means one who has reached the final stage of life, the third portion of a hundred-year lifespan. It is said that the Blessed One taught this sutta in the year of his Parinibbāna. Therefore, he spoke thus: 'My age has reached eighty.' 'Paramāya' means with supreme power. In the words beginning with 'satiyā,' the power to grasp even a hundred or a thousand phrases while they are being recited is called 'sati' (mindfulness/memory). The power to retain and firmly bind that which has been grasped is called 'gati' (retention/course). The lesson thus grasped and retained...
357:
The energy capable of performing recitation is called dhiti (fortitude). The state of being capable of demonstrating the meaning and the cause (Pali) of those things learned, retained, and recited is called paññāveyyattiya (proficiency of wisdom).

'Daḷhadhammā dhanuggaho' refers to an archer who stands holding a strong bow. A 'daḷhadhanu' (strong bow) refers to a bow that can bear a weight of two thousand. A bow that can bear a weight of two thousand means a bow that, when the weight of copper, iron, lead, etc., tied to the fixed bowstring is held by the bow-staff and lifted to the length of an arrow, can be released from the ground. 'Sikkhito' refers to one who has studied the arts under a teacher for ten or twelve years. 'Katahattho' refers to the fact that some people only learn the art but lack manual dexterity; this archer, however, is one who has manual dexterity due to having practiced and attained mastery (vasībhāva). 'Katūpāsano' refers to one who has already demonstrated his art in the presence of royalty and so on. 'Lahukena asanena' refers to shooting with an extremely light arrow that has been made hollow inside, filled with cotton etc., and finished with a coating of lac. Because it is made this way, an arrow capable of reaching a distance of one usabha goes two usabhas; an arrow capable of reaching eight usabhas goes sixteen usabhas. 'Appakasirena' means without difficulty (easily). 'Atipāteyya' means it would surpass or exceed.

'Evaṃ adhimattasatimanto' means that just as that archer can swiftly cause an arrow to surpass a shadow the length of a span and four finger-breadths, so too are they capable of learning, retaining, and reciting hundreds of phrases and thousands of phrases, and of investigating their meanings and causes. 'Aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitā' means that eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting must be performed by the Blessed One as well as by the bhikkhus. Therefore, it is stated by setting aside the time spent merely for such eating and drinking.

'Apariyādinnāyeva' means only while not yet exhausted. If one bhikkhu asks about the contemplation of the body, another about the contemplation of feelings, another about the contemplation of the mind, and another about the contemplation of mental objects—they do not look at one another thinking, 'I will ask what this person asks.' Even when this is the case, their turns are evident. In this way, however, the turn of the Buddhas is not evident; even before the shadow surpasses the length of a span and four finger-breadths, the Blessed One expounds the fourteen-fold contemplation of the body, the nine-fold contemplation of feelings, the sixteen-fold contemplation of the mind, and the five-fold contemplation of mental objects. Or let those four stay for a while. If four others were to ask questions on the right efforts, others on the bases of power, another five on the faculties, another five on the powers, another seven on the factors of enlightenment, and another eight on the path factors, the Blessed One would expound those as well. Or let those eight stay for a while. If another thirty-seven persons were to ask regarding the factors of enlightenment...
358:
...were to ask questions, the Blessed One would answer those questions at that very moment. Why? Because in the time it takes for ordinary worldly people to speak one word, the Elder Ānanda can speak eight words. While the Elder Ānanda is speaking just one word, the Blessed One can speak sixteen words. Why? Because the Blessed One's tongue is soft, his lips and teeth are well-aligned, his speech is uninterrupted, and the transition of his life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is rapid. Therefore, He said: 'Sāriputta, the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata is indeed undiminished.'

In that context, 'dhammadassanā' means the establishment of the Pali text. 'Dhammapadabyañjana' means the phrasing of the Pali, the syllables that express each respective meaning. 'Pañhapratibhāna' means the answering of questions. What is shown by this? In the past, when the Tathāgata was young, He was able to combine syllables to speak a word, combine words to speak a verse, and speak the meaning of a verse composed of four, eight, or sixteen syllables. Now, in old age, it is not the case that He is unable to combine syllables to speak a word, or combine words to speak a verse, or speak the meaning of a verse. He shows this fact: that in both youth and old age, all this remains undiminished for the Tathāgata. The phrase 'even if I must be carried by a litter' was spoken by imagining it only to demonstrate the power of the Buddha. There is no time when the Possessor of Ten Powers is placed on a litter and carried around villages, market towns, and royal capitals. This is because the Tathāgatas, in the fifth stage of life, pass away into Parinibbāna without being overcome by broken teeth and so on, before the golden-colored body reaches discoloration, and only at a time when they are beloved and pleasing to devas and humans.

'Nāgasamālo' is the name of that Elder. Within the first twenty years after the Enlightenment, this Elder was also an attendant of the Blessed One, just like the Elders Upavāna, Nāgita, and Meghiya. 'Vījayamāno' means creating a pleasant temperature for the Blessed One with the gentle breeze of a palmyra-leaf fan. 'He said this' means that having heard the entire sutta and having become confident by referring to the difficult practices performed by the Blessed One in the past, he spoke these words: 'It is wonderful, Bhante,' and so on. In that context, 'acchariya' (wonderful) refers to something that makes one want to snap one's fingers. 'Abbhuta' (marvelous) refers to something unprecedented that has come into being. By both terms, he demonstrates his own amazement. 'What is the name of this discourse, Bhante?'—this was said with the intention: 'This Dhamma discourse is truly excellent; indeed, I shall request the Blessed One to give it a name.' Then, the Blessed One, wishing to give it a name, said: 'Therefore, then, you...' and so on. The meaning of that is: 'Since your hair has stood on end upon hearing this sutta, therefore...'
359:
"Nāgasamāla, you should remember this legal exposition as the 'Lomahaṃsana Pariyāya' (The Hair-raising Discourse)," He said.

## The explanation beginning with Saṃsārasuddhi is finished.

## In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī,

## The explanation of the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta. In that Sutta, according to the Vinaya method, three persons are called "sambahulā" (many monks); more than three is called a "Saṅgha." According to the Sutta method, three are just three; more than three are called "sambahulā." In this Sutta, it should be understood according to the Sutta method as "sambahulā." "They entered for alms" refers to those who have already entered; however, since those monks had not yet entered but had set out with the intention "we will enter," it is said "they entered." For example, a person who has set out saying "I will go to the village," even if he has not yet reached that village, when asked "Where is so-and-so?", it is said "He has gone to the village." This is the same. "Paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo" refers to the park of the wanderers of other sects located not far from the Jetavana monastery. "Friends, the recluse" means "Friends, your teacher is the Recluse Gotama." "Full understanding of sensual pleasures" means He prescribes the abandonment and transcending of sensual pleasures. The same method applies to forms and feelings.

In that context, the wanderers, while knowing their own doctrines, might prescribe the full understanding of sensual pleasures while speaking of the first jhāna; they might prescribe the full understanding of forms while speaking of the formless realm; they might prescribe the full understanding of feelings while speaking of the realm of non-percipient beings. However, they do not even know, "This is the first jhāna, this is the form realm, this is the formless realm." Although they are unable to prescribe it, they merely say, "We prescribe it, we prescribe it." The Tathāgata prescribes the full understanding of sensual pleasures through the Path of Non-returning, and the full understanding of forms and feelings through the Path of Arahantship. Even though such great distinctions exist, those wanderers said, "Friends, what is the distinction in this teaching?" and so forth.

In that context, "idha" (here) means in this prescribing. "Dhamma-desanāya vā dhamma-desanaṃ" means: if one were to speak of the distinction between the Recluse Gotama's teaching and our teaching, or our teaching and the Recluse Gotama's teaching, what would that distinction be? In the second phrase, the method is the same.
360:
The explanation is: Thus, like gold broken in the middle, they placed their own views on equal footing with the Dispensation merely by words. "They did not delight" means they did not accept it, thinking, "This word is true as you say." "They did not contradict" means they did not prohibit it, thinking, "This is not so." Why? It is said that those wanderers are like blind people; thinking that they might speak whether they know or not, they did not delight in it. Because of the word "pariññā" (full understanding), they felt there was a slight scent of the Dispensation, so they did not contradict it. Or perhaps, being residents of the countryside, they were not very skilled in their own doctrines or the doctrines of others, so they did neither.

"They will not be able to satisfy" means they will not be able to speak in a way that is consistent and complete. "Further distress" means they will encounter further suffering because of their inability to satisfy the explanation. Indeed, suffering arises for those who are unable to speak completely. "Monks, in what is not one's domain"—here "yathā" is a word indicating cause, and "taṃ" is merely a particle. The meaning is: because a question was asked in a domain that is not theirs. "The world with its devas" means the world together with devas. The same method applies to "with its Māras," etc. Thus, by including three places in the world and two types of beings, and by encompassing the entire world of beings with these five, He shows: "In this world with its devas, Māras, etc., I do not see such a deva or human [who could satisfy these questions]." Or else, "having heard from this Dispensation" means having heard from my Dispensation, even one who is not a Buddha or a disciple of a Buddha could satisfy and please [the mind]. He shows that there is no other way of satisfying.

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to show the satisfaction of the mind by answering those questions, said "Monks, what is it?" and so forth. "Kāmaguṇa" (cords of sensual pleasure): they are "kāma" in the sense of being desirable. They are "guṇa" in the sense of fettering. In the passage, "Monks, I allow a double-layered outer robe (saṅghāṭi) made of new cloth," "guṇa" means a layer. In the passage, "Times pass by, nights fly past, the stages of life (vayo-guṇa) leave one in succession," "guṇa" means a mass or group. In the passage, "A hundredfold benefit (sata-guṇa) is to be expected," "guṇa" means benefit. In the passage, "The large intestine, the small intestine... one should make many garlands (mālā-guṇa)," "guṇa" means a bond or fetter. Here too, this sense of a bond is intended; therefore, it is said, "They are guṇa in the sense of fettering."
361:
"Cognizable by the eye" (cakkhuviññeyyā) refers to visual forms that are to be seen by eye-consciousness. In this same manner, the meaning of terms such as "cognizable by the ear" (sotaviññeyyā) and so forth should be understood. "Desirable" (iṭṭhā) means sense objects that are naturally wished for, whether they are actively sought after or not. "Lovely" (kantā) refers to objects that are pleasing and endearing. "Agreeable" (manāpā) refers to objects that expand or gladden the mind. "Charming" (piyarūpā) refers to objects that are dear in nature. "Connected with sensual desire" (kāmūpasaṃhitā) refers to objects associated with the defilement of sensuality that arises when they are made an object of focus. "Lust-inducing" (rajanīyā) means objects that are enticing or the cause for the arising of passion.

In the passages beginning with "If by manual arithmetic" (yadi muddāya), "manual arithmetic" (muddā) refers to the art of counting by making marks on the finger-joints. "Counting" (gaṇanā) refers to continuous counting such as one, two, and so forth. "Calculation" (saṅkhāna) refers to estimation by groups or masses. Through such calculation, people look at a field and know, "In this field, this much grain will be produced"; they look at a tree and know, "On this tree, this many fruits will grow"; they look at the sky and know, "In this sky, there will be this many birds."

"Farming" (kasī) refers to the work of agriculture. "Trade" (vaṇijjā) refers to trade routes such as peddling on foot or land-based commerce. "Cattle-rearing" (gorakkha) refers to the livelihood of tending one's own or others' cattle and selling the five products of the cow. "Archery" (issattha) refers to the service of attending upon someone while bearing weapons. "Royal service" (rājaporisa) refers to performing royal duties and serving with weapons. "Other crafts" (sippaññatara) refers to remaining arts such as elephant-riding and horse-riding. "Facing the cold" (sītassa purakkhato) means being in the presence of cold as a target is before an arrow; the meaning is being afflicted by the cold. The same method applies to heat. In the terms beginning with "gadflies" (ḍaṃsa), "gadflies" (ḍaṃsā) refers to yellow flies. "Mosquitoes" (makasā) refers to all kinds of mosquitoes and flies. "Reptiles" (sarīsapā) refers to any creatures that move by crawling. "Suffering" (rissamāno) means being weary or afflicted. "Dying" (mīyamāno) means passing away. Monks, this is the danger caused by factors such as cold, arising on account of making a living through arts such as manual arithmetic. "Danger in sensual pleasures" (kāmānaṃ ādīnavo) means the misfortune or calamity occurring within sensual pleasures. "Visible" (sandiṭṭhiko) means that which is to be seen for oneself in the present life. "Mass of suffering" (dukkhakkhandho) is a heap of pain.

In the terms beginning with "due to sensual pleasures" (kāmahetu), they are called "kāmahetu" because sensual pleasures are the cause of this suffering in the sense of being a condition. They are called "kāmanidāna" because sensual pleasures are the source of this suffering in the sense of being a root. Due to grammatical gender inflection, it is stated as "kāmanidānaṃ." They are called "kāmādhikaraṇa" because sensual pleasures are the basis of this suffering in the sense of being a reason. Due to gender inflection, it is stated as "kāmādhikaraṇaṃ." The phrase "solely due to sensual pleasures" (kāmānameva hetu) is a restrictive statement, meaning that it arises certainly and only on account of sensual pleasures.
362:
"For one who strives" (uṭṭhahato) refers to one who exerts effort and energy that gives rise to a livelihood. "For one who exerts" (ghaṭato) refers to one who applies that energy continuously from beginning to end. "For one who endeavors" (vāyamato) refers to one who makes persistent effort, exertion, and application. "They are not accomplished" (nābhinipphajjanti) means the works are not completed or do not come into one's hands. "He grieves" (socati) means he sorrows with intense grief arisen in the mind. "He becomes weary" (kilamati) means he is exhausted by the suffering arisen in the body. "He laments" (paridevati) means he wails by speaking various words. "Beating the breast" (urattāḷiṃ) means striking one's own chest. "He cries" (kandati) means weeping. "He falls into bewilderment" (sammohaṃ āpajjati) means he becomes utterly confused like one who has lost consciousness. "Vain" (moghaṃ) means empty. "Fruitless" (aphalo) means without result. "On account of guarding" (ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ) means because of the reason of protection. "By what means?" (kintī) means by what strategy or method? "Whatever wealth I had" (yampi me) refers to the wealth that was acquired by performing farming and so forth. "That too is no longer with us" (tampi no natthi) means that wealth is no longer in our possession now.

Furthermore, monks, by the words "due to sensual pleasures" (kāmahetu) and so forth, the Buddha shows the danger only after demonstrating the cause. In that passage, "due to sensual pleasures" (kāmahetu) means that even kings quarrel with kings on account of sensual pleasures. "Kāmanidānaṃ" is a neuter abstract noun, meaning they quarrel making sensual pleasures the source. "Kāmādhikaraṇaṃ" is also a neuter abstract noun, meaning they quarrel making sensual pleasures the basis. "Solely due to sensual pleasures" (kāmānameva hetu) means they quarrel solely for the sake of sensual pleasures such as positions of village headman, market-town headman, city governor, general, or royal chaplain. "They attack" (upakkammanti) means they strike one another. "Sword and shield" (asicammaṃ) refers to the sword and protective gear such as shields. "Having bound the bow and quiver" (dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā) means taking the bow and fastening the quiver of arrows. "Arrayed on both sides" (ubhatobyūḷhaṃ) refers to the formation of armies into masses on both sides. "They charge in" (pakkhandanti) means they enter the fray. "Among arrows" (usūsu) means amidst the shafts. "While they are flashing" (vijjotalantesu) means while they are flying and moving about. "Those there" (te tattha) refers to those people on that battlefield.

In the phrase "ramparts plastered with wet mud" (addāvalepanā upakāriyo), people build the base of the city walls with bricks in the shape of a horse's hoof and plaster the top with lime. Such city wall bases are called "upakāriya." When they are smeared with wet mud, they are called "addāvalepanā." "They charge in" (pakkhandanti) means that even though they are pierced by sharp iron spikes and so forth at the foot of those walls, and even though they are unable to climb due to the slipperiness of the ramparts, they still rush forward. "With rotting cow dung" (chakaṇakāyā) means with putrid cow manure. "With a hundred-toothed weapon" (abhivaggenā) refers to a weapon called satadanta. Having made that weapon in a form with eight edges, [they strike] the city gate...
363:
“Let us break the door and enter,” saying thus, those who came were crushed by the momentum of the elephant after those standing above the door cut the elephant's binding ropes.

“They also break through the joints of the house” means breaking the joints of the house walls. “Nillopa” means attacking a village and committing a great robbery. “Ekāgārika” means surrounding about 50 or 60 people and capturing them alive. “They also stand on the path” means committing robbery and destruction on the road. “With short sticks” means hitting with clubs (muggara) or with short sticks made by cutting a four-cubit-long stick into two pieces.

“Bilaṅgathālika” (The Gruel-Pot) is a torture performed like boiling in a vinegar pot. In doing so, they remove the skull, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and pour it into the skull. Because of this pouring, the brain boils and overflows. “Saṅkhamuṇḍika” (The Shell-Shave) is a torture called Saṅkhamuṇḍaka. In doing so, they cut the skin from the upper lip, both sides of the ears, and the hollow of the neck, gather all the hair together, twist it with a stick, and pull it off. The skin comes off along with the hair. Then, they rub and wash the skull with rough stones to make it as white as a conch shell.

“Rāhumukha” (Rāhu's Mouth) is a torture called Rāhumukha. In doing so, they tear open the mouth with an iron hook and light a lamp inside the mouth. Or, they dig into the mouth with a chisel starting from the ears. Blood flows and fills the mouth. “Jotimālika” (The Garland of Fire) means wrapping the whole body in oil-soaked cloth and setting it on fire. “Hatthapajjotika” (The Hand-Torch) means wrapping the hands in oil-soaked cloth and lighting them like lamps. “Eraka-vattika” (The Grass-Roll) is a torture called Eraka-vatta. In doing so, they cut the skin into strips starting from the neck down to the ankles. Then, they tie the person with ropes and pull them. That person trips on their own skin strips and falls. “Cīrakavāsika” (The Bark-Dress) is a torture called Cīrakavāsika. In doing so, they cut the skin into strips in the same way and leave them at the waist. Then they cut from the waist down to the ankles. The upper and lower parts of the body look as if they are wearing a bark garment. “Eṇeyyaka” (The Antelope-Knee) is a torture called Eṇeyyaka. In doing so, they put iron rings on both elbows and both knees and strike them with iron spikes. That person stands fixed to the ground by four iron spikes. Then, they surround him and set him on fire. “The Eṇeyyaka is surrounded by fire...”
364:
The word “Yathā” also carries this meaning in the context where it appears. In that torture, they occasionally remove the spikes and let the person stand on only the four bone-ends. Such forms of torture no longer exist.

Baḷisamaṃsika (The Fish-Hook) means striking with double-headed iron hooks and tearing out the skin, flesh, and sinews. Kahāpaṇika (The Penny-Cut) means cutting the whole body with sharp adzes, starting from the extremities, into pieces the size of a kahāpaṇa coin. Khārāpatacchika (The Alkali-Rinse) means striking the body in various places with weapons and then rubbing alkali with brushes. The skin, flesh, and sinews melt and flow away, leaving only the skeleton. Palighaparivattika (The Pin-Pivot) means making the person lie on one side, driving an iron spike through the ear into the ground to fix them to the earth. Then, they take the feet and spin them around. Palālapīṭhaka (The Straw-Seat) means a skilled executioner breaks the bones with grinding stones without breaking the skin, and then lifts the person by the hair. At that time, the body becomes like a large mass of flesh, and they carry it by wrapping it in the hair itself. It is made and wrapped like a bundle of straw. “Also by dogs” means feeding the person to hungry dogs after not giving them food for several days. Those dogs turn the person into a skeleton in a moment. Samparāyika refers to the result (vipāka) experienced in the next life, the second existence.

Chandarāgavinaya and Chandarāgappahāna refer to Nibbāna. Because desire and lust (chandarāga) for sensual pleasures are disciplined and abandoned through Nibbāna, Nibbāna is called Chandarāgavinaya and Chandarāgappahāna. “They will personally understand sensual pleasures” means they will personally understand those sensual pleasures through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). Tathattāya means for the sake of such a state. Yathāpaṭipanno refers to the practice as it has been practiced.

The phrase “Or a princess,” etc., is mentioned to show rebirth in a place where one can obtain clothes, ornaments, etc., due to extensive and vast wholesome kamma. Pannarasavassuddesikā refers to a person fifteen years of age. The same applies to the second term. Why is the age mentioned? To show the perfection of complexion. For women, even if born in a poor family, the complexion gradually becomes clear at this age. For men, however, it becomes clear and radiant only at the age of twenty or twenty-five. By the words “not too tall,” etc., the perfection of the body, free from the six defects, is shown. Vaṇṇanibhā refers to the complexion itself.
365:
Jiṇṇa means old and decrepit. Gopānasivaṅka means crooked like the rafters of a house. Bhogga means bent; this term also indicates the person's crooked state. Daṇḍaparāyaṇa means relying on a staff, having a staff as a companion. Pavedhamāna means trembling. Ātura means afflicted due to old age. Khaṇḍadanta means having broken teeth due to old age. Palitakesa means having grey hair. Vilūna means baldness as if the hair had been plucked out. Khalitasira means a very bald head. Valina means the appearance of wrinkles. Tilakāhatagatta means a body scattered with white and black freckles. Ābādhika means being diseased. Dukkhita means having reached suffering.

Bāḷhagilāna means severely ill. Sivathikāya chaḍḍita means discarded in a cemetery where corpses are thrown. The rest of the words in this sutta should be understood as stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. In this sutta as well, Nibbāna itself is the removal of desire and lust (chandarāga).

"At that time, also for one's own harm" means at that time, not intending even for one's own suffering. Abyābajjhaṃ means simply being free from suffering.

Monks, in saying "feeling is impermanent," it means: Monks, because feeling is impermanent, therefore this aspect of impermanence and so on is the danger (ādīnava) of feeling. The escape (nissaraṇa) should be understood as previously stated.

## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta
"Thus have I heard" and so on is the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta. Therein, "among the Sakyans" (Sakkesu) means in the district of that name. That district is called "Sakya" because it is the dwelling place of the Sakyan princes. The origin of the Sakyans should be understood as it appears in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. "In Kapilavatthu" (Kapilavatthusmiṃ) means in the city of that name. That city is called "Kapilavatthu" because it was built on the site where the sage Kapila lived. He [the Buddha] stayed there, making it his resort for alms. "In Nigrodha's Park" (Nigrodhārāme) means the Sakyan named Nigrodha built a monastery in his own park and offered it to the Blessed One when He arrived at Kapilavatthu during the gathering of His relatives. It means He was staying in that monastery. "Mahānāma" is the elder brother of Venerable Anuruddha and the son of the Blessed One's paternal uncle.
366:
Suddhodana, Sukkodana, Sakkodana, Dhotodana, and Amitodana—these five persons were brothers. The queen named Amitā was their sister. Venerable Tissa was the son of that Queen Amitā. The Tathāgata and Venerable Nanda were the sons of King Suddhodana; Mahānāma and Venerable Anuruddha were the sons of King Sukkodana. Venerable Ānanda was the son of King Amitodana and was the younger brother of the Blessed One. Mahānāma was the elder and was a Noble Disciple who was a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī).

By the word "for a long time" (dīgharattaṃ), he shows, "I have known this for a long time since I attained the fruit of Once-returning." "States of greed" (lobhadhammā) means the states known as greed; it refers only to greed of various kinds. The same method applies to the other two [hatred and delusion]. "They remain overwhelming" (pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti) means they remain having exhausted [the mind]. This term pariyādāna appears in the sense of "seizing" in this passage (from the Saṃyutta Nikāya): "Having seized the entire elephant corps, having seized the entire cavalry, having seized the entire chariot corps, having seized the entire infantry, he should release him while still alive." It appears in the sense of "exhausting" in this passage: "Monks, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, exhausts all sensual lust." Here too, the sense of exhausting is intended. Therefore, it is said, "pariyādiyitvā means having exhausted."

By the words "whereby at times states of greed also [overwhelm my mind]," he asks, "For what reason do states of greed also at times remain overwhelming my mind?" It is said that this king had the notion that "greed, hatred, and delusion are abandoned without remainder by the path of Once-returning." While he knows "I still have unabandoned defilements," based on those unabandoned defilements, he also has the notion: "Do abandoned defilements return again?" Does such a doubt arise in a Noble Disciple? Yes, it does. Why? Because of lack of skill in designations (paṇṇatti). For even a Noble Disciple who is unskilled in the designation "this defilement is to be abandoned by such-and-such a path," such a doubt can occur. Does he not have reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā)? He does. However, that reviewing knowledge is not complete for everyone. One person reviews only the abandoned defilements. One reviews only the remaining defilements, one only the path, one only the fruit, and one only Nibbāna. Among these five kinds of reviewing knowledge, it is not possible not to obtain one or two. Thus, for one whose reviewing knowledge is incomplete, this occurs because of lack of skill in the designation of defilements to be abandoned by the path.
367:
"So eva kho te" means that although those states of greed, hatred, and delusion have not yet been abandoned in your mental continuum, you were under the impression that they had been abandoned. "So ca hi te" refers to those very states of greed, hatred, and delusion of yours. "Kāme" refers to the two kinds of sensual pleasures. "Na paribhuñjeyyāsī" indicates that you should go forth as a monk like the Buddha.

"Appassādā" means having little gratification or happiness. "Bahudukkha" means that in these sensual pleasures, there is much suffering in both the present life and future lives. "Bahupāyāsā" means that in these sensual pleasures, there is much despair and defilement in both the present and future lives. "Ādīnavo" means many dangers and faults in the present and future lives. "Ettha bhiyyo" means that in these sensual pleasures, this danger is indeed great. Gratification (assāda), however, is extremely small, like a mustard seed compared to Mount Himavanta. "Iti cepi mahānāma" means "Mahānāma, if it were thus for the noble disciple." "Yathābhūtaṃ" means according to reality or nature. It shows that it is well seen through wisdom with the correct method and reason. In that context, "paññāya" (through wisdom) means through insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), specifically through the knowledge of the two lower paths.

"So ca" refers to that noble disciple who has seen the danger of sensual pleasures through those two paths. By the term "pītisukhaṃ," the two jhānas accompanied by rapture are shown. "Aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ" refers to the other two higher jhānas and the two paths which are more peaceful than those two jhānas. "Neva tāva anāvaṭṭī kāmesu hoti" means that although that noble disciple remains having penetrated the two paths, because he has not yet attained the higher jhānas or the higher paths, he is not yet one who does not return to sensual pleasures; he does not yet have the mental orientation of one who does not return. He still has the mental orientation of one who returns. Why? Because there is no abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna) through the four jhānas, nor abandoning by eradication (samucchedappahāna) through the [higher] two paths.

"Mayhampi kho" means not only for you, but also for the Buddha. "Pubbeva sambodhā" means even before attaining the enlightenment of the path. In this context, "paññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hoti" refers to the wisdom that abandons the harem and dancers. "Pītisukhaṃ nājjhagamaṃ" means not having attained the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. "Aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ" in this context refers to the two higher jhānas and the four paths. "Paccaññāsiṃ" means having known through penetration.

"Ekamidāhaṃ mahānāma samayaṃ"—why is this phrase started? This is a separate connection (anusandhi). Below, the gratification and danger of sensual pleasures...
368:
...the escape (nissaraṇa) has not yet been taught, so this teaching is undertaken to teach that escape. Devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) is one extreme, and devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) is another extreme. This teaching is also undertaken to show the entire Dispensation, which is free from these two extremes, by taking the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) in the higher stages as the head.

"On the Gijjhakūṭa mountain" means that on that mountain, there is a peak resembling a vulture; therefore, it is called Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture Peak). Or, it is called Gijjhakūṭa because vultures live on its peaks. "On the side of Isigili" means on the side of the Isigili mountain. "At Kāḷasilā" means on the surface of a black-colored rock. "They remain standing" (ubbhaṭṭhakā honti) means they remain only standing up, not sitting down. "Exertion-born" (opakkamikā) means produced by their own exertion such as standing upright. Since the Nigaṇṭhas could not state any other reason, they threw the responsibility onto the Nigaṇṭha [leader]. "Sabbaññū sabbadassāvī" (all-knowing, all-seeing) means that our teacher knows and sees everything—past, future, and present. "Claims knowledge and vision without remainder" means that our teacher, knowing all things without remainder, claims the knowledge and vision called "without remainder," and when claiming, he claims thus: "Whether I am walking or standing... it is present." In that context, "satataṃ" means constantly. "Samitaṃ" is a synonym for that same meaning.

"Friends Nigaṇṭhas, do you know that this much suffering has been exhausted?" The Blessed Lord said this to show that a person knows what he does. When one takes a debt of twenty kahāpaṇas and pays back ten, he knows, "I have given ten, ten remain." When he pays those back too, he knows, "All has been given." After reaping one-third of a field, he knows, "One part is reaped, two parts remain." When he reaps another part, he knows, "Two parts are reaped, one part remains." When that remaining part is also reaped, he knows, "All is finished." In this way, just as one knows what is done and what is not yet done in all tasks, the Buddha shows that you too should know in that manner. "The abandoning of unwholesome states" is a question asking whether there is any Nigaṇṭha in your dispensation who, having abandoned the unwholesome and developed the wholesome, has reached purity.

"This being so" means when you have such a state of not knowing. "Luddā" (cruel) means those of cruel behavior. "Lohitapāṇino" (bloody-handed) means those whose hands are smeared with blood from depriving beings of life. Even for one who kills a being, if his hand is not smeared with blood...
369:
(The blood of a being) is smeared (on the hand); such a person is also called 'lohitapāṇī' (one with blood-stained hands). 'Kurūrakammantā' refers to those who perform cruel deeds. It means those who wrong their mother, father, or righteous recluses and brahmins, or those who perform harsh acts such as hunters who kill prey.

"Not so, friend Gotama"—thinking, "This ascetic Gotama blames our doctrine; let us also find fault in his doctrine," the Nigaṇṭhas began these words. The meaning is: "Friend Gotama, you all, wearing exquisite robes, eating fine rice with meat, and living in a Perfumed Chamber like a divine mansion, attain happiness through a pleasant practice. Happiness is not to be attained through such a pleasant practice. Rather, just as we experience various kinds of suffering through practices such as squatting, happiness is to be attained only through a painful practice."

"Friend, if happiness could be attained through a pleasant practice, then King (Bimbisāra) would attain it"—this was said to show (the Nigaṇṭhas' view). In that context, 'Māgadha' refers to the ruler of the Magadha kingdom. 'Seniya' is his name. 'Bimbī' is the name for the physical body (attabhāva). Because that king possessed an excellent essence, was beautiful, inspiring, and had a perfect physical form, he is called 'Bimbisāra'. The Nigaṇṭhas said "one who lives more happily" referring to the King's enjoyment of luxury with dancers of three different ages in his three palaces. 'Addhā' means certainly. 'Sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā' means acting suddenly without reflection, or speaking without consideration. It shows that (the Nigaṇṭhas) spoke their words just as one speaks under the influence of lust, hatred, or delusion.

In that context, 'paṭipucchissāmi' means "I will ask back regarding that matter." 'Yathā vo khameyya' means "as it may please you" (according to your wish). 'Pahoti' means "is able."

'Aniñjamāno' means being firm without wavering. 'Ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī' means experiencing uninterrupted happiness. "Friends Nigaṇṭhas, I am able... (etc.) ...to experience uninterrupted happiness"—this was said to show his own happiness of the Attainment of Fruition (phalasamāpatti). Here, to establish the conversation, the questioning began from seven days on the King's side. If it is said that one is not able for seven days and seven nights, then it is possible to easily ask about six, five, or four days. However, in the 'pure section' (suddhavāra), after saying seven days, it is not surprising to say six, five, or four days again; therefore, the teaching was given starting from one day. The remaining meanings are clear.

## The Commentary on the Cūḷadukkhandha Sutta
## in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary known as Papañcasūdanī is finished.
370:
## 5. Anumāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Anumāna Sutta. In that sutta, "Bhaggesu" means in the country named Bhagga; the grammatical derivation (vacanattha) here should be understood following the method already mentioned. "Susumāragire" means in the city named Susumāragira. It is heard that on the day the site for that city was being marked out, a crocodile made a sound and uttered a cry in a nearby pond. Thus, when the city was completed, they named it "Susumāragira" (Crocodile's Cry). "Bhesakaḷāvane" means in the forest named Bhesakaḷā. There is also a reading "Bhesagaḷāvane". "Migadāye" is so called because that forest was established as a sanctuary for animals and birds.

"Pavarēti" means "invites" or "requests." "Vadantu" means "let them speak by way of advice and instruction," meaning "let them instruct." "Vacanīyomhi" means "I am one who should be spoken to, instructed, and advised by you." "So ca hoti dubbaco" means that person is difficult to speak to; he cannot endure being spoken to. "Dovavacassakaraṇehi" means by the sixteen qualities that make one difficult to speak to, which will be mentioned below. "Appadakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ" refers to a person who, when spoken to or instructed, says, "Why do you speak to me? I know what is suitable or unsuitable for myself, what is blameworthy or blameless, and what is beneficial or harmful." Such a person does not take the instruction "clockwise" (respectfully) but takes it "counter-clockwise" (disrespectfully); therefore, he is called "appadakkhiṇaggāhī" (one who does not receive instruction respectfully).

"Pāpikānaṃ icchānaṃ" means of the evil desires to manifest qualities that one does not possess. "Paṭippharati" means he stands in opposition like an enemy. "Apasādeti" means he disparages or insults thus: "What is the use of the words of a fool and an ignorant person like you? Do you also think you are someone who should speak?" "Paccāropeti" means he counter-accuses thus: "You too have committed such-and-such an offense; first remedy that offense yourself."

"Aññenāññaṃ paṭicarati" means he conceals one matter or statement with another matter or statement. When told, "You have committed an offense," he says, "Who committed it? What was committed? In what matter was it committed? To whom are you speaking? What are you saying?" When asked, "Did you see anything of this sort?" he brings his ear close (pretending not to hear) and says, "I do not hear." How does he divert the talk to something external? When asked, "Have you committed such-and-such an offense?" he says, "I went to Pāṭaliputra," and then (the speaker says), "We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputra..."
371:
When it is said, "We ask about the offense," he says, "After that, I went to Rājagaha." Or when it is said, "Go to Rājagaha, or go to the brahmin's house; you have committed an offense," he says things like, "I obtained pork in that Rājagaha," and so on—how does he deflect the conversation externally?

"Apadāna" means one's own conduct. "Incomplete" means: "Friend, where do you live? Depending on whom do you live?" or "To whom do you say, 'I saw this monk committing an offense'?" or "What were you doing at that time? What was this monk doing? Where were you staying? Where was this monk staying?" When asked about his conduct in such ways, he is unable to answer completely.

"Tatrāvuso" means: Friends, among those sixteen things. "One should compare oneself with oneself in this way" means: In this way, one should compare, weigh, and investigate oneself by oneself.

"Should be reflected upon" means it should indeed be reflected upon. "Ahorattānusikkhinā" means by training during the day and during the night; by training in wholesome states throughout the day and night, one should arouse only joy and gladness (pīti-pāmojja).

"In a clear bowl of water" means in a clear vessel for holding water. "Mukhanimittaṃ" means the reflection of the face. "Rajaṃ" means adventitious dust. "Aṅgaṇaṃ" means a freckle or a pimple born on that face. By the words "All these evil unwholesome states have been abandoned," he speaks of total abandoning. How? For one who arouses reflection that "These many unwholesome states are unsuitable for a renunciant," abandoning by reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna-pahāna) is spoken of. For one who, based on virtue, undertakes the preliminary work for kasina and produces the eight attainments, abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) is spoken of. For one who, based on the attainments, develops insight, abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna) is spoken of. For one who, having developed insight, develops the path, abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna) is spoken of. Abandoning by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna) when the fruit is reached, and abandoning by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna) when Nibbāna is reached—thus, in this sutta, all types of abandoning are indeed spoken of.

Ancient teachers say this sutta is called the "Bhikkhu Pātimokkha." This sutta should be reflected upon three times a day. Early in the morning, having entered the dwelling place and sitting down, one should reflect: "Do these many defilements exist in me or not?" If one sees that they exist, one should strive to abandon them. If one does not see them...
372:
...one should be joyful, thinking, "I have gone forth well." After finishing the meal, sitting in either the night quarters or the day quarters, one should also reflect. In the evening, sitting in the dwelling place, one should also reflect. A monk who is unable to reflect three times should reflect twice. If unable to reflect twice, he must certainly reflect once; they say it is not proper to remain without reflecting. All the remaining words have clear meanings.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Anumāna Sutta is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Cetokhila Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Cetokhila Sutta. In that sutta, "Cetokhila" (wilderness of the heart) refers to the state of the mind being stiff, like rubbish, or like a stump. "Cetaso vinibandha" (mental shackles) are so called because they bind the mind and seize it as if holding it in a fist. In the terms "Vuddhi" and so on, it means growth through virtue, increase through the path, and expansion through Nibbāna. Or, growth through virtue and concentration, increase through insight and the path, and expansion through the fruit and Nibbāna. "Satthari kaṅkhati" (doubts the Teacher) means he doubts the physical body or the qualities of the Teacher. Doubting the physical body, he doubts: "Does the body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man really exist or not?" Doubting the qualities, he doubts: "Does the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing the past, future, and present really exist or not?" "Vicikicchati" (is perplexed) means while investigating, he becomes weary, falls into suffering, and is unable to decide. "Nādhimuccati" (is not convinced) means not obtaining the conviction that "This is so." "Na sampasīdati" (is not settled) means being unable to settle with clarity through the absence of doubt by entering into the qualities, and being unable to be undisturbed. "Ātappāya" means for the purpose of making effort that burns up defilements. "Anuyogāya" means for the purpose of repeated application. "Sātaccāya" means for the purpose of constant action. "Padhānāya" means for the purpose of exertion. "Ayaṃ paṭhamo cetokhilo" means this first state of mental stiffness, known as doubt in the Teacher, has not been abandoned by this monk. "Dhamme" (in the Dhamma) refers to both the Dhamma of scripture (pariyatti) and the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha). Doubting the Dhamma of scripture, he doubts: "They say the word of the Buddha in the Three Piṭakas consists of eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma; does that Dhamma really exist or not?" Doubting the Dhamma of realization, he doubts: "They say the path is the result of insight, the fruit is the result of the path, and Nibbāna is the relinquishment of all conditioned things; does that Dhamma really exist or not?" "Saṅghe kaṅkhati" (doubts the Saṅgha) means by virtue of the terms such as "Suppaṭipanno" (practicing well), such a practice...
373:
The Saṅgha is the collection of eight persons: the four standing in the paths (maggaṭṭha) and the four standing in the fruits (phalaṭṭha), who have practiced well. One doubts whether such a Saṅgha exists or not. One who doubts the training (sikkhā) is said to doubt the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā); he doubts whether these trainings exist or not. This fifth stiffness of the mind refers to the fifth stiffness of the mind known as anger towards fellow practitioners, which is like being rubbish or a stump.

Among the bonds (vinibandha), 'sensuality' (kāma) refers to both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma). 'Body' (ကာယ) refers to one's own physical body. 'Form' (ရူပ) refers to external forms. 'Yāvadatthaṃ' means as much food as one desires. 'Udarāvadehakaṃ' means eating until the belly is full. It is called 'udarāvadehakaṃ' because it fills the belly. 'Seyyasukhaṃ' is the pleasure derived from lying on a couch or bed, or pleasure derived from the climate. 'Passasukhaṃ' is the pleasure that arises for one who is sleeping by turning from the right side to the left side repeatedly. 'Middhasukhaṃ' is the pleasure derived from sleep and torpor. 'Anuyutto' means one who lives in constant application.

'Paṇidhāya' means having aspired. Among the terms beginning with virtue (sīla), 'sīla' refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). 'Vata' is the undertaking of a practice. 'Tapa' is the practice of effort that burns away defilements. 'Brahmacariya' is abstinence from sexual intercourse. 'I will become a deity' means becoming either a great deity of high status or one among the deities of lesser status.

Among the bases of power (iddhipāda), concentration based on desire is 'chanda-samādhi'. The volitional formations of striving are 'padhāna-saṅkhāra'. 'Samannāgataṃ' means being endowed with those qualities. It is called 'iddhipāda' because it is the cause of success (iddhi) or because it is the foundation that is success. The same method applies to the remaining bases of power; this is the summary here. The detailed explanation is as it appears in the Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga. Its meaning is also illustrated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, through these four bases of power, abandoning by suppression (vikkhamphana-pahāna) is taught. 'Ussoḷhī' is the fifth; here, 'ussoḷhī' shows the energy (vīriya) to be applied in all matters. One endowed with fifteen factors including ardor (ussoḷhī)—namely, the five abandonings of the wilderness of the mind, the five abandonings of the bonds, the four bases of power, and ardor—is fit to break through defilements with knowledge, to realize the four paths (sambodha), and to attain the supreme Arahantship, which is the security from the four yokes (yogakkhema). 'Seyyathā' is a particle used in the sense of a simile. 'Pi' is used in the sense of emphasis. Both together as 'seyyathāpi nāma, bhikkhave' illustrate the simile.
374:
In the phrase "the eggs of a hen, whether eight, ten, or twelve," although a hen may have fewer or more eggs than the stated number, it is said this way for the sake of smooth phrasing. Only when said thus is speech considered smooth in the world. "Tānassu" is "tāni assu," meaning "those eggs should be." "Well sat upon by the hen" means they are well sat upon by that mother hen who spreads her wings and sits over those eggs. "Well warmed" means they are well warmed and heated all around by letting them receive the right temperature from time to time. "Well scented" means they are well scented all around from time to time, meaning they are made to receive the scent of the hen.

"Even if it occurs to that hen" means that even if that hen, through performing these three actions, acts with diligence, the wish "may they hatch" might not arise. "Nevertheless, those chicks are capable (of hatching)" means those chicks are fit to break out safely according to the method described. Because the hen protects those eggs in these three ways, the eggs do not rot. The sticky moisture within them also reaches exhaustion, the shell becomes thin, the tips of the claws and the beak become hard, and they mature naturally. Because the shell is thin, the light from outside is perceived within. Therefore, desiring to emerge, thinking, "We have lain for a long time in a cramped place with limbs curled; now the light from outside is seen; here will be our happy dwelling," they kick the shell with their feet and stretch their necks. Then the shell breaks in two. Then those chicks, shaking their wings and chirping appropriately for that moment, emerge. Having emerged, they wander about, beautifying the village fields.

"Even so" is the application of this simile. It should be understood by comparing the meaning thus: The monk's endowment with fifteen factors including ardor (ussoḷhī) is like the hen's performing the three actions upon the eggs. The non-decline of insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) in a monk endowed with fifteen factors, through the completion of the three types of contemplation (anupassanā), is like the eggs not rotting due to the hen's completion of the three actions. The exhaustion of the moisture of attachment (nikanti-sineha) following the three realms in that monk, through the completion of the three contemplations, is like the exhaustion of the sticky moisture in the eggs through the hen's performing the three actions. The thinning of the eggshells...
375:
The thinning of the monk's eggshell of ignorance is like (the thinning of a chicken's eggshell). Just as the tips of the claws and the beaks of young chicks become hard and sharp, the monk's insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) possesses the nature of being sharp, piercing, clear, and courageous. The period when the monk's insight knowledge matures, increases, and takes hold of the 'womb of insight' should be understood as being like the time when the young chicks reach maturity. Just as the young chicks break the eggshell with the tips of their claws or their beaks and emerge safely, flapping their wings, so too should one understand the time when a monk—who dwells having taken hold of that womb of insight knowledge, having obtained suitable climate (utu-sappāya), suitable food (bhojana-sappāya), suitable persons (puggala-sappāya), and suitable hearing of the Dhamma (dhammassavana-sappāya), and who develops insight while sitting in a single seat—breaks the eggshell of ignorance through the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) attained in due order, and reaches the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) safely, flapping the wings of direct knowledge (abhiññā). Just as the mother hen, knowing the maturity of her chicks, breaks the eggshell for them, so too the Teacher, knowing the maturity of the knowledge of a monk endowed with such maturity of wisdom, emits a radiance and strikes the eggshell of ignorance with a verse in this manner:

## Cut off your own affection, as with the hand an autumn lotus;
## Cultivate only the path to peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.

'Cut off your own moisture of craving (taṇhā-sineha), just as one would pluck an autumn lotus with the hand. Cultivate only the path to peace, and realize the Nibbāna taught by the Blessed One.' At the end of the verse, that monk breaks the eggshell of ignorance and reaches the Fruition of Arahantship. From then on, just as those young chicks wander about beautifying the village fields, this great Arahant (khīṇāsava) wanders about beautifying the monastery (saṅghārāma), dwelling in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object.

Thus, in this Sutta, four types of abandoning (pahāna) are taught. How? By the abandoning of the mental barrenness (cetokhila) and the mental shackles (cetovinibandha), abandoning by reflection (paṭisaṅkhānappapahāna) is taught. By the bases of power (iddhipāda), abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhanappapahāna) is taught. When the Path arises, abandoning by eradication (samucchedappapahāna) is taught. When the Fruition arises, abandoning by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhippapahāna) is taught. All the remaining words have clear meanings.

## The Explanation of the Cetokhila Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya (Papañcasūdanī) is finished.
376:
## 7. Vanapatthapariyāya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the Vanapatthapariyāya Sutta, which begins with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," the term "Vanapatthapariyāya" means the cause of the forest thicket or the teaching concerning the forest thicket.

"He dwells in dependence on a forest thicket" means he dwells practicing the Dhamma of a recluse in dependence on a forest dwelling that is beyond the vicinity of human habitation. In the words beginning with "anupaṭṭhitā," it means that even though he dwells in dependence on that forest, mindfulness (sati) which has not appeared before does not appear; the mind which was not concentrated before does not become concentrated; the taints (āsava) which were not yet exhausted do not reach exhaustion; and he does not attain the unsurpassed security from bondage (yogakkhema) known as the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) which he had not attained before.

"Jīvitaparikkhāra" refers to the four requisites which are the supports of life. "Samudānetabbā" means they should be acquired. "Kasirena samudāgacchanti" means they are obtained with difficulty and hardship. "Whether in the night portion or in the day portion" refers to the division of the night or the division of the day. Herein, one who realizes this while reflecting during the night should depart during the night itself; if there are dangers from fierce wild beasts and so on at night, he should wait until dawn. One who realizes this during the day should depart during the day itself; if there are dangers during the day, he should wait until sunset.

"Saṅkhāpi" (having reflected) means having known the state of the non-accomplishment of the recluse's Dhamma. In the subsequent passage, "saṅkhāpi" means having known the state of the accomplishment of the recluse's Dhamma.

"Yāvajīvaṃ" means he should dwell there as long as life lasts.

The phrase "that person" is connected with the words "should not be followed." "Anāpucchā" here means he should depart without asking permission from that person.

"Saṅkhāpi" means having known the state of the non-accomplishment of the recluse's Dhamma, that person should not be followed, and one should depart after asking permission from him.

"Even if being driven out" means even if being expelled. If a person of such nature is made to carry a hundred bundles of wood, or a hundred jars of water, or a hundred bags of sand, or even if he is driven out with the command "Do not stay here," he should endure and apologize to that person and dwell there for the rest of his life.

## The Explanation of the Vanapatthapariyāya Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
377:
## 8. Commentary on the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta

This sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," is the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta. In that Madhupiṇḍika Sutta, 'Mahāvana' refers to a natural forest that is contiguous with the Himālaya mountains and not planted by humans; it is not like the forest near the city of Vesālī, which is a mixture of planted and naturally grown trees. 'Divāvihārāya' means for the purpose of solitary seclusion during the day. 'Beluvalaṭṭhikāya' means near a young wood-apple (bael) tree. 'Daṇḍapāṇi' does not mean one who holds a staff because of being old and weak. Although this Sakyan prince Daṇḍapāṇi was in the first stage of life (youth), he had a mind that took pleasure in a staff (or was skilled in the art of the staff) and wandered about carrying a golden staff. Therefore, he is called 'Daṇḍapāṇi' (one with a staff in hand). 'Jaṅghāvihāraṃ' means walking on foot to dispel the fatigue of the legs. 'Anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno' means wandering here and there for the purpose of seeing the monastery grounds, the forest, the mountains, and so on. It is said that this prince would only occasionally leave the palace to wander in this manner. 'Daṇḍamolubbha' means that he stood in one place, leaning on his staff for support like a young cowherd, placing the staff in front of him, resting both hands on the head of the staff, and pressing his chin against the back of his hands.

'Kiṃvādī' is a question asking what kind of view he holds. 'Kimakkhāyī' is a question asking what doctrine he teaches. This prince, without paying homage to the Blessed One, merely exchanged polite greetings and then asked the question. Furthermore, that questioning was not out of a desire to know, but was asked with a disrespectful and indifferent mind. Why? It is said that this prince was a partisan of Devadatta. Devadatta used to create division between the Tathāgata and those who came to him. It is said that Devadatta used to speak thus: "The ascetic Gotama is an enemy to our clan; he does not wish for the prosperity of our clan. My sister was worthy of enjoying the status of a Universal Monarch's queen, yet he made her renounce the world and leave the palace, saying, 'Let this woman be ruined.' Knowing that my nephew was the seed of a Universal Monarch, and not being pleased with the growth of our clan, he made him renounce the world even while he was a child, saying, 'Let this boy be ruined.' I myself, being unable to live without that nephew, followed him into renunciation. Even though I have renounced in this way, from the day of my renunciation, he has never looked at me with straight eyes. When speaking in the midst of the assembly, he speaks as if striking with a great axe, saying, 'Devadatta is one destined for hell,' and so forth." Thus, this prince Daṇḍapāṇi was also one who had been influenced by Devadatta's divisiveness, and that is why he acted in this (disrespectful) manner.

Then the Blessed One thought, "So that this prince cannot say that I did not answer when he asked a question," and also, "So that he will not understand the meaning of the words I speak..."
378: ...thinking, "I will speak to this Daṇḍapāṇi in this way," and wishing to speak words suitable for him, He uttered the words beginning with "Yathāvādī kho." In that passage, "does not stand in dispute with anyone in the world" means that He does not engage in disputatious talk or quarrel with anyone in the world. Indeed, the Tathāgata does not dispute with the world. However, it is the world that disputes with the Tathāgata; when He says "impermanent," they say "permanent," and when He says "suffering, non-self, and foul," they say "happiness, self, and beautiful," thus they dispute. Therefore, He said: "Monks, I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me. Monks, one who speaks according to the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world; it is only one who does not speak according to the Dhamma (adhamma-vādī) who disputes." (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.94). "Yathā" means by whatever reason. "Kāmehi" refers to both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective defilements (kilesa-kāma). "Taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ" refers to that Arahant whose taints are destroyed. "Akathaṃkathiṃ" means one who is free from doubt (vicikicchā). "Chinnakukkuccaṃ" is called such because both the worry of remorse (vippaṭisāra) and the restlessness of hands and feet (hatthapāda-kukkucca) have been cut off. "Bhavābhave" refers to repeated existence, or low and high existence; for high existence that has reached prosperity is called "abhava." "Saññā" refers to the perception of defilements (kilesa-saññā). Here, the defilements themselves are called by the name 'perception.' Therefore, the meaning is: I speak of the reason why perceptions of defilement do not underlie that Arahant who lives detached from sense pleasures and who has no clinging to views in the world. In this way, the Blessed One shows His own state of being one whose taints are destroyed. "Nillāḷetvā" means having stuck out (the tongue) and moved it about. "Tivisākhaṃ" refers to a three-pronged (wrinkle). "Nalāṭikaṃ" refers to the act of frowning so that three lines appear on the forehead. "Daṇḍamolubbha" means pressing upon (leaning on) the staff. There is also a variant reading "daṇḍamālubbha," which means he took hold of it and departed. There was a certain monk whose name was not well-known. He was skilled in connecting the sequence of the discourse. When the Blessed One said, "I have spoken in such a way that Daṇḍapāṇi cannot understand," that monk, taking up the sequence and thinking, "Why did the Blessed One speak the question in an incomprehensible way? I shall request the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) to make this question clear to the Saṅgha," rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and raising his joined palms brilliant with ten fingernails, asked, "But, Bhante, what is the Blessed One's doctrine?" and so forth.
379:
The term "yatonidānaṃ" is a neuter of state (bhāvanapuṃsaka), meaning "due to which cause" or "when which cause exists." In the phrase "papañcasaññāsaṅkhā," the word "saṅkhā" means a portion or a group. "Papañcasaññā" refers to perception associated with the proliferations (papañca) of craving, conceit, and views; or, the proliferations themselves are referred to by the name of perception. Therefore, the meaning here is "the group of proliferations." "Samudācaranti" means they occur or arise.

"Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ" means that when the causes known as the twelve sense bases (āyatana) exist, the reckonings of perceptions of proliferation arise. Among those twelve sense bases, if there is not even a single sense base that should be delighted in, asserted as 'mine,' or clung to, this is the meaning. In those terms, "abhinanditabbaṃ" means to be delighted in as 'I' or 'mine.' "Abhivaditabbaṃ" means to be asserted as 'I' or 'mine.' "Ajjhositabbaṃ" refers to that which should be clung to by overwhelming, swallowing, and completely grasping it. By this, it is taught that craving and so forth do not arise in these sense bases. "Esevanto" means that this absence of delight and so forth is the end (cessation) of the latent tendencies of lust (rāgānusaya) and so forth. This same method applies in all places.

Regarding the terms such as "daṇḍādāna" (taking up the rod): the intention (cetanā) by which one takes up a rod or a stick is called "daṇḍādāna." The intention by which one takes up or handles a weapon is called "satthādāna." A quarrel that has reached its peak is called "kalaha." A dispute based on various views is called "viggaha." A contention based on various words is called "vivāda." The act of insulting one another as "you! you!" is called "tuvaṃtuvaṃ." Slander that causes separation between loved ones is called "pesuñña." Making a statement that is not in accordance with reality is to be known as "musāvāda" (false speech).

"Etthete" refers to these defilements (kilesa) that arise in these twelve sense bases. For when defilements arise, they arise depending on the twelve sense bases; and when they cease, they cease within the twelve sense bases themselves. Thus, where they arise, there they cease. This meaning should be explained by the question on the truth of the origin (samudayasacca):

"Where does that craving arise when it arises? Where does it settle when it settles?" Having asked this, it is taught: "Whatever in the world is endearing and agreeable, there this craving arises when it arises, there it settles when it settles. And what in the world is endearing and agreeable? The eye (cakkhu) is endearing and agreeable in the world," and so forth. In this manner, the arising and cessation of that craving is taught in the twelve sense bases themselves. Just as craving, having arisen in the twelve sense bases, is said to have ceased in the sense bases because it no longer occurs in them upon reaching Nibbāna, so too should it be understood that these evil unwholesome states cease in the sense bases. Alternatively, this absence of delight and so forth...
380:
...is called the end of the latent tendencies of lust (rāgānusaya) and so forth. In Nibbāna, which is designated as the end of these latent tendencies of lust and so forth, evil unwholesome states cease without remainder. For whatever is not present in a certain place is said to have ceased there. This meaning should be explained by the question on cessation (nirodha). For it has been said: "For one who has attained the second jhāna, verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra) consisting of applied and sustained thought (vitakkavicāra) are stilled," and so forth.

"Satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito" means he is also praised by the Teacher (the Buddha). "Viññūnaṃ"—this word is also in the possessive case (sāmivacana) with the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa), meaning he is also esteemed by the wise and by fellow practitioners of the holy life. "Pahoti" means he is able.

"Atik္kammeva mūlaṃ atik္kamma khandhaṃ" means that what is called the heartwood (sāra) might be in the root or in the trunk; it means having surpassed even that root and trunk. "Evaṃsampadaṃ" means endowed with such perfection, of such a nature. "Atisitvā" means having surpassed. He is said to be "jānaṃ jānāti" (knowing, he knows) in the sense that he knows only what should be known. He is said to be "passaṃ passati" (seeing, he sees) in the sense that he sees only what should be seen. Otherwise, some people, by grasping wrongly, do not know even though they know, and do not see even though they see; but the Blessed One is not like that. When the Blessed One knows, he truly knows; when he sees, he truly sees. He is "Cakkhubhūta" (become vision) in the sense of being the leader of vision. He is "Ñāṇabhūta" (become knowledge) in the sense of performing the act of knowing. He is "Dhammabhūta" (become Dhamma) because he has an undistorted nature, or because he sets in motion the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma), or because his nature is the Dhamma that he has thought with his heart and expressed with his speech. He is "Brahmabhūta" (become sublime) in the sense of being supreme. Alternatively, he is "Cakkhubhūta" because he is like an eye; thus should the meaning of these terms be understood.

That Blessed One is "Vattā" (the speaker) because he teaches the Dhamma. He is "Pavattā" (the setter in motion) because he causes it to be set in motion. He is "Atthassa ninnetā" (the leader to the meaning) because of his ability to extract and show the meaning. He is "Amatassa dātā" (the giver of the Deathless) because he gives the practice for the attainment of the Deathless Nibbāna. "Agaruṃ katvā" means without making it difficult by making us request repeatedly, and without making it hard to understand—as if one were standing on the power of his own disciple's knowledge and lifting a grain of sand from under Mount Sineru—but rather, it means "please teach us by making it easy to understand without making us request repeatedly."

In the phrase "yaṃ kho no āvuso," although it should have been said "yaṃ kho vo" (that which to you), those monks said "yaṃ kho no" (that which to us) by including themselves. Or it is because the brief summary (uddesa) had already been taught to them. The Blessed One, however, also to the Elder Sāriputta...
381:
To those monks also, it was the Blessed One himself (who pointed out the summary). Therefore, with reference to the word 'Bhagavā' (the Blessed One), it is said: "The Blessed One, our Lord, having pointed out a summary to you in brief..."

In the phrases beginning with "Friends, [dependent on] the eye," the meaning is as follows: Friends, dependent on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) as the support (nissaya) and visible forms (rūpa) produced by the four causes as the object (ārammaṇa), what is called eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) arises. "The meeting of the three is contact (phassa)" means that due to the meeting of those three, the state called contact arises. Dependent on that contact, through the power of the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) and so forth, feeling (vedanā) arises due to contact. Whatever object one feels with that feeling, perception (saññā) perceives that very object. Whatever object perception perceives, thought (vitakka) thinks about that very object. Whatever object thought thinks about, mental proliferation (papañca) proliferates that very object. "Due to that cause" means due to these causes such as the eye and visible forms. "Perceptions and categories of mental proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā) assail the person" means that the groups of mental proliferation overwhelm and assail that person whose causes are not fully understood; the meaning is that they occur to that person.

Among those states, contact, feeling, and perception arise together with eye-consciousness. Thought, however, should be understood as occurring in the thought-accompanied consciousnesses that arise immediately after eye-consciousness and so forth. The categories of mental proliferation arise together with the impulsion consciousness (javana). If this is so, why are the past and future included? Because they arise in that manner. Just as the mental proliferation occurring at the eye-door at the present time arises dependent on the eye, visible forms, contact, feeling, perception, and thought, so too, desiring to show the arising of that mental proliferation in relation to visible forms cognizable by eye-consciousness in the past and future, he spoke in this way.

In the phrases beginning with "Friends, [dependent on] the ear," the method is the same. In the sixth door, however, "mind" (mana) refers to the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta). "Mental objects" (dhamma) refers to the objects of the three planes. "Mind-consciousness" (mano-viññāṇa) refers to either the adverting (āvajjana) or the impulsion (javana) consciousness. If adverting is taken, contact, feeling, perception, and thought arise together with the adverting consciousness. Mental proliferation arises together with the impulsion. If impulsion is taken, the life-continuum together with the adverting is called "mind"; in that case, all states beginning with contact arise together with the impulsion consciousness only. Since all objects of various kinds such as the past can occur at the mind-door, it is indeed appropriate to say "in the past, future, and present."

Now, desiring to show the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), he began the teaching with "So vata āvuso" (Indeed, friends, that...). "He will describe the designation of contact" (phassa-paññattiṃ paññapessati) means he will designate or show the designation of contact, saying that a state called contact arises. This method is the same in all places. Having thus shown the entire round of suffering by way of the twelve bases (āyatana) as "when this exists, this occurs," he now began with "So vata āvuso" desiring to show the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) by way of the rejection of the twelve bases.
382:
He began the teaching with "When there is no eye..." (cakkhusmiṃ asati). The meaning in that text should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

Having thus answered the question, he spoke the words beginning with "And if you should desire..." (ākaṅkhamānā ca pana), wishing to urge them: "Do not have any doubt that 'the disciple has answered the question'; this Blessed One sits holding the balance of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa); if you desire, approach that Blessed One himself and be free from doubt."

"By these modes" (imehi ākārehi) means by these causes, both by the specific causes for the arising of mental proliferation and by the causes for the round and the cessation of the round. "By these words" (imehi padehi) means by these collections of syllables. "By these phrasings" (byañjanehi) means by the individual syllables. "Wise" (paṇḍito) means endowed with wisdom. Or, one is wise through four reasons: being skilled in elements (dhātu-kusala), skilled in bases (āyatana-kusala), skilled in dependent origination (paccaya-ākāra-kusala), and skilled in what is and what is not a cause (kāraṇa-akāraṇa-kusala). "Of great wisdom" (mahāpañño) means endowed with great wisdom capable of comprehending great meanings, great doctrines, great linguistics, and great perspicuity. "As it was [explained] by Mahākaccāna" (yathā taṃ mahākaccānena) means just as it was explained by the Venerable Mahākaccāna; the word 'taṃ' (that) refers to that Venerable's explanation. The meaning is: "Just as it was explained by Mahākaccāna, I too would explain it in that very same way."

"Honey-ball" (madhupiṇḍikaṃ) means a large molasses cake or a ball of flour mixed with molasses. "Delicious in itself" (asecanakaṃ) means not needing any other flavor to be poured over it. It is a well-blended flavor such that one cannot say of the ghee, molasses, honey, or sugar, "this is too little" or "this is too much." "By mind" (cetaso) means one who is of a reflective nature. "Of a wise nature" (dabbajātiko) means one who has the nature of a wise person. "What is the name of this [discourse]?" (ko nāmo ayaṃ) means that the Elder Ānanda, having thought, "This Dhamma discourse is exceedingly excellent; I shall have its name given by the Lord of Ten Powers (Dasabala) through his omniscience alone," asked the question. Therefore, because it is sweet like a honey-ball, he said, "Remember it as the 'Honey-ball Discourse' (Madhupiṇḍika-pariyāya)." All the remaining words have clear meanings.

## The Explanation of the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
383:
## 9. Commentary on the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta

This discourse beginning with "Me sutaṃ" is the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta. In that sutta, the phrase "dvidhā katvā dvidhā katvā" means having made into two parts, having made into two parts. "Kāma-vitakka" (thought of sensuality) refers to thought connected with sensual pleasures. "Byāpāda-vitakka" (thought of ill-will) refers to thought connected with ill-will (the desire to destroy). "Vihiṃsā-vitakka" (thought of cruelty) refers to thought connected with cruelty (the desire to harm). "Ekaṃ bhāgaṃ" (one part) means that whether it arises within one's own continuity or externally, whether it is gross or subtle, all such thought belongs only to the unwholesome side; therefore, he made all three—thoughts of sensuality, ill-will, and cruelty—into a single group (one part).

Thought connected with renunciation, which is the departure from sensual pleasures, is called "nekkhamma-vitakka" (thought of renunciation); that thought can occur up to the first jhāna.
