Thought connected with non-ill-will (loving-kindness) is called "abyāpāda-vitakka"; that thought can occur from the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā-pubbabhāga) up to the first jhāna. Thought connected with non-cruelty (compassion) is called "avihiṃsā-vitakka"; that thought can occur from the preliminary stage of compassion (karuṇā-pubbabhāga) up to the first jhāna. "Dutiyaṃ bhāgaṃ" (the second part) means he made the thoughts belonging to the entire wholesome side into the second group. By these words, the time when the Bodhisatta suppressed his thoughts is described.

For the Bodhisatta who was practicing striving (padhāna) for six years, thoughts of renunciation and so forth occurred in abundance, like the flow of water in a great river. However, when mindfulness was lost, thoughts of sensuality and so forth would suddenly arise, cutting off the wholesome sequence and remaining as a sequence of unwholesome impulsions (javana). Then the Bodhisatta thought: "These thoughts of sensuality and so forth of mine remain, having cut off the wholesome sequence; indeed, I shall dwell having divided these thoughts into two parts." Thus, he made one group of the unwholesome side, such as thoughts of sensuality, and one group of the wholesome side, such as thoughts of renunciation.

Then he thought again: "I shall suppress the thought that comes from the unwholesome side, like one squeezing and catching a cobra with a mantra, or like one treading on the neck of an enemy; I shall not allow it to grow. But the thought that comes from the wholesome side, I shall make it grow quickly, like a cloud in the rainy season, or like a fine young rice plant in a good field." Having done so, he suppressed the unwholesome thoughts and developed the wholesome thoughts. In this way, it should be understood that the time of the Bodhisatta's suppression of thoughts is described.

Now, wishing to show how those thoughts arose and how he suppressed them, he said the words beginning with "Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave." Therein, "appamattassa" means...
384:
To one dwelling without being free from mindfulness means to one dwelling without being separated from mindfulness. "Ātāpino" means to one possessing ardent energy (ātāpa-vīriya) that burns away defilements. "Pahitattassa" means to one whose mind is sent forth towards Nibbāna. "Kāma-vitakka arises" means that for the Bodhisatta who was practicing striving (dukkara-cariyā) for six years, what is called a thought of sensuality had never arisen before, whether concerning royal happiness, or palaces, or dancers, or the harem, or any kind of prosperity. However, when he reached the limit of extreme exhaustion through the cutting off of food while performing austere practices, it occurred to that Bodhisatta: "It is not possible to produce distinction by the cutting off of food; what if I were to consume solid food?"

That Bodhisatta entered the village of Uruvelā for alms. People thought: "This Great Man previously did not take even food that was brought and offered; now surely his heart's desire has reached its pinnacle, therefore he has come by himself," and they offered very excellent food. The Bodhisatta's physical body returned to its normal state before long. Indeed, an old and decayed body does not return to its normal state even after obtaining suitable food. But the Bodhisatta was young. Therefore, as he consumed suitable food, his body became normal before long; his faculties became clear, his skin-complexion was pure, and his body became adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, like the sky when the host of stars has arisen. Looking at his body, he thought: "This physical body, which was so exhausted, has thus returned to its normal state." Due to the greatness of his wisdom, he took even such a slight thought and classified it as a thought of sensuality (kāma-vitakka).

While sitting in front of his leaf-hut, he saw herds of animals such as the yak (camarī), the pasada deer, the gavaya ox, and the rohita deer; groups of birds such as peacocks and jungle fowl calling with pleasant sounds; ponds covered with blue lotuses, white water-lilies, and red lotuses; forest groves with branches covered with various flowers; and the river Nerañjarā with a flow of water as clear as a mass of jewels. To him, it occurred: "How beautiful indeed are these animals, these groups of birds, the ponds, the forest groves, and the river Nerañjarā!" He took even such a slight thought and made it a thought of sensuality; therefore he said, "Kāma-vitakka arises."

"For one's own affliction also" means for one's own suffering also. This same method applies everywhere. But is there such a thing as a thought that leads to the suffering of both for the Great Being? There is not. However, the thought of one who remains without full understanding (apariññāya) can lead to the affliction of both; therefore, it receives these three names, and thus he spoke. "Paññānirodhiko" means that which obstructs wisdom...
385:
It is called 'destroyer of wisdom' (paññānirodhika) because it does not allow the unarisen mundane and supramundane wisdom to arise, and it completely cuts off and abandons even the mundane wisdom that has arisen through the power of the eight attainments and five higher knowledges. 'Belonging to the side of distress' (vighātapakkhika) means being part of the mass of suffering. It is called 'not leading to Nibbāna' (anibbānasaṃvattanika) because it prevents one from realizing the unconditioned, known as Nibbāna. 'Goes to destruction' (abbatthaṃ gacchati) means reaching the state of ending or non-existence. It vanishes like a water bubble. 'Just abandoning' (pajaham eva) means simply giving up. 'Just dispelling' (vinodam eva) means simply removing. 'I made an end of it' (byantam eva naṃ akāsiṃ) means I have brought that thought to an end without any remainder; I have limited it.

The 'thought of ill-will' (byāpāda-vitakka) in the mind of the Bodhisatta is not a thought associated with the desire to kill or harm others. Rather, it refers to the transformation of the mind caused by excessive rain, extreme heat, or extreme cold; it is with reference to this state that it is called 'thought of ill-will.' Similarly, 'thought of cruelty' (vihiṃsā-vitakka) for the Great Being (Mahāsatta) is not a thought associated with the desire to cause suffering to others. It is the occurrence of restlessness and lack of concentration in the mind that is called 'thought of cruelty.' For instance, while sitting at the door of his leaf-hut, he sees wild beasts like lions and tigers harming smaller animals like pigs and deer. Then the Bodhisatta feels compassion, thinking, 'Even in this forest, which should be free from fear, these animals have enemies; the strong eat the weak, and the devouring by the strong continues.' He also sees others like cats eating chickens and mice. When entering a village for alms, he sees people being oppressed, bound, or killed by king's men, and feels compassion, thinking, 'They are unable to live by doing their own work like farming or trading.' It is with reference to this that it is said, 'a thought of cruelty arises.'

'In that way, in that way' (tathā tathā) means by those various manners. The meaning is this: as long as one thinks of any thought among sensual thoughts and so on, as long as one causes any thought to occur, the mind does not become the state of sensual thought etc., by that manner. 'He abandons the thought of renunciation' means he gives up the thought of renunciation. 'He made much of' means he did it repeatedly. 'For the mind of that person to become a sensual thought' means for the purpose of the mind of that person to become a sensual thought.
386:
It means the mind associated with sensual thought arises and inclines in such a way. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Now, to show a simile that clarifies the meaning, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'Just as' (seyyathāpi). In that simile, 'in a field crowded with crops' (kiṭṭhasambādhe) means in a field area full of crops and thus narrow. 'He would strike' (ākoṭeyya) means striking directly on the back. 'He would strike back' (paṭikoṭeyya) means striking sideways on the ribs. 'He would check' (sannirundheyya) means blocking or obstructing. 'He would restrain' (sannivāreya) means not allowing it to go here and there. 'Because of that' (tatonidānaṃ) means for that reason. The meaning is: because of the reason that those unprotected cows eat the crops of others. Indeed, a foolish cowherd, by not protecting the cows in this way, suffers dangers such as being beaten by the owners of the cows and the owners of the fields, who say, 'This man only eats the food and wages we give him; he cannot even protect the cows properly, and he causes us to have grudges with other families.'

A wise cowherd, however, seeing these four dangers well, protects the cows properly. This statement was made with reference to such guarding after seeing the danger. 'Danger' (ādīnavaṃ) means misfortune. 'Baseness' (okāraṃ) means lowliness or entering into the five aggregates. 'Defilement' (saṃkilesaṃ) means the state of being soiled. 'In renunciation' (nekkhamme) means in the state of renunciation. 'Benefit' (ānisaṃsaṃ) means the side of purity. 'The side of purification' (vodānapakkha) is a synonym for that benefit. It means seeing the side of purity in renunciation among wholesome states. 'Renunciation' (nekkhamma) refers to all wholesome states that have emerged from sensual pleasures. If taken as a single state, it is Nibbāna itself. The comparison with the simile is as follows: The field crowded with crops is like the five sense objects such as visible forms. The rogue cow with a bell is like the crooked mind. The wise cowherd is like the Bodhisatta. The four dangers are like the thoughts that lead to the affliction of oneself and others. Just as the wise cowherd, seeing the four dangers, protects the cows without negligence among the crops, so the Bodhisatta, while practicing his striving for six years, saw the dangers such as self-affliction and guarded his mind so that sensual thoughts and so on would not arise regarding sense objects like visible forms.

In the terms beginning with 'leading to the growth of wisdom' (paññāvuddhika), it is called 'leading to the growth of wisdom' because it leads to the arising of unarisen mundane and supramundane wisdom and to the growth of wisdom that has already arisen. It is called 'not belonging to the side of distress' (avighātapakkhika) because it does not lead to a mass of suffering. It is called 'leading to Nibbāna' (nibbānasaṃvattanika) because it leads to the realization of the element of Nibbāna. 'Even if, monks, I were to think such a thought for a whole night' (rattiṃ cepi naṃ bhikkhave anuvitakkeyyaṃ) means even if I were to cause that thought to proceed for the entire night. 'Because of that' (tatonidānaṃ) means based on that thought. 'Would be harmed' (ohanyeyya) means being affected or damaged due to restlessness...
387:
It means 'it would lead to (distraction)'. 'Ārā' means in a distant place. 'From concentration' (samādhimhā) means from both access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi).

'Monks, I (settle) the mind internally' means 'Monks, I well-place the mind internally, thinking "May my mind not be far from concentration"; I place it on the internal object.' 'I settle it' means making that mind stay well on that very object. 'I make it one-pointed' means producing one-pointedness (ekaggatā). 'I properly establish' means to place well, to fix well upon the object. 'Lest my mind be distressed' means 'May my mind not be distressed, may it not lead to distraction.'

In the passage 'The thought of non-ill will arises... the thought of non-harming arises,' the thought that arises together with the young insight (taruṇa-vipassanā) mentioned below is called 'thought of renunciation' (nekkhamma-vitakka) because it opposes sense-desire. That same thought is called 'thought of non-ill will' (abyāpāda-vitakka) because it opposes ill will, and 'thought of non-harming' (avihiṃsā-vitakka) because it opposes harming.

By this much, the time of establishing insight by relying on the Bodhisatta's meditative attainment (samāpatti) is described. Indeed, for that Bodhisatta whose concentration is young and whose insight is also young, when he sits for a long time establishing insight, his body becomes weary, heat rises within like a fire, sweat flows from his armpits, and it is as if steam rises from his head; the mind is distressed, oppressed, and agitated. That Bodhisatta, having entered meditative attainment again, tames that weariness, makes it supple, and having found relief, establishes insight once more. When he sits for a long time again, it happens in the same way. Then he enters meditative attainment again and does the same. Indeed, meditative attainment is of great benefit to insight.

For example, just as an armory (phalakakoṭṭhaka) is of great benefit to a soldier. Relying on that armory, he enters the battlefield. Having performed his duties there with elephants, horses, and soldiers, when his weapons are exhausted or when he wishes to eat and so on, he retreats and enters the armory, takes new weapons, rests, eats, drinks water, and puts on his armor again. Having done these various tasks, he enters the battlefield again. Having served in the battle again, he enters the armory again because of being pressed by the need to defecate or urinate, or for some other business. Having strengthened himself in that armory...
388:
...he enters the battlefield again. In this way, just as the armory is to the soldier, meditative attainment is of great benefit to insight.

Even more than meditative attainment, insight is of greater benefit than the soldier's armory for overcoming the battlefield. For although one establishes insight relying on meditative attainment, insight that has gained strength also protects meditative attainment. It makes it strong.

For example, on land, people make a boat and the goods carried by the boat into a cartload. But upon reaching water, they make the cart, the cart's goods, and the yoked oxen into a boatload. Just as the boat cuts across the current and reaches a safe harbor without danger, in the same way, although one establishes insight relying on meditative attainment, insight that has gained strength also protects meditative attainment and makes it strong. Meditative attainment is like the cart upon reaching land. Insight is like the boat upon reaching water. Thus, it should be understood that by this much, the time of establishing insight by relying on the Bodhisatta's meditative attainment is described.

The passage beginning with 'yannadeva' should be understood according to the method stated in the dark side (kaṇhapakkha). Here too, to show an illustrative analogy, He said the passage beginning with 'seyyathāpi'. In that passage, 'gāmantasambhatesu' means among the cattle brought near the village. 'Only mindfulness is to be exercised' means it is only necessary to produce the mindfulness that 'these are cows.' There is no longer the task of going here and there and striking them. 'These states' (ete dhammā) means in these states of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), it is only necessary to produce mindfulness. By this, the time when the Bodhisatta's serenity and insight have gained strength is described. At that time, it is said that while he sits to reach absorption (appanā) in meditative attainment, the eight attainments appear to his mind with a single reflection; when he sits having established insight, the seven contemplations (anupassanā) are ascended all at once.

What is shown here by the word 'seyyathāpi'? This is a separate sequence (anusandhi). The Blessed One began this teaching desiring to show His practice for the welfare of beings and the perfection of His state as a Teacher. In that passage, 'araññe' means in the great forest. 'Pavane' means in a woodland grove. In meaning, these two are the same; the second is a synonym (vevacana) for the first. 'Ayogakkhemakāmo' means one who does not desire the security from the four yokes (Nibbāna) but desires only danger...
389:
One who desires. 'Sovatthiko' means that which brings safety and well-being. 'Pītigamanīyo' means that which leads to joy. Alternatively, there is a variant reading 'Pītagamanīyo'. 'Pidahayya' means one should obstruct or close off with branches and such. 'Vivareyya' means one should make a clear opening and leave it open. 'Kummagga' refers to a wrong path, one that is not a true path, being obstructed by water, forests, mountains, and so forth. 'Should place an okacara' means one should place a decoy deer in a certain spot, as if it were grazing in the area where those deer frequent. 'Okacārika' refers to a female deer bound by a long rope.

Indeed, a deer hunter goes to the forest where the deer dwell and observes, 'They live here, they exit by this path, they graze here, they drink water here, and they re-enter by this path.' Having noted this, he closes the right path, opens a wrong path, places the decoy deer and the female decoy, and then waits, holding a spear, in a concealed place. Then, in the evening, the deer, having grazed in the forest where they feel safe and having drunk water, come near their dwelling place while frolicking with their fawns. When they see the decoy deer and the female decoy, they enter without suspicion, thinking, 'Our companions have arrived.' When they see the right path closed, they think, 'This is not the path; this must be the path,' and they enter the wrong path. The deer hunter does not do anything immediately; only after the deer have entered does he slowly strike the very last deer. That deer becomes terrified, and consequently, all the deer become terrified. Thinking, 'Danger has arisen,' they look ahead and see the path obstructed by water, forest, or mountains. Being unable to enter the thick forest on either side, which is like interlaced fingers, they attempt to exit by the same path they entered. When the hunter realizes they are turning back, he slaughters thirty or forty deer, starting from the first. With reference to this, it was said: 'In this way, bhikkhus, that great herd of deer would fall into ruin and disaster at a later time.'

In the phrase, 'This is a designation for delight and lust (nandīrāga), this is a designation for ignorance (avijjā),' it is because these beings, being devoid of knowledge through ignorance and bound by delight and lust, are led toward sense objects such as forms and are slaughtered by the spear of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). Therefore, the Blessed One showed the decoy deer (okacara) as delight and lust, and the female decoy (okacārika) as ignorance.

Sometimes, the deer hunter rubs his body with branches to remove the human scent, places the decoy deer in one spot, releases the female decoy along with the rope, and stands near the decoy deer holding a spear while concealing himself. The female decoy heads toward the place where the herd of deer grazes...
390:
(The female decoy) goes. Seeing her, the deer stand with their heads raised. She also stands with her head raised. Those deer, thinking, 'She is of the same species as us,' begin to graze. She also approaches slowly as if eating grass. The leader of the forest herd, catching her scent, abandons his own mate and heads toward her. For beings, that which is new is always dear.

The female decoy, without giving the forest deer a chance to get too close, retreats while facing him and goes toward the male decoy. Wherever her rope gets snagged, she strikes it with her hoof to free it. The forest deer, seeing the male decoy and being intoxicated with lust for the female decoy, feels jealousy toward the male decoy and stands there shaking his head with his back hunched. At that moment, even if he licks the spear with his tongue, he does not realize, 'What is this?' The male decoy also hunches his back if it is easy to strike the forest deer from the upper part. If it is easy to strike from the lower part, he raises his chest. Then the hunter strikes the forest deer with the spear, kills him right there, and leaves taking the meat. 

Just as that deer, being intoxicated with lust for the female decoy and feeling jealousy toward the male decoy, knows nothing even while licking the spear with his tongue; similarly, these beings, intoxicated by ignorance and becoming blind, knowing nothing of the nature of things, approach delight and lust (nandīrāga) for forms and so forth, and are slaughtered by the spear of the suffering of the round of rebirths. Thus, the Blessed One showed the male decoy as delight and lust, and the female decoy as ignorance.

In the statement, 'Thus, bhikkhus, the safe path has been opened by me,' it means: 'Bhikkhus, by practicing for the welfare of these beings, after attaining Supreme Enlightenment, I did not remain seated in silence thinking "I am the Buddha," but rather, starting from the Setting in Motion of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana), by teaching the Dhamma, I have opened the safe Noble Eightfold Path. I have closed the wrong path. I have split in two and cast down delight and lust, which is like the male decoy that disturbs the minds of capable persons (babbapuggala) such as Aññātakoṇḍañña. I have destroyed ignorance, which is like the female decoy, eradicating it entirely.' Thus, he showed his own service for their welfare. All the remaining words are clear in meaning.

## The explanation of the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
391:
## 10. Commentary on the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta

This sutta, beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', is the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta. In that sutta, 'adhicittamanuyuttena' means: the mind that arises by virtue of the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) is merely mind; however, the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti), which serve as the basis for insight (vipassanā), are superior to that mind, and are thus called 'adhicitta' (higher mind). 'Anuyuttena' refers to one who practices this higher mind repeatedly and persistently, or one who exerts successive efforts in that higher mind.

In this context, when a monk, having wandered for alms in the forenoon and returned from his alms-round after his meal, takes his sitting mat and sets out thinking, 'I will perform the recluse's duties at the root of such-and-such a tree, or in a forest grove, or at the foot of a mountain, or in a mountain cleft'; even while he is removing grass and leaves from his sitting place with his hands or feet upon arrival, he is still one 'devoted to the higher mind'. After sitting down, washing his hands and feet, sitting cross-legged, and dwelling while taking up his primary meditation subject (mūlakammaṭṭhāna), he is likewise one 'devoted to the higher mind'.

'Nimittāni' refers to causes or signs. 'Kālena kālaṃ' means from time to time, or at all times. Indeed, should not a meditation subject be attended to continuously without abandoning it even for a moment? Why, then, did the Blessed One say 'from time to time'? In the Pali texts, thirty-eight meditation subjects are classified and explained. Among them, as long as no defilement arises while a monk sits having taken up a meditation subject of his choice, there is no need for the task of attending to these signs (nimitta). However, when defilements do arise, one should take up these signs to remove the 'growth' (defilement) that has arisen in the mind; it is to show this that the Blessed One spoke thus.

'Chandūpasaṃhitā' means those (thoughts) accompanied by desire or associated with lust. The field (khetta) and the object (ārammaṇa) of these three types of thought (vitakka) should be understood. Among them, the field for thoughts associated with desire is the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed (lobhasahagata); for thoughts associated with hatred, it is the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure (domanassasahagata); and for thoughts associated with delusion, it is all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. The two consciousnesses associated with doubt and restlessness, however, are the specific field for those thoughts of delusion. The objects of all these thoughts are both beings (satta) and formations (saṅkhāra); for they arise regarding beings and formations that are pleasant (iṭṭha), unpleasant (aniṭṭha), or neutrally regarded (asamapekkhita).

'Aññampi nimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ' means that another sign (nimitta) connected with the wholesome, other than that (unwholesome) sign, should be attended to. In this context, 'another sign' means: when thoughts associated with desire arise regarding beings, the meditation on foulness (asubhabhāvanā) is called 'another sign'. When they arise regarding formations, the reflection on impermanence (anicca) is 'another sign'...
392:
is called 'another sign'. When thoughts associated with hatred arise regarding beings, the meditation on loving-kindness (mettābhāvanā) is 'another sign'. When they arise regarding formations, the attention to elements (dhātumanasikāra) is 'another sign'. When thoughts associated with delusion arise regarding anything whatsoever, resorting to the five things is 'another sign'.

When greed arises regarding beings in such ways as, 'This person's hands are beautiful, the feet are beautiful,' and so on, one should reflect by way of foulness (asubha). 'In what are you enamored? Are you enamored in the hair of the head? In the hair of the body? ... In the urine?' This so-called 'individual form' (attabhāva) is erected by three hundred bones, bound by nine hundred tendons, smeared with nine hundred pieces of flesh, wrapped in moist skin, covered by the complexion of the skin, and from nine orifices and ninety-nine thousand pores, impure filth flows out; it is full of corpses, foul-smelling, disgusting, loathsome, and merely a collection of thirty-two impurities. There is no essence or excellence in this body. For one who reflects by way of foulness in this manner, the greed that has arisen regarding beings is abandoned. Thus, his reflection by way of foulness is called 'another sign'.

When greed arises regarding formations such as alms-bowls and robes, it is abandoned for one who attends to them by way of being ownerless (assāmika) and temporary (tāvakālika), according to the method stated in the commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, thereby establishing equanimity towards formations. For him, the reflection by way of impermanence (anicca) is called 'another sign'. When hatred arises regarding beings, loving-kindness (mettā) should be developed by virtue of the removal of resentment (āghātavinaya) and the Simile of the Saw (kacopamovāda), etc. For one who develops it, hatred is abandoned. For him, the meditation on loving-kindness is called 'another sign'. When hatred arises regarding stumps, thorns, grass, leaves, and so on, for one who performs attention to elements (dhātumanasikāra) in such ways as, 'At whom are you angry? Is it at the earth element? Or at the water element? Or who is this that is called angry? Is it the earth element? Or the water element?', hatred is abandoned. For him, the attention to elements is called 'another sign'.

When delusion arises regarding anything whatsoever:

'Living with teachers, learning, 
Inquiring into what was learned, 
Listening to the Dhamma at the right time, 
And discerning what is a ground and what is not— 
By resorting to these five things, the element of delusion is abandoned.'
393:
These five things should be relied upon. Indeed, a monk living in dependence on a teacher, (reflecting) thus: "The teacher imposes a penalty, such as fetching a hundred jars of water, upon one who enters the village without asking permission, or one who does not perform the duties at the time they should be performed," becomes one who is diligent and careful; then, delusion (moha) is abandoned in him. Also, one who is learning the Pali texts, (reflecting) thus: "The teacher imposes a penalty upon one who does not learn at the time of learning, or one who recites disrespectfully," becomes one who is diligent and careful; in this way too, delusion is abandoned in him. One who approaches respected monks and asks, "Venerable Sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?" dispels doubt; in this way too, delusion is abandoned in him. For one who goes to the place of hearing the Dhamma at the proper time and listens respectfully, the meaning becomes clear in various places; in this way too, delusion is abandoned in him. He becomes skilled in discerning what is a cause and what is not a cause, thinking, "This is the cause of this benefit, this is not the cause"; in this way too, delusion is abandoned in him. Because of such abandoning, the reliance on these five things is called another sign (nimitta).

Furthermore, for one who develops any of the thirty-eight meditation objects, these unwholesome thoughts are indeed abandoned. However, these signs (nimittas) are direct opposites and act as adversaries. Lust (rāga) and other defilements abandoned by these signs are well-abandoned. For example, one can indeed extinguish a fire by beating it with wet wood, dust, or branches; however, water is the direct opposite of fire, and a fire extinguished by that water is well-extinguished. Similarly, lust and other defilements abandoned by these signs are well-abandoned. Therefore, it should be understood that these signs were taught.

'Kusalūpasaṃhita' means associated with the wholesome, or being a cause for the wholesome. 'Ajjhattameva' means only within one's own internal objective field. 'Palagaṇḍa' means a carpenter. 'Sukhumāya āṇiyā' means with a fine wooden peg made of heartwood, which is finer than the peg one wishes to remove. 'Oḷārikaṃ āṇiṃ' means an uneven peg driven into a sandalwood board or a board made of heartwood. 'Abhinihaneyya' means one should drive it in by striking it with a mallet. 'Abhinīhareyya' means one should remove it from the board by thus driving it in. 'Abhiniwasseyya' means knowing that many have now come out, shaking it with the hand...
394:
...and should remove it. In that analogy, the mind is like the board; the unwholesome thoughts are like the uneven peg in the board; the other wholesome signs, such as the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā), are like the fine peg; and the removal of those thoughts by wholesome signs like the meditation on foulness should be understood as the removal of the coarse peg by the fine peg.

The phrase beginning with 'ahikuṇapena' is spoken to show a carcass that is extremely loathsome and repulsive. 'Kaṇṭhe āsattena' means (a carcass) brought by some enemy and tied or fastened around the neck. 'Aṭṭiyeyya' means one would be oppressed and distressed. 'Harāyeyya' means one would be ashamed. 'Jiguccheyya' means one would feel disgust.

'Pahīyanti' means that for this reason also, for one who investigates with the power of one's own wisdom that these unwholesome states are blameworthy and have painful results, and who is disgusted by them as if they were a snake carcass and so on, these unwholesome states are abandoned. If, however, one is unable to investigate with the power of one's own wisdom, one should approach a teacher, a preceptor, another respected fellow practitioner, or an Elder of the Saṅgha, and after striking the gong to assemble the Saṅgha of monks, one should inform them. In a large assembly, there will certainly be at least one wise person; he will say, "The danger in these thoughts should be seen in this way," or he will suppress those thoughts with discourses such as the 'Discourse on the Cutting up of the Body' (Kāyavicchindanīya-kathā).

'Asati-amanasikāro āpajjitabbo' means that thought should not be remembered, nor should it be attended to; one should be occupied with something else. Just as a man who does not wish to see a visual object would close his eyes, even so, a monk who is sitting and firmly grasping his original meditation subject should, if a thought arises in the mind, be occupied with something else. If he does this, that thought will be abandoned; when it is abandoned, he should sit again grasping the meditation subject.

If it is still not abandoned, if there is a sequence of Dhamma discourses that has been learned, he should recite it loudly. If, even while being occupied with something else in this way, it is not abandoned, and if there is a book in his bag in which the qualities of the Buddha and the Dhamma are written, he should take it out and read it, being occupied with something else. If, even after doing this, it is not abandoned, he should take out the fire-drill and fire-making materials from his bag and...
395:
Reflecting, "This is the upper fire-stick, this is the lower fire-stick," one should be one whose mind is inclined toward another object. Even if one does so, if the unwholesome thought is not yet abandoned, one should take out the case of writing materials and, reflecting on the requisites, "This is called a long-pointed stylus, this is called a slate, this is called a nail-cutter, this is called a needle," one should be one whose mind is inclined toward another object. Even if one does so, if it is not yet abandoned, one should take the needle and sew the worn-out parts of the robe, thus being one whose mind is inclined toward another object. In this way, as long as it is not abandoned, one should be one whose mind is inclined toward another object by performing various wholesome deeds. When the thought is abandoned, one should sit down and take up the original meditation subject (mūlakammaṭṭhāna) again; however, one should not start a new work (navakamma). Why? Because when thoughts are cut off, there is an opportunity for the attention to be directed toward the meditation subject.

Wise ones of the past, however, cut off thoughts even while performing new work. In this regard, there is this story—it is said that the preceptor of Tissa Sāmaṇera lived in the Tissa Mahāvihāra. Tissa Sāmaṇera said, "Venerable Sir, I am dissatisfied (with the holy life)." Then the Elder said to him, "Bathing water is difficult to find in this monastery; take me and let us go to Cittalapabbata." He did as he was told. There, the Elder said, "This monastery belongs entirely to the Saṅgha; make a private place for a single person." The novice replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and from the beginning, he simultaneously undertook three tasks: reciting the Saṃyutta Nikāya, cleaning the cave, and practicing the preliminary work for the fire-kasina (tejo-kasiṇa). He brought the meditation subject to absorption (appanā), completed the recitation of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, and finished the work on the cave. Having done everything, he gave a signal to his preceptor. The preceptor said, "Novice, you have worked with great hardship; for today, you yourself stay there." That night, while staying in the cave, having obtained suitable weather (utu-sappāya), he developed insight (vipassanā), attained Arahantship, and attained parinibbāna right there. Taking his relics, they built a stupa. Even today, it is known as the Tissa Thera Cetiya. This section is called the Section on Non-attention (Asati-pabba).

Wishing to show the section on cutting the root of thoughts, thinking that one who is unable to suppress thoughts by staying in this (Asati-pabba) will suppress them by staying in this (Vitakkamūlabheda-pabba), the Buddha said, "Puna tassa ce bhikkhave," and so on. In that Pali, regarding the phrase "the form of thought-formations (vitakka-saṅkhāra-saṇṭhāna) should be attended to"—it is called 'saṅkhāra' because it conditions; it means the cause, the condition, the root. It is called 'saṇṭhāna' because it stays there; the place where thought-formations stay is the 'vitakka-saṅkhāra-saṇṭhāna.' That should be attended to. What is meant is this: one should attend to the root and the root-of-the-root of thoughts, asking, "Due to what cause, due to what condition, due to what reason has this thought arisen?" How? "Am I..."
396:
"For what reason am I walking fast? What benefit is there for me in walking fast like this? It would be better if I walked slowly; I will walk slowly," he thinks. "That person should walk slowly" means that the person, having thought thus, walks slowly. This method should be understood in the same way for all terms.

In that analogy, the time of that man walking fast is like the time when this monk is mounted by thought (when thought occurs). The time of his walking slowly is like the time when this monk cuts the range of thought. The time of his standing is like the time when this monk, having cut the range of thought, enters the original meditation subject. The time of his sitting is like the time when this monk, having developed insight, attains the Fruition of Arahantship. The time of his lying down is like the time when this monk spends the day in the Attainment of Fruition (phalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object. In such reflection, for one who searches for the successive roots of thoughts, asking, "What is the cause of these thoughts? Due to what condition do they arise?", the range of thoughts becomes weakened. When they have become weakened and reach the end, the thoughts cease entirely. This meaning should also be illustrated by the Duddubha Jātaka—

It is said that while a young hare was sleeping at the foot of a bael tree (beluva), a bael fruit broke from its stalk and fell near its ear. Due to that sound, the hare thought, "The earth is breaking!" and getting up, fled with great speed. Seeing the hare fleeing, other four-footed animals in front also fled. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a lion. He thought, "This earth only breaks at the time of the destruction of the world-cycle; there is no such thing as the earth breaking in the interval. It would be well if I go to the root-of-the-root and investigate." That lion, starting from the noble elephant down to the hare, asked, "Friend, did you see the earth breaking?" The hare said, "Yes, Lord." The lion said, "Friend, come and show me." The hare said, "Lord, I do not dare." "Friend, come, do not be afraid," the lion said, and coaxing him, took him along. The hare, standing not far from the tree, spoke this verse:

"Venerable Sir, the sound 'Duddubha' occurred in the place where I live;
'Aham petaṃ na jānāmi, kimetaṃ duddubhāyatīti'—I myself do not know why this 'Duddubha' sound occurred."

The Bodhisatta said, "You stay right here," and going to the foot of the tree, he saw the place where the hare had slept, he saw the bael fruit, and looking up, he saw the stalk. Having seen this, he thought, "This hare was sleeping here, and while he was sleeping, this bael fruit's..."
397:
Having heard a sound falling near his ear, he ran away with the perception that 'the earth is breaking.' Knowing this, [the Bodhisatta] questioned the hare about the cause. The hare replied, "Yes, Great King."

The Bodhisatta spoke this verse:

"Hearing the falling of the bael fruit, the hare ran, thinking 'duddubha' (the sound of the earth breaking). Hearing the hare's words, the frightened herd of animals ran."

Then the Bodhisatta comforted the herd of animals, saying, "Do not be afraid." In this way, for one who follows thoughts to their very root, the thoughts are abandoned.

To show that a monk who, while remaining in this section of analyzing the root of thoughts, is unable to suppress thoughts, should suppress them in this way, He spoke again, beginning with: "If, bhikkhus, to that monk..."

"Clenching the teeth with the teeth" means placing the upper teeth upon the lower teeth. "Mind with the mind" means the unwholesome mind should be specially suppressed by the wholesome mind. "Just as a strong man" means just as a strong man, full of strength and great power, might seize a weak man by the head, neck, or shoulders and suppress him, squeeze him, and cause him great heat, making him like one who is exhausted, weary, and fainting; even so, a monk should become a wrestler against thoughts, and by overcoming them with the thought, "Who are you? Who am I?", he should suppress thoughts by exerting great energy (mahāvīriya), thinking: "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain in the body; let the flesh and blood dry up." To show this, He brought forth this simile which illustrates the meaning.

"Bhikkhus, when..."—this passage is called the section on total eradication (pariyādānabhājanīya); its meaning is clear. For example, a teacher trains a prince who has come from another country in the art of the five weapons and sends him off, saying, "Go, take the kingship in your own country. If robbers rise up against you on the way, proceed by using the bow. If your bow is lost or broken, use the spear, the sword..." In this way, showing the actions to be done with the five weapons, he sends him off. The prince does as instructed, goes to his country, takes the kingship, and enjoys royal prosperity. In the same way, when the Blessed One sends off a monk devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta) to attain Arahantship, [He intends that] "If unwholesome thoughts arise in him in the meantime, he should stay in the section on other signs (aññanimittapabba), suppress those thoughts, and develop insight..."
398:
That monk will attain the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). In attaining this, if he is unable while established in the section on other signs (aññanimittapabba), then [he tries] while established in the section on drawbacks (ādīnavapabba); if unable there, while established in the section on non-attention (asatipabba); if unable there, while established in the section on the removal of the root of thoughts (vitakkamūlabhedapabba); and if unable there, while established in the section on forceful suppression (abhiniggaṇhanapabba), he suppresses the thoughts, develops insight (vipassanā), and will attain the fruit of Arahantship—thus He taught these five sections (pabba). (This is like a master archer teaching a prince the five weapons and sending him forth.)

"Mastery in the paths of the ways of thought" (vasī vitakkapariyāyapathesu) refers to one who has mastery, being practiced and proficient in the paths where thoughts range. The phrase "Whatever thought he desires" is spoken to show the manner in which that monk has attained mastery. Previously, this monk could not think the thoughts he wished to think, and would think the thoughts he did not wish to think. But now, having attained mastery, if he wishes to think a certain thought, he thinks only that thought. If he does not wish to think a certain thought, he does not think it. Therefore, He said: "Whatever thought he desires, that thought he will think. Whatever thought he does not desire, that thought he will not think."

All the phrases beginning with "He has cut off craving" (acchecchi taṇhaṃ) are just as taught in the Sabbāsava Sutta.

## In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta is finished.
## The Explanation of the Second Division (Vagga) is finished.
## The first part of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Commentary is finished.
